title: Accounting Basics and Double Entry
lines: USAT-COM asks about ten Accounting questions at ICom Principles of Accounting level. In this topic expect two kinds: naming the concept behind a practice, and short transactions where you pick the account to debit or the effect on the accounting equation. Every question is solvable by hand in about a minute.
## Concepts and conventions
Accounting rests on a few basic assumptions. Learn each with one example, because questions describe a practice and ask which concept it follows.
| Concept | What it says | Typical example
| Business entity | The business is separate from its owner | The owner's private house is not a business asset
| Going concern | The business will continue for the foreseeable future | Fixed assets shown at cost less depreciation, not at break-up value
| Money measurement | Only items measurable in money are recorded | Staff loyalty is not recorded
| Historical cost | Assets are recorded at what they cost | Land bought for Rs 2,000,000 stays at that figure
| Dual aspect | Every transaction has two equal effects | The basis of double entry
| Realisation | Revenue is recorded when goods are delivered | A sale is not recorded when the order arrives
| Matching (accruals) | Expenses are matched with the revenue of the same period | Unpaid December wages charged in December's year
| Accounting period | Life of the business is split into periods, usually a year | Annual income statement
| Consistency | The same methods are used year after year | No switching of depreciation methods
| Prudence | Provide for all likely losses; do not anticipate gains | Stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value
| Materiality | Trivial items need not be treated strictly | A Rs 400 stapler written off at once
| Objectivity | Records rest on verifiable evidence | Entries supported by invoices and receipts
! Prudence and matching are the two most often confused. Prudence is about caution with gains and losses; matching is about putting an expense in the right year.
## The accounting equation
Everything the business owns was financed either by the owner or by outsiders:
- Assets = Capital + Liabilities
- Capital = Assets − Liabilities
- Closing capital = Opening capital + Net profit + Additional capital − Drawings

Every transaction keeps the equation in balance. Only four patterns are possible: an asset rises and another falls (totals unchanged); assets and liabilities rise or fall together; assets and capital rise or fall together; or one claim replaces another.
> Bilal starts a business with Rs 400,000 cash, buys furniture on credit for Rs 60,000 and withdraws Rs 15,000 for personal use.
> Cash 385,000 + Furniture 60,000 = Assets Rs 445,000
> Check: 385,000 + 60,000 = 445,000. The equation balances.
## Debit and credit rules
A debit is an entry on the left side of an account and a credit on the right. Which side increases an account depends on its type. The modern rule, remembered as DEAD CLIC, is:
| Increase with a debit | Increase with a credit
| Drawings | Liabilities
| Expenses (and losses) | Income (and gains)
| Assets | Capital
A decrease is always entered on the opposite side. So an asset falls with a credit, and a liability falls with a debit.
Many Pakistani textbooks also teach the traditional (golden) rules, which give the same answers:
- Personal accounts (people, firms, banks): debit the receiver, credit the giver.
- Real accounts (assets such as cash, furniture, goodwill): debit what comes in, credit what goes out.
- Nominal accounts (expenses, losses, incomes, gains): debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.
> Goods are sold on credit to Kamran for Rs 20,000.
> Kamran receives the goods: personal account, debit Kamran.
> Sales is an income: nominal account, credit Sales.
> Entry: Kamran Dr 20,000; Sales Cr 20,000.
## Owner's transactions
Because of the entity concept, anything the owner takes out is drawings, and anything he puts in is capital.
- Cash or goods taken for personal use: Drawings Dr, Cash or Purchases Cr. Goods are credited to Purchases at cost, not to Sales.
- Private bills paid from the business: Drawings Dr, Bank Cr, never an expense.
- Owner brings in an asset or pays a business debt privately: the asset or creditor Dr, Capital Cr.
> Ayesha's capital at the start was Rs 250,000. Profit Rs 60,000, drawings Rs 24,000, new capital Rs 30,000.
## Source documents
Every entry starts from a document that proves the transaction happened.
| Document | Issued by | Records
| Invoice | Seller | A credit sale (a purchase for the buyer)
| Cash memo | Seller | A cash sale
| Debit note | Buyer | Goods returned to the seller
| Credit note | Seller | Reduction of what the buyer owes
| Receipt | Person receiving money | Cash received
| Cheque counterfoil | Payer | A payment by cheque
| Pay-in slip | Depositor | Money paid into the bank

! A credit note issued to a customer reduces what he owes, so his account is credited. Do not let the word 'credit' in the document's name mislead you on the buyer's side: the buyer debits the seller.
! Drawings are a debit balance, but they are not an expense. They never appear in the profit and loss account.
## Quick check
- Can you name the concept behind writing off a Rs 400 stapler at once? (Materiality)
- Which side increases capital, and which side increases drawings?
- What is the effect on the equation of paying a creditor by cheque?
- Which document does a buyer send with returned goods?

title: Final Accounts and Adjustments
lines: Final accounts questions on USAT ask you to find cost of goods sold, gross or net profit from a few figures, classify an item as capital or revenue, say where an item appears, or correct a draft profit for one or two adjustments. Keep a clear picture of which statement each item belongs to.
## The income statement
For a sole trader, the income statement has two parts. The trading account finds gross profit; the profit and loss account finds net profit.
- Net sales = Sales − Returns inwards
- Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases − Returns outwards + Carriage inwards − Closing stock
- Gross profit = Net sales − Cost of goods sold
- Net profit = Gross profit + Other incomes − Expenses
> Opening stock Rs 40,000, purchases Rs 260,000, carriage inwards Rs 6,000, returns outwards Rs 10,000, closing stock Rs 55,000.

Items in the profit and loss account include salaries, rent, carriage outwards, depreciation, bad debts and discount allowed (debits), and discount received, commission received and rent received (credits).
! Carriage inwards goes in the trading account as part of the cost of goods; carriage outwards is a selling expense in profit and loss. This pair is tested again and again.
## Mark-up and margin
Gross profit can be expressed on cost (mark-up) or on sales (margin). If goods are sold at cost plus 25 %, then sales are 125 % of cost and gross profit is 25/125 = 20 % of sales.
> Sales Rs 300,000 at cost plus 25 %. Cost = 300,000 × 100/125 = 240,000. Gross profit = Rs 60,000.
## The balance sheet

The balance sheet shows the position on one date. It lists non-current assets (land, buildings, machinery, vehicles, furniture, goodwill), current assets (stock, debtors, prepaid expenses, accrued income, bank, cash), capital, non-current liabilities (long-term loans) and current liabilities (creditors, outstanding expenses, income received in advance, bank overdraft).
- Closing capital = Opening capital + Net profit − Drawings
- Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities
## Capital and revenue

Capital expenditure buys or improves a fixed asset that benefits more than one year: buying a van, extending a building, and the carriage, installation and legal costs needed to bring an asset into use. Revenue expenditure maintains the business from day to day: repairs, repainting, fuel, wages, rent. Capital receipts come from non-recurring sources (sale of a fixed asset, loans, new capital); revenue receipts come from normal trading (sales, commission, interest).
! Wages paid for installing a new machine are capital expenditure, added to the machine's cost. Ordinary wages are revenue. Treating capital expenditure as revenue understates both profit and assets.
## Adjustments

The trial balance shows what has been recorded. Adjustments bring each year's income and expense into line with the matching concept. Each adjustment has two effects: one in the income statement and one in the balance sheet.
| Adjustment | Income statement | Balance sheet
| Outstanding expense | Add to the expense | Current liability
| Prepaid expense | Deduct from the expense | Current asset
| Accrued income | Add to the income | Current asset
| Income received in advance | Deduct from the income | Current liability
| Depreciation | Expense in profit and loss | Deduct from the asset
| Further bad debts | Expense in profit and loss | Deduct from debtors
| Provision for doubtful debts | Charge the increase (or credit a decrease) | Deduct from debtors
| Closing stock | Credit of trading account | Current asset
| Goods taken by owner | Deduct from purchases | Add to drawings
> Insurance of Rs 36,000 is paid on 1 April for one year; the year ends on 31 December.
> April to December = 9 months: expense = 36,000 × 9/12 = Rs 27,000
> Prepaid (January to March) = Rs 9,000, a current asset
## Bad and doubtful debts
Bad debts are written off first; the provision for doubtful debts is then worked on the debtors that remain. Only the change in the provision affects this year's profit.
> Debtors Rs 200,000; write off Rs 5,000; provision 5 %.
> Remaining debtors 195,000; provision = 9,750
> Balance sheet: debtors 195,000 − 9,750 = Rs 185,250
! If the old provision was Rs 6,000 and the new one must be Rs 8,500, charge only Rs 2,500. A fall in the provision is a gain credited to profit and loss.
## Depreciation

Straight-line depreciation = (Cost − Residual value) ÷ Useful life, the same each year. Reducing balance applies a fixed percentage to the book value, so the charge falls each year. When an asset is bought during the year and the question says depreciation is for the time held, charge only the months owned.
## Correcting a draft profit
Work through each item and ask: does it raise or lower profit?
> Draft profit Rs 120,000; rent outstanding Rs 6,000; insurance prepaid Rs 2,000; depreciation of Rs 10,000 not charged.
An overstated closing stock raises this year's profit and, as next year's opening stock, lowers next year's profit by the same amount.
## Quick check
- Where do carriage inwards and carriage outwards go?
- How is income received in advance shown in the balance sheet?
- Why is only the increase in the provision charged?
- Is installation of a new machine capital or revenue expenditure?

title: Journal, Ledger and Trial Balance
lines: USAT questions on this topic give a short transaction and ask for the journal entry, ask which subsidiary book records it, or give a few ledger figures and ask for a balance. Some show a small trial balance in a table with one figure missing.
## The journal

The journal is a book of original (prime) entry: each transaction is first recorded here, in date order, from its source document. Each entry shows the date, the account debited, the account credited, the ledger folio (L.F.) and a short narration such as 'Being goods sold to Ali on credit'.
- A simple entry has one debit and one credit.
- A compound entry has more than one debit or credit, but total debits always equal total credits.
- An opening entry brings last year's assets, liabilities and capital into the new books: debit the assets, credit the liabilities and capital.
> Goods of Rs 60,000 are bought from Tariq; Rs 20,000 is paid at once by cheque.
> Purchases Dr 60,000
>     To Bank 20,000
>     To Tariq 40,000
> (Being goods bought, part paid by cheque)
## Discounts

Trade discount is a reduction from the list price given to traders. It is deducted on the invoice and never recorded in any account. Cash discount is given for prompt payment and is recorded: Discount Allowed (a loss, debit) by the seller, Discount Received (a gain, credit) by the buyer.
> List price Rs 80,000, trade discount 20 %, cash discount 5 % for immediate payment.
> After trade discount: 80,000 × 80 % = 64,000
> Cash discount: 5 % of 64,000 = 3,200
> Cash received: 64,000 − 3,200 = Rs 60,800
! Apply the two discounts one after the other, not added together. 25 % of 80,000 gives a wrong Rs 60,000.
## Subsidiary books
Busy businesses split the journal into special books for repeated transactions.
| Book | Records | Source document
| Purchases book | Credit purchases of goods for resale | Invoices received
| Sales book | Credit sales of goods | Copies of invoices issued
| Purchases returns book | Goods returned to suppliers | Debit notes
| Sales returns book | Goods returned by customers | Credit notes issued
| Cash book | All cash and bank receipts and payments | Receipts, counterfoils, pay-in slips
| Journal proper | Everything else: opening, closing, adjusting and correcting entries, credit purchase or sale of fixed assets | Vouchers

Posting: each personal account is posted individually, and the book's periodic total goes to the nominal account. From the sales book, each customer is debited and the total is credited to Sales. From the purchases book, each supplier is credited and the total is debited to Purchases.
! A computer bought on credit by a cloth shop goes in the journal proper, not the purchases book, which holds only goods for resale.
## The ledger

The ledger holds one account for each asset, liability, capital, income and expense. Posting moves each journal line to its account. On the debit side write 'To' and the name of the other account; on the credit side write 'By'.
To balance an account, total both sides, write the difference on the smaller side as 'Balance c/d', and bring it down on the larger side as 'Balance b/d'. The balance is named after the larger side.
> Ali (supplier): purchases from him Rs 40,000 and Rs 25,000 (credits); payment Rs 30,000 and returns Rs 3,000 (debits).
> Credits 65,000 − debits 33,000 = Rs 32,000 credit balance: the business still owes Ali.
Nominal accounts (purchases, sales, expenses) are closed to the trading or profit and loss account at the year end; real and personal accounts are carried down to the next year.
## The cash book

The cash book is both a book of original entry and the cash and bank accounts themselves. A single column cash book has a cash column; a double column cash book has cash and bank columns; a triple column cash book adds a discount column.
- A contra entry is one with both sides in the cash book, such as cash paid into the bank (debit bank, credit cash). It is marked 'C' and not posted to the ledger.
- The cash column can never have a credit balance. The bank column can: that is an overdraft.
- The discount columns are memorandum columns. The debit side total is posted to Discount Allowed (debit), the credit side total to Discount Received (credit).
- Petty cash is often kept on the imprest system: at the end of each period the petty cashier is given exactly what was spent, restoring the float.
## The trial balance

A trial balance lists every ledger balance on a date, debits in one column and credits in the other. If the totals agree, the double entry is arithmetically correct. Debit balances: assets, expenses, drawings, purchases, returns inwards, discount allowed. Credit balances: capital, liabilities, sales, returns outwards, discount received, a bank overdraft.
> A trial balance has debits of Rs 325,000 and credits, other than capital, of Rs 248,000.

Agreement does not prove the books are free of errors. Errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry and compensating errors all leave the totals equal. Closing stock is normally given as a note, not in the trial balance, because it is not yet in the ledger.
! A posting to one side only, a wrong amount on one side, or a casting error does make the trial balance disagree. Work out the difference by asking which side was affected and by how much.
## Quick check
- Which book records goods returned by customers, and from which document?
- How is the total of the purchases returns book posted?
- What does a credit balance in the bank column mean?
- Name two errors the trial balance cannot reveal.

title: Bank Reconciliation, Errors and Partnership
lines: This topic mixes several ICom chapters. USAT questions are short: find a bank statement or cash book balance, name an error or pick the correcting entry, work out depreciation or a book value, share partnership profit, or find the due date or proceeds of a bill of exchange.
## Bank reconciliation
The cash book (bank column) and the bank statement rarely agree on the same date. Reasons fall into two groups.
- Timing differences: cheques issued but not yet presented; cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank.
- Items known only to the bank: bank charges, interest, direct credits from customers, dividends collected, dishonoured cheques. These are first entered in the cash book to update it.

Starting from an updated cash book debit balance: add unpresented cheques and deduct uncleared deposits to reach the bank statement balance. Working from the bank statement back to the cash book, do the reverse.
> Cash book debit balance Rs 48,000; unpresented cheques Rs 12,000; uncleared deposits Rs 7,500; bank charges Rs 600 not yet in the cash book.
> Updated cash book = 48,000 − 600 = 47,400

! A favourable balance is a debit in the cash book but a credit on the bank statement. With an overdraft, reverse every adjustment: unpresented cheques make the bank's overdraft smaller, uncleared deposits make it larger.
## Errors and their correction
| Error | Meaning | Trial balance
| Omission | Transaction not recorded at all | Agrees
| Commission | Posted to the wrong account of the same class | Agrees
| Principle | Capital and revenue confused | Agrees
| Original entry | Wrong amount in the book of prime entry | Agrees
| Compensating | Two errors cancel out | Agrees
| One-sided | Wrong side, wrong amount on one side, or casting error | Disagrees

When the trial balance disagrees, the difference is placed in a suspense account on the shorter side. Each error that affected only one side is then corrected with the suspense account as the other half of the entry.
> The sales book is undercast by Rs 1,000. Sales received too little credit.
> Correction: Suspense Dr 1,000; Sales Cr 1,000
! An amount posted to the wrong side must be corrected with twice the amount: once to cancel the wrong entry and once to make the right one.
## Depreciation methods
- Straight-line (fixed instalment): (Cost − Residual value) ÷ Life, equal each year; book value can reach zero or the residual value.
- Reducing balance (diminishing balance): a fixed percentage of the opening book value; the charge falls each year and the book value never reaches zero.
- Land is normally not depreciated. With a provision account, the entry is Depreciation Dr, Provision for Depreciation Cr, and the asset stays at cost.
- On sale: profit or loss = Sale proceeds − Book value (cost − accumulated depreciation).
> Machine Rs 100,000 at 10 % reducing balance: 90,000, then 81,000, then Rs 72,900 after three years.
## Partnership basics

A partnership is an association of persons who share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them. In Pakistan it is governed by the Partnership Act, 1932. Partners have unlimited liability. Their agreement, preferably written as a partnership deed, settles capital, profit-sharing ratio, interest, salaries and drawings.
If there is no agreement, the Act applies:
- Profits and losses are shared equally.
- No interest on capital and no interest on drawings.
- No salary to any partner.
- Interest at 6 % a year on a partner's loan to the firm.

Profit is divided in the profit and loss appropriation account: add interest on drawings, deduct interest on capital and salaries, then share the remainder in the agreed ratio. With fixed capitals these items pass through the partners' current accounts.
> Profit Rs 200,000. Interest on capital 10 %: Faisal 40,000, Ghazala 30,000. Salary to Ghazala 24,000. Remainder 106,000 shared equally, 53,000 each.
> Faisal 93,000; Ghazala 107,000; total 200,000.
## Bills of exchange

A bill of exchange is an unconditional written order, drawn by a creditor (drawer) on a debtor (drawee), to pay a sum on demand or at a fixed future time. The drawee signs to accept it. A promissory note is the reverse: a written promise by the debtor (maker) to pay.
- Due date of a time bill = date plus the period plus 3 days of grace (Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881).
- Drawer, on acceptance: Bills Receivable Dr, Debtor Cr. Drawee: Creditor Dr, Bills Payable Cr.
- Discounting: the bank deducts interest for the unexpired period. Discount = Amount × Rate × Months/12.
- Dishonour: the bill is cancelled and the debtor is again charged with the amount plus any noting charges.
> A bill of Rs 100,000 with three months to run is discounted at 12 % a year.
! For a bill 'after date' counted in days, do not count the date of drawing. A bill of 15 January for 60 days falls on 16 March; with grace, 19 March (in a non-leap year).
## Quick check
- From a cash book debit balance, do you add or deduct unpresented cheques?
- Which errors leave the trial balance in agreement?
- What rate of interest does a partner's loan earn without an agreement?
- How many days of grace are added to a time bill?

title: Cell Biology and Biomolecules
lines: USAT-M Biology asks short fact-recall and one-step reasoning questions on this topic: which organelle does a job, how prokaryotes differ from eukaryotes, which bond joins which monomers, how enzymes behave, and where each stage of respiration and photosynthesis happens. Most questions take under a minute if the tables below are learnt by heart.
## The cell and its organelles

The cell theory says that all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and new cells come only from existing cells. The plasma membrane follows the fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972): a phospholipid bilayer with proteins floating in it, plus cholesterol in animal cells.
| Organelle | Main job
| Nucleus | holds DNA; controls the cell; double membrane with pores
| Nucleolus | makes rRNA and assembles ribosomes
| Rough ER | carries ribosomes; makes proteins for export
| Smooth ER | makes lipids and steroids; detoxifies drugs (liver)
| Golgi apparatus | modifies, packages and secretes proteins; forms lysosomes
| Lysosome | holds hydrolytic enzymes; digests worn-out parts (autophagy)
| Mitochondrion | aerobic respiration; own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes
| Chloroplast | photosynthesis; own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes
| Ribosome | protein synthesis; 80S in eukaryotic cytoplasm, 70S in prokaryotes
| Centriole | forms spindle fibres in animal cells; absent in most plant cells
| Vacuole | large central sap vacuole in plants keeps the cell turgid
## Prokaryotes and eukaryotes
- Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nuclear membrane: the DNA lies in a nucleoid, is circular and has no histones. Extra small rings of DNA are plasmids.
- They have 70S ribosomes, a peptidoglycan (murein) cell wall, and no mitochondria, ER or Golgi. Respiratory enzymes sit on the cell membrane.
- Eukaryotes have a true nucleus, linear chromosomes with histones, 80S ribosomes and membrane-bound organelles. Plant walls are cellulose; fungal walls are chitin; animal cells have no wall.
## Movement across the membrane
- Diffusion: high to low concentration, no energy. Facilitated diffusion uses carrier or channel proteins, still no ATP.
- Osmosis: water moves through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a concentrated one.
- Active transport: against the concentration gradient, using carrier proteins and ATP (for example the Na⁺/K⁺ pump).
- Endocytosis brings material in (phagocytosis for solids, pinocytosis for liquids); exocytosis sends secretions out.

! In a concentrated (hypertonic) solution a plant cell loses water and its membrane pulls away from the wall: plasmolysis. In pure water a plant cell becomes turgid but does not burst because of its wall; a red blood cell has no wall and bursts (haemolysis).
## Biomolecules
Carbohydrates, proteins and lipids are built from small units joined by condensation (water is removed) and broken by hydrolysis (water is added).
| Molecule | Monomer | Bond
| Polysaccharide (starch, glycogen, cellulose) | glucose | glycosidic
| Protein | amino acid (20 kinds) | peptide
| Triglyceride (fat) | glycerol + 3 fatty acids | ester
| Nucleic acid (DNA, RNA) | nucleotide (sugar + phosphate + base) | phosphodiester
- Monosaccharides: glucose, fructose, galactose (all C₆H₁₂O₆). Disaccharides: maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose), lactose (glucose + galactose).
- Starch is the plant store, glycogen the animal store (liver and muscle), cellulose the plant cell wall. Iodine turns starch blue-black.

- Proteins have four levels of structure: primary (amino acid sequence), secondary (α-helix or β-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds), tertiary (3-D folding of one chain) and quaternary (two or more chains, as in haemoglobin with 2α and 2β chains).
- A phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails, so it forms bilayers in water. Cholesterol and the sex hormones are steroids, also lipids.

- DNA has deoxyribose and the bases A, T, G, C; RNA has ribose and uracil in place of thymine. In DNA, A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds) and G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds), so A = T and G = C (Chargaff's rule).
> A double-stranded DNA sample has 35 % cytosine. What percentage is thymine?
> A + T = 100 − 70 = 30 %, and A = T, so thymine = 15 %.
> A polypeptide chain has 120 amino acids. How many peptide bonds does it contain, and how many water molecules were released in making it?
> n amino acids in one chain are joined by n − 1 peptide bonds: 119 bonds.
> Each bond releases one water molecule: 119 water molecules.
## Enzymes

Enzymes are biological catalysts, nearly all proteins. They speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy and are not used up. Each acts on a specific substrate because the shape of its active site fits that substrate: Fischer's lock-and-key model, refined by Koshland's induced-fit model, in which the active site moulds itself around the substrate.
- Temperature: the rate rises to an optimum (about 37 °C for human enzymes), then falls as the enzyme denatures. Cold only slows enzymes.
- pH: each enzyme has an optimum, for example pepsin about 2 and salivary amylase about 6.8.
- Substrate concentration: the rate rises and then levels off when all active sites are busy (saturation). Only more enzyme raises it further.
- Cofactors: a prosthetic group is tightly bound and organic (haem); a coenzyme is loosely bound and organic (NAD⁺, FAD, often from vitamins); an activator is a metal ion (Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺).

- A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and blocks the active site; extra substrate overcomes it. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape; extra substrate does not help.
> The rate of an enzyme reaction stops rising even though more substrate is added. Temperature and pH are at their optimum. What will raise the rate?
> All active sites are already occupied, so the enzyme is saturated.
> Only adding more enzyme provides new active sites; more substrate does nothing.
## Bioenergetics
ATP is the energy currency of the cell. Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose; respiration releases it as ATP.
- Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, in light, with chlorophyll.
- Light-dependent reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes (grana). Water is split (photolysis), releasing O₂; ATP and NADPH are made.
- The Calvin cycle (light-independent) occurs in the stroma. The enzyme rubisco fixes CO₂ onto RuBP, and ATP and NADPH from the light reactions turn the product into sugar.
| Stage of respiration | Site | Products per glucose
| Glycolysis | cytoplasm | 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP, 2 NADH
| Link reaction | mitochondrial matrix | 2 acetyl CoA, 2 CO₂, 2 NADH
| Krebs cycle (2 turns) | mitochondrial matrix | 4 CO₂, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP
| Electron transport chain | inner membrane (cristae) | most of the ATP; O₂ accepts electrons and forms water
Aerobic respiration gives about 36-38 ATP per glucose. Without oxygen only glycolysis runs, giving a net 2 ATP: muscle turns pyruvate into lactic acid, and yeast turns it into ethanol and CO₂.
> How many molecules of CO₂ are released from one glucose molecule in complete aerobic respiration, and where?
> Link reaction: 1 CO₂ per pyruvate × 2 = 2.
> Krebs cycle: 2 CO₂ per turn × 2 turns = 4.
> Total 6 CO₂, all in the mitochondrial matrix; glycolysis releases none.
! Glycolysis does not need oxygen and happens in the cytoplasm, not in the mitochondrion. Oxygen is used only at the very end of the electron transport chain, as the final electron acceptor.
! The O₂ given off in photosynthesis comes from water, not from CO₂.
## Quick check
- Which two organelles have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes? (mitochondria and chloroplasts)
- Which bond joins two amino acids? (peptide bond)
- DNA with 22 % adenine: what is guanine? (28 %)
- Which inhibitor can be beaten by adding more substrate? (competitive)
- Where does the Calvin cycle happen? (stroma)
- Net ATP from anaerobic respiration of one glucose? (2)

title: Diversity of Life
lines: USAT-M Biology tests this topic with recall questions: the order of taxonomic ranks, how a scientific name is written, which kingdom or phylum an organism belongs to, the features of plant groups, and ecology ideas such as food chains, the 10 % energy rule, nutrient cycles and the relationships between species.
## Classification and naming

Organisms are grouped in a hierarchy of ranks, from the largest to the smallest: kingdom, phylum (division in plants), class, order, family, genus, species. A species is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
- Binomial nomenclature was introduced by Carolus Linnaeus. Each organism has a two-part Latin name: genus then species, for example Homo sapiens (humans) or Mangifera indica (mango).
- The genus starts with a capital letter, the species name with a small letter. The name is printed in italics or underlined when handwritten.
## The five kingdoms
Robert Whittaker (1969) proposed five kingdoms.
| Kingdom | Cells | Nutrition | Examples
| Monera (Prokaryotae) | prokaryotic, mostly single cells | varied | bacteria, cyanobacteria
| Protista (Protoctista) | eukaryotic, mostly single cells | varied | Amoeba, Paramecium, Plasmodium, algae
| Fungi | eukaryotic, mostly hyphae; chitin walls | absorb food (saprotrophs, parasites) | yeast, Penicillium, mushrooms
| Plantae | eukaryotic, many cells; cellulose walls | photosynthesis | mosses, ferns, pine, mango
| Animalia | eukaryotic, many cells; no walls | ingest food | sponges to mammals

- Viruses are not placed in any kingdom. They are acellular, contain DNA or RNA (never both) inside a protein coat (capsid), and reproduce only inside a living host cell. A virus that infects bacteria is a bacteriophage. HIV is an RNA virus (retrovirus) that attacks helper T cells.

- Bacteria are named by shape: cocci (spheres), bacilli (rods), spirilla (spirals), vibrios (commas). They reproduce mainly by binary fission. The Gram stain separates them by cell-wall type: Gram-positive walls have thick peptidoglycan.
- Rhizobium lives in root nodules of legumes and fixes atmospheric nitrogen. Plasmodium (a protist) causes malaria and is carried by the female Anopheles mosquito.
- A lichen is a mutualistic partnership of a fungus and an alga (or cyanobacterium).
## Plants
| Group | Vascular tissue | Seeds | Dominant generation | Example
| Bryophytes | none | no (spores) | gametophyte | mosses, liverworts
| Pteridophytes | yes | no (spores) | sporophyte | ferns
| Gymnosperms | yes | naked seeds, in cones | sporophyte | pine, cycads
| Angiosperms | yes | seeds inside fruits; flowers | sporophyte | wheat, rose, mango
Bryophytes need water for the male gametes to swim to the egg, so they grow in damp, shady places.
| Feature | Monocot | Dicot
| Cotyledons in seed | one | two
| Leaf veins | parallel | net (reticulate)
| Flower parts | in threes | in fours or fives
| Roots | fibrous | tap root
| Examples | wheat, rice, maize, grasses | pea, gram, rose, mango
> A plant has xylem and phloem and reproduces by spores. It has no flowers or seeds. To which group does it belong?
> Vascular tissue rules out bryophytes; having no seeds rules out gymnosperms and angiosperms.
> It is a pteridophyte, such as a fern.
## Animals
| Phylum | Key features | Examples
| Porifera | pores in body wall; no true tissues | sponges
| Cnidaria | radial symmetry, stinging cells, one opening | Hydra, jellyfish
| Platyhelminthes | flat, unsegmented worms | tapeworm, liver fluke, planaria
| Nematoda | round, unsegmented worms | Ascaris
| Annelida | segmented worms | earthworm, leech
| Arthropoda | jointed legs, chitin exoskeleton; the largest phylum | insects, spiders, crabs
| Mollusca | soft body, often a shell | snail, mussel, octopus
| Echinodermata | spiny skin, tube feet, all marine | starfish, sea urchin
| Chordata | notochord, dorsal nerve cord, gill slits (at some stage) | fish to mammals
- Vertebrate classes: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals. Birds and mammals are warm-blooded (endothermic); the others are cold-blooded (ectothermic).
- Heart chambers: fish 2, amphibians 3, most reptiles 3 (crocodiles 4), birds 4, mammals 4.
- Mammals have hair, mammary glands and (mostly) give birth to live young; the platypus is an egg-laying mammal.
> An animal has a segmented body, a hard exoskeleton containing chitin and six jointed legs. Name its phylum and class.
> Jointed legs with a chitin exoskeleton place it in Arthropoda.
> Six legs (three pairs) make it an insect (class Insecta). Spiders have eight legs and are arachnids.
! A whale, a bat and a dolphin are mammals, not fish or birds. A starfish is not a fish: it is an echinoderm.
## Ecology

An ecosystem is a community of living things plus their non-living surroundings. Producers (green plants, algae) make food by photosynthesis; consumers eat other organisms; decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead matter and recycle nutrients.
- Food chain: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake. Each step is a trophic level. Food chains link into a food web.
- Only about 10 % of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next; the rest is lost mostly as heat in respiration. This limits chains to 4 or 5 levels.
- Carbon cycle: photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration, decay and burning of fuels return it.
- Nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium, lightning), nitrification (ammonia → nitrite by Nitrosomonas, nitrite → nitrate by Nitrobacter), and denitrification (nitrate → N₂ gas).
| Relationship | Effect on the two species | Example
| Mutualism | both gain | lichen; Rhizobium and a legume
| Commensalism | one gains, the other is unaffected | epiphyte orchid on a tree
| Parasitism | one gains, the host is harmed | tapeworm in a human
| Predation | predator gains, prey is killed | hawk and sparrow
- A population grows until it reaches the carrying capacity: the largest number the environment can support.
- Acid rain comes mainly from SO₂ and nitrogen oxides. CO₂ and methane are greenhouse gases. CFCs damage the ozone layer.
> Producers in a pond store 50,000 kJ of energy. Using the 10 % rule, how much reaches the tertiary consumers?
> Primary consumers: 10 % of 50,000 = 5,000 kJ.
> Secondary consumers: 10 % of 5,000 = 500 kJ.
> Tertiary consumers: 10 % of 500 = 50 kJ.
! Count the levels carefully: tertiary consumers are three steps above the producers, so multiply by 0.1 three times, not four.
## Quick check
- Which rank comes between class and family? (order)
- Which kingdom has chitin walls and absorbs its food? (Fungi)
- Which plant group has naked seeds? (gymnosperms)
- Which phylum includes the tapeworm? (Platyhelminthes)
- Which relationship benefits both partners? (mutualism)
- Which bacterium turns nitrite into nitrate? (Nitrobacter)

title: Genetics and Evolution
lines: USAT-M Biology asks two kinds of genetics question: terms and facts (Mendel's laws, DNA structure, the genetic code, tools of biotechnology, theories of evolution) and short crosses that you solve with a Punnett square or a probability rule. Practise the crosses until each takes under a minute.
## Key terms
- Gene: a length of DNA that codes for one protein or trait. Alleles: different forms of the same gene, at the same place (locus) on a pair of chromosomes.
- Genotype: the alleles an organism has (TT, Tt, tt). Phenotype: the trait that shows (tall, dwarf).
- Homozygous: two identical alleles (TT or tt). Heterozygous: two different alleles (Tt).
- Dominant allele: shows its effect even in a heterozygote. Recessive allele: shows only when homozygous.
## Mendel's laws
Gregor Mendel, the father of genetics, worked with garden peas.
- Law of segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate, so each gamete gets only one.
- Law of independent assortment: genes on different chromosomes are sorted into gametes independently of each other.
| Cross | Phenotype ratio | Genotype ratio
| Tt × Tt (monohybrid) | 3 : 1 | 1 : 2 : 1
| Tt × tt (test cross) | 1 : 1 | 1 : 1
| RrYy × RrYy (dihybrid) | 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 | 9 genotypes
| RrYy × rryy (dihybrid test cross) | 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 | 1 : 1 : 1 : 1
A test cross mates an individual showing the dominant trait with a homozygous recessive. If any recessive offspring appear, the parent was heterozygous.
> In peas, round (R) is dominant to wrinkled (r). Two heterozygous plants are crossed and give 800 seeds. About how many seeds are wrinkled?
> Rr × Rr gives RR : Rr : rr = 1 : 2 : 1, so ¼ are rr.
> ¼ × 800 = 200 wrinkled seeds.
- Number of gamete types = 2ⁿ, where n is the number of heterozygous gene pairs. AaBbCc gives 2³ = 8 types.
- To find the chance of one offspring type, split the cross into single genes and multiply. From RrYy × RrYy, the chance of rryy is ¼ × ¼ = 1/16.
## Beyond simple dominance
- Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is in between. In the four o'clock plant, red × white gives pink F₁, and the F₂ is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
- Codominance: both alleles show fully. Blood group AB shows both A and B antigens.
- Multiple alleles: the ABO gene has three alleles, IA, IB and i. IA and IB are codominant; both are dominant to i.
| Blood group | Possible genotypes
| A | IA IA or IA i
| B | IB IB or IB i
| AB | IA IB
| O | i i
> A man of group A (IA i) and a woman of group B (IB i) have a child. What are the chances of each blood group?
> Gametes: IA or i from the father; IB or i from the mother.
> Offspring: IA IB (AB), IA i (A), IB i (B), i i (O), each ¼.
> So all four groups are possible, each with probability ¼.
## Sex determination and sex linkage
- Humans have 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. Females are XX, males XY. The father's sperm decides the sex of the child.
- Haemophilia and red-green colour blindness are X-linked recessive. A male has only one X, so one recessive allele is enough to show the disorder; this is why they are more common in males.
- A father passes his X to all daughters and his Y to all sons, so he never passes an X-linked allele to his son.
> A carrier woman (XH Xh) marries a man with normal blood clotting (XH Y). What fraction of their sons may have haemophilia?
> Sons receive Y from the father and one X from the mother: XH Y or Xh Y.
> Half of the sons may be haemophiliac. Daughters get XH from the father, so none is affected, but half are carriers.
! Read whether the question asks about sons, daughters or all children. Here ½ of sons are affected, but only ¼ of all children.
- Chromosome number disorders: Down syndrome (trisomy 21, 47 chromosomes), Klinefelter syndrome (XXY male), Turner syndrome (XO female, 45 chromosomes).
## DNA and protein synthesis

- Watson and Crick described the double helix in 1953, using X-ray work of Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins. The two strands are antiparallel and are held by hydrogen bonds between bases: A with T, G with C.

- Replication is semi-conservative: each new molecule keeps one old strand (shown by Meselson and Stahl). DNA polymerase builds new strands only in the 5′ to 3′ direction, so the lagging strand is made in short Okazaki fragments, joined by DNA ligase.
- Transcription: DNA → mRNA in the nucleus; uracil replaces thymine. Translation: mRNA → protein on ribosomes; tRNA brings amino acids; rRNA forms part of the ribosome.

- The genetic code is a triplet code: 64 codons for 20 amino acids. It is degenerate (most amino acids have more than one codon) and almost universal. AUG is the start codon; UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.
> A DNA template strand reads TAC CGT. What mRNA is made from it?
> Pair each base: T → A, A → U, C → G, G → C.
> TAC → AUG and CGT → GCA, so the mRNA is AUG GCA. AUG is the start codon.
- A gene mutation is a change in the base sequence. In sickle-cell anaemia one base change replaces one amino acid in haemoglobin.
## Biotechnology
- Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific base sequences; DNA ligase joins pieces. A plasmid is the usual vector for carrying a gene into a bacterium.
- Recombinant DNA technology lets bacteria such as E. coli make human insulin and growth hormone.
- PCR (polymerase chain reaction) copies a piece of DNA many times using heat-stable Taq polymerase; after n cycles there are 2ⁿ copies.
- Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size; it is used in DNA fingerprinting for crime and paternity cases.
- Genetically modified crops include Bt cotton, which makes its own insecticidal protein. Dolly the sheep (1996) was the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell.
## Evolution
- Lamarck: use and disuse, and the inheritance of acquired characters. This idea is rejected.

- Darwin: natural selection (On the Origin of Species, 1859). Organisms overproduce; there is variation and a struggle for existence; those with favourable inherited variations survive and reproduce more. Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea independently.

- Evidence: fossils; homologous organs (same basic structure, different jobs, such as the forelimbs of a human, bat and whale) show common ancestry; analogous organs (same job, different origin, such as bird and insect wings) do not. Vestigial organs, such as the human appendix, are reduced remains.
- Example of selection: dark peppered moths became common in sooty industrial areas because birds ate the light ones that showed up on dark trees.

- Origin of life: Oparin and Haldane proposed that simple gases formed organic molecules; Miller and Urey (1953) made amino acids by passing sparks through methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour.
- Hardy-Weinberg: in a large, randomly mating population with no selection, mutation or migration, allele frequencies stay constant. p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
> In a population, 16 % of people show a recessive trait. What percentage are heterozygous carriers?
! Antibiotics do not cause resistance in bacteria. Resistant variants already exist; the drug kills the others, and the resistant ones multiply.
## Quick check
- Phenotype ratio of a monohybrid F₂? (3 : 1)
- Which blood group shows codominance? (AB)
- Chromosomes in a person with Down syndrome? (47)
- Which enzyme joins Okazaki fragments? (DNA ligase)
- Codons in the genetic code? (64)
- Forelimbs of a bat and a whale are which kind of organ? (homologous)

title: Human Physiology
lines: Human physiology is the largest biology topic in USAT-M. Questions ask where a process happens, which enzyme or hormone does a job, how blood flows through the heart, how the kidney makes urine, how nerve impulses travel, and how the body defends itself. Learn the tables; most questions are one-step recall.
## Digestion
| Region | Juice or enzyme | Action
| Mouth | salivary amylase | starch → maltose
| Stomach | HCl and pepsin (from pepsinogen) | HCl kills microbes and activates pepsin; proteins → polypeptides
| Duodenum | bile (from liver, stored in gall bladder) | emulsifies fat; has no enzyme
| Duodenum | pancreatic amylase, trypsin, lipase | starch → maltose; proteins → peptides; fats → fatty acids + glycerol
| Small intestine wall | maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidases | disaccharides → monosaccharides; peptides → amino acids
- Absorption happens mainly in the ileum, through millions of villi. Sugars and amino acids enter the blood capillaries; fats enter the lacteals (lymph).
- The large intestine (colon) absorbs water and salts. Its bacteria make vitamin K.
- The liver makes bile, stores glycogen, turns excess amino acids into urea (deamination) and breaks down toxins.
- Gut hormones: gastrin (stomach) increases gastric juice; secretin and cholecystokinin (duodenum) stimulate the pancreas, and cholecystokinin also empties the gall bladder.
! Trypsinogen is activated by enterokinase, not by HCl. Bile emulsifies fat but digests nothing.
## Blood and circulation

- Plasma (about 55 % of blood) carries dissolved food, CO₂, hormones and urea. Red cells carry O₂ on haemoglobin; mature red cells have no nucleus. White cells fight infection; platelets start clotting.
- ABO groups depend on antigens on red cells: group A has antigen A, B has B, AB has both, O has neither. O negative is the universal donor; AB positive is the universal recipient.

- The heart has four chambers. Deoxygenated blood: venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs. Oxygenated blood: pulmonary veins → left atrium → bicuspid (mitral) valve → left ventricle → aorta → body. This is double circulation.
- The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood round the whole body.
- The beat starts in the sinoatrial (SA) node, the pacemaker in the right atrium. The impulse passes to the AV node, the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres.
- The first heart sound (lubb) is the closing of the AV valves; the second (dub) is the closing of the semilunar valves.

- Arteries have thick, elastic walls and carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. Veins have thin walls and valves and carry blood back. Capillaries are one cell thick and exchange materials with tissues. Normal adult blood pressure is about 120/80 mmHg.
> A person's heart beats 75 times a minute. How long is one cardiac cycle?
> 60 s ÷ 75 beats = 0.8 s per cycle.
> At this rate: atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, complete diastole 0.4 s.
! The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood. Arteries and veins are named by direction (away from or towards the heart), not by oxygen content.
## Breathing and gas exchange
- Air passes: nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. C-shaped cartilage rings keep the trachea open.
- Gas exchange happens by diffusion across the thin, moist walls of millions of alveoli, which give a huge surface area.
- Inhaling: the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs, chest volume rises, pressure falls and air rushes in. Quiet exhaling is mostly passive.
- About 97 % of O₂ travels as oxyhaemoglobin. Most CO₂ travels as bicarbonate ions in plasma. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than O₂, so it cuts O₂ transport.
- The breathing rate is controlled by the medulla, which responds mainly to the CO₂ level of the blood.
> Tidal volume is 500 mL, inspiratory reserve volume 3,000 mL and expiratory reserve volume 1,100 mL. Find the vital capacity.
> Vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV = 500 + 3,000 + 1,100 = 4,600 mL.
> Residual volume is not included: it can never be breathed out.
## Excretion
- The kidneys remove urea, excess water and salts. Urea itself is made in the liver.

- The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney. Ultrafiltration happens from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule: water, glucose, salts and urea pass through, but blood cells and plasma proteins stay in the blood.
- Selective reabsorption: the proximal convoluted tubule takes back all the glucose and amino acids and most of the water and salts. The loop of Henle helps concentrate urine.

- Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), released from the posterior pituitary, makes the collecting duct reabsorb more water, so less but more concentrated urine is made. Aldosterone increases Na⁺ reabsorption.
- Urine path: kidney → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra.
> A patient's urine regularly contains glucose. What is the most likely reason?
> Normally all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.
> In diabetes mellitus, blood glucose is so high that the filtered glucose exceeds what the tubule can reabsorb, so the extra appears in urine. Protein in urine instead points to damaged glomeruli.
## Nervous system and senses

- The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system is the nerves. A neuron has dendrites, a cell body and an axon, often covered by a myelin sheath that speeds conduction.
- At rest the inside of a neuron is about −70 mV. In an action potential, Na⁺ ions rush in (depolarisation), then K⁺ ions move out (repolarisation). The impulse is all-or-none.
- At a synapse a neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine crosses the gap, so impulses travel in one direction only.
- Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron in the spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (muscle or gland).
| Brain part | Main job
| Cerebrum | thinking, memory, voluntary movement, senses
| Cerebellum | balance and coordination of movement
| Medulla oblongata | breathing, heart rate, blood pressure
| Hypothalamus | temperature, thirst, hunger; controls the pituitary

- Eye: in short sight (myopia) the image forms in front of the retina; it is corrected by a concave lens. In long sight (hypermetropia) the image forms behind the retina; a convex lens corrects it. Rods work in dim light; cones see colour.
## Endocrine system
| Gland | Hormone | Effect
| Pituitary (anterior) | growth hormone, TSH, FSH, LH | growth; controls other glands
| Pituitary (posterior) | ADH, oxytocin | water reabsorption; uterine contraction in childbirth
| Thyroid | thyroxine (contains iodine) | sets the metabolic rate
| Pancreas (islets of Langerhans) | insulin; glucagon | lowers blood glucose; raises it
| Adrenal medulla | adrenaline | fight or flight
| Testes | testosterone | male secondary sexual characters
| Ovaries | oestrogen, progesterone | female characters; maintain the uterus lining
The pituitary is called the master gland because it controls many other glands, but it is itself controlled by the hypothalamus. Lack of iodine causes goitre.
## Immunity
- Innate (non-specific) defences: skin, mucus, stomach acid, phagocytes and inflammation.

- Specific immunity uses lymphocytes. B cells become plasma cells that secrete antibodies (humoral immunity). T cells mature in the thymus; killer T cells destroy infected cells and helper T cells coordinate the response (cell-mediated immunity).
- Memory cells make the second response to the same antigen faster and stronger.

- Active immunity: the body makes its own antibodies after infection (natural) or vaccination (artificial). Passive immunity: ready-made antibodies from the mother through the placenta or milk (natural) or by injection (artificial). Passive immunity is quick but short-lived.
## Reproduction

- Male: sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules of the testes, mature in the epididymis, and pass through the vas deferens and urethra. Seminal vesicles, the prostate and Cowper's glands add fluid.
- Female: an ovary releases an egg into the oviduct (Fallopian tube), where fertilisation happens. The embryo implants in the uterus.

- In a 28-day menstrual cycle, menstruation takes about days 1-5, FSH makes a follicle grow and secrete oestrogen, a surge of LH causes ovulation around day 14, and the corpus luteum then makes progesterone. If no pregnancy occurs, progesterone falls and menstruation starts again.
- Gametes are made by meiosis and carry 23 chromosomes; fertilisation restores 46.
! Many students write that the pituitary makes ADH. ADH is made in the hypothalamus and stored and released by the posterior pituitary; MCQs usually accept "posterior pituitary" as the source.
## Quick check
- Where does protein digestion begin? (stomach)
- Which valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle? (bicuspid or mitral)
- Which muscle flattens when you breathe in? (diaphragm)
- Where does ultrafiltration take place? (glomerulus into Bowman's capsule)
- Which ion rushes in during depolarisation? (Na⁺)
- Which hormone lowers blood glucose? (insulin)
- Antibodies from mother's milk give which immunity? (natural passive)

title: Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
lines: This topic gives USAT many quick marks: mole calculations, Avogadro's number, molar volume, empirical formulas and limiting reactants; the gas laws and kinetic theory; types of solids and intermolecular forces; and atomic structure up to quantum numbers and electronic configurations. Arithmetic is light, so accuracy with formulas and molar masses decides the mark.
## The mole
One mole is the amount of substance containing Avogadro's number of particles, Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³.
| You know | Moles n =
| mass m (g) | m ÷ molar mass M
| number of particles N | N ÷ Nₐ
| volume of gas at STP | V ÷ 22.4 dm³
| solution | molarity × volume (dm³)
- STP means 0 °C (273 K) and 1 atm.
- Read the question: molecules, atoms or ions? One mole of H₂SO₄ contains 7 moles of atoms, including 4 of oxygen.
> Example 1. How many molecules and how many atoms are there in 4.4 g of CO₂ (C = 12, O = 16)?
> M = 44 g/mol, so n = 0.1 mol. Molecules = 0.1 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²². Each has 3 atoms, so atoms = 1.81 × 10²³.
## Formulas and stoichiometry
- Percentage of an element = (mass of that element in one formula ÷ molar mass) × 100.
- Empirical formula: divide each mass (or percentage) by the atomic mass, then divide by the smallest result to get a whole-number ratio.
- Molecular formula = n × empirical formula, where n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass. Glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ has the empirical formula CH₂O.
> Example 2. A compound contains 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula.
> C 40.0 ÷ 12 = 3.33; H 6.7 ÷ 1 = 6.7; O 53.3 ÷ 16 = 3.33. Dividing by 3.33 gives 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH₂O.
- Limiting reactant: divide the moles of each reactant by its coefficient in the balanced equation; the smallest result is the limiting reactant and fixes the amount of product.
- Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100.
> Example 3. 28 g of N₂ reacts with 4 g of H₂: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Which is limiting, and what mass of NH₃ forms?
> N₂: 1 mol ÷ 1 = 1. H₂: 2 mol ÷ 3 = 0.67. H₂ is limiting. NH₃ formed = ⅔ × 2 mol = 4/3 mol = 4/3 × 17 ≈ 22.7 g.
## Gases
- Boyle: PV = constant at fixed T. Charles: V/T = constant at fixed P (T in kelvin). Combined: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
- Ideal gas equation PV = nRT, with R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ or 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
- Avogadro: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules.
- Dalton: total pressure = sum of partial pressures; each partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.
- Graham: rate of diffusion ∝ 1/√M. Hydrogen diffuses four times as fast as oxygen. A gas that diffuses half as fast as O₂ has M = 4 × 32 = 128 g/mol.
- Kinetic theory: gas molecules move randomly and collide elastically; their average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature.
- Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour most at high pressure and low temperature. The van der Waals equation corrects for molecular attraction (a) and molecular volume (b).
## Liquids and solids
- Intermolecular forces, weakest to strongest for molecules of similar size: London (dispersion) forces < dipole-dipole forces < hydrogen bonds.
- Hydrogen bonding needs H joined to F, O or N. It explains why water is a liquid while H₂S is a gas, and why ice floats.
- A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure, so water boils below 100 °C on a mountain and above it in a pressure cooker.
| Solid | Particles and forces | Example
| Ionic | ions, ionic bonds | NaCl, MgO
| Covalent network | atoms, covalent bonds | diamond, SiO₂
| Molecular | molecules, intermolecular forces | ice, iodine
| Metallic | cations in a sea of electrons | copper, iron
## Atomic structure
- Electron: discovered through cathode rays (J. J. Thomson); mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, charge −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Proton: from positive rays. Neutron: discovered by Chadwick (1932).
- Rutherford's α-scattering showed that an atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
- Atomic number Z = protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z and different numbers of neutrons.
- Bohr: the electron in hydrogen occupies fixed orbits; energy is emitted or absorbed only when it jumps between them.
- Quantum numbers: n (shell, 1, 2, 3 …), l (subshell, 0 to n − 1: s, p, d, f), m (orientation, −l to +l) and s (spin, ±½).
- A shell holds 2n² electrons; subshells hold s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14.
## Filling orbitals
- Aufbau: fill in order of increasing (n + l); for equal (n + l), lower n first. Order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s.
- Pauli: no two electrons have the same four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two, with opposite spins.
- Hund: electrons enter degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing.
- Exceptions: Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, because half-filled and filled d subshells are extra stable.
> Example 4. How many unpaired electrons do Cr and Fe²⁺ have?
> Cr is 3d⁵ 4s¹: all six electrons are unpaired. Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²; Fe²⁺ loses the 4s electrons first, leaving 3d⁶ with 4 unpaired.
! The reactant with fewer moles is not always limiting; compare moles divided by coefficients.
! Use kelvin in all gas-law work: heating from 27 °C to 127 °C raises V by 400/300, not by 127/27.
! There is no 2d or 1p orbital: l can only run from 0 to n − 1.
## Quick check
- Volume of 0.5 mol of a gas at STP? (11.2 dm³)
- Moles of ions from one mole of CaCl₂? (3)
- Maximum electrons in the n = 3 shell? (18)
- Which fills first, 4s or 3d? (4s)
- Which gas diffuses faster, NH₃ or HCl? (NH₃, lower molar mass)

title: Inorganic Chemistry
lines: Inorganic questions in USAT test the periodic table and its trends, the chemistry of the s, p and d blocks, and the main industrial processes. Most are recall questions: a trend and its exception, a formula, a colour, a catalyst or the condition used in a process. Learn the reasons behind the trends, because questions often ask why.
## The periodic table
- The modern table is arranged by atomic number (Moseley), not atomic mass (Mendeleev). It has 7 periods and 18 groups.
- Period lengths: 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32. The period number is the highest shell in use.
- s block: groups 1-2 (ns¹⁻²). p block: groups 13-18 (ns² np¹⁻⁶). d block: groups 3-12. f block: lanthanides and actinides.
> Example 1. An element has Z = 35. Find its configuration, period, group and block.
> [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵: highest shell n = 4, so period 4; seven outer electrons in s and p, so group 17 in the p block. It is bromine.
## Periodic trends
| Property | Across a period | Down a group
| Atomic radius | decreases | increases
| Ionisation energy | increases | decreases
| Electronegativity | increases | decreases
| Metallic character | decreases | increases
- Across a period the nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell, so they are pulled in more tightly. Down a group new shells are added and inner electrons shield the outer ones.
- Ionisation energy dips: Be > B and Mg > Al (a p electron is easier to remove than an s² electron); N > O and P > S (half-filled p³ is extra stable).
- Chlorine has a higher electron affinity than fluorine because the small fluorine atom crowds the incoming electron.
- Cations are smaller than their atoms; anions are larger. In an isoelectronic series, more protons mean a smaller ion.
> Example 2. Arrange O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺ in order of decreasing size.
> All have 10 electrons; the nuclear charge rises from 8 to 13. So O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺.
- Period 3 oxides change from basic (Na₂O, MgO) through amphoteric (Al₂O₃) to acidic (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇).
## The s block
- Group 1 (alkali metals) and group 2 (alkaline earth metals) are reactive metals; reactivity rises down each group as ionisation energy falls.
- Flame colours: Li crimson, Na golden yellow, K lilac, Ca brick red, Sr crimson red, Ba apple green.
- Down group 2, hydroxides become more soluble and sulphates less soluble (BaSO₄ is insoluble). Carbonates become more stable to heat.
- Lithium resembles magnesium, and beryllium resembles aluminium (diagonal relationship). BeO is amphoteric.
- Compounds to know: NaOH from the electrolysis of brine; Na₂CO₃ by the Solvay process; quicklime CaO from heating limestone; slaked lime Ca(OH)₂; gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O and plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O.
## The p block
- Boron and aluminium (group 13): borax Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O; boric acid H₃BO₃ is a weak Lewis acid. Al₂O₃ and Al(OH)₃ are amphoteric. Alum purifies water by coagulating suspended particles.
- Group 14: catenation is strongest for carbon. Down the group the +2 state becomes more stable (inert pair effect), so Pb²⁺ is the stable lead ion and PbO₂ is an oxidising agent.
- Nitrogen and phosphorus (group 15): N₂ is unreactive because of its strong triple bond. White phosphorus is very reactive and stored under water; red phosphorus is far more stable.
- Oxygen and sulphur (group 16): ozone O₃ in the stratosphere absorbs ultraviolet. Concentrated H₂SO₄ is a dehydrating agent (it chars sugar) and an oxidising agent.
- Halogens (group 17): oxidising power F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂, so chlorine displaces bromine and iodine from their salts. With silver nitrate, Cl⁻ gives a white precipitate, Br⁻ cream and I⁻ yellow.
- Noble gases (group 18) are very unreactive, but xenon forms fluorides such as XeF₂, XeF₄ and XeF₆.
## The d block (transition elements)
- Electrons enter the (n − 1)d subshell; on forming ions the 4s electrons are lost first.

- Typical properties: variable oxidation states (Mn reaches +7 in KMnO₄), coloured ions (due to d-d transitions), paramagnetism from unpaired electrons, complex formation and catalytic activity (Fe in Haber, V₂O₅ in the contact process, Ni in hydrogenation).
- Ions with d⁰ or d¹⁰ configurations (Sc³⁺, Zn²⁺) are colourless. Zinc is not a typical transition element.
- Magnetic moment (spin only) = √(n(n + 2)) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
- In acid, purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺ (gaining 5 electrons) and orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ to green Cr³⁺ (6 electrons per ion).
> Example 3. Find the number of unpaired electrons and the spin-only magnetic moment of Fe³⁺ (Z = 26).
> Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²; Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵ with 5 unpaired electrons. μ = √(5 × 7) = √35 ≈ 5.9 BM.
## Industrial chemistry
| Process | Reaction | Catalyst, conditions
| Haber (ammonia) | N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ | iron; about 450 °C, about 200 atm
| Contact (sulphuric acid) | 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ | V₂O₅; about 450 °C, 1-2 atm
| Ostwald (nitric acid) | 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O | platinum-rhodium gauze
- Both Haber and contact reactions are exothermic, so a moderate temperature is a compromise between yield and rate.
- In the contact process SO₃ is absorbed in 98 % H₂SO₄ to give oleum, which is then diluted; SO₃ added straight to water forms a fine acid mist.
- Urea CO(NH₂)₂ is made from ammonia and carbon dioxide and contains about 46.7 % nitrogen, more than any other common solid fertiliser.
- Portland cement is made by heating limestone with clay; a little gypsum is added to slow the setting.
- Acid rain comes mainly from SO₂ and oxides of nitrogen; CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone.
> Example 4. Find the percentage of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃ (N = 14, H = 1, O = 16).
! Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶, not [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s²: the 4s electrons leave first.
! The strongest bond among the halogens is Cl-Cl, not F-F, yet fluorine is still the strongest oxidising agent.
! A catalyst in the Haber process does not raise the yield of ammonia; it only gets to equilibrium faster.
## Quick check
- Element with the highest electronegativity? (fluorine)
- Flame colour of potassium? (lilac)
- Catalyst in the contact process? (vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅)
- Why is Zn²⁺ colourless? (3d¹⁰: no d-d transitions)
- Which has the larger first ionisation energy, N or O? (N)

title: Organic Chemistry
lines: Organic chemistry has the most chemistry questions in USAT. They ask for IUPAC names, functional groups, isomers, the type of a reaction and its product, simple tests that tell compounds apart, and facts about biomolecules and polymers. Learn the reaction type of each family: that one fact predicts most products.
## Basics
- Carbon forms four bonds and links to itself in chains and rings (catenation), giving millions of compounds.
- A homologous series has the same functional group and general formula; neighbouring members differ by CH₂. Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.
| Family | Group | Name ending | Example
| Alcohol | –OH | -ol | ethanol C₂H₅OH
| Aldehyde | –CHO | -al | ethanal CH₃CHO
| Ketone | C=O in the chain | -one | propanone CH₃COCH₃
| Carboxylic acid | –COOH | -oic acid | ethanoic acid CH₃COOH
| Ester | –COOR | -oate | ethyl ethanoate CH₃COOC₂H₅
| Amine | –NH₂ | -amine | ethylamine C₂H₅NH₂
- IUPAC naming: find the longest chain containing the main group, number it from the end nearer that group, then list side chains as prefixes with their positions.
> Example 1. Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂OH.
> The longest chain holding the OH has three carbons (propanol); number from the OH end: OH on C-1, methyl on C-2. The name is 2-methylpropan-1-ol.
## Isomerism

- Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures: chain (butane and 2-methylpropane), position (propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol) and functional group (ethanol and methoxymethane).
- Geometric (cis-trans) isomers need a C=C with two different groups on each carbon, such as but-2-ene.
- Optical isomers contain a chiral carbon: one carrying four different groups, as in lactic acid.
- Counts worth knowing: C₄H₁₀ has 2 isomers, C₅H₁₂ has 3, and C₄H₁₀O has 4 alcohols.
## Reaction types
- Homolytic bond fission gives free radicals; heterolytic fission gives ions.
- Electrophiles seek electrons (H⁺, NO₂⁺, Br⁺); nucleophiles donate a lone pair (OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O).
| Family | Typical reaction
| Alkanes | free-radical substitution (Cl₂ in light)
| Alkenes, alkynes | electrophilic addition
| Benzene | electrophilic substitution
| Alkyl halides | nucleophilic substitution or elimination
| Aldehydes, ketones | nucleophilic addition
## Hydrocarbons
- Alkenes decolourise bromine water and cold alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's test); alkanes do not.
- Markovnikov's rule: when HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, H goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens. With peroxide, HBr adds the other way.
- Ethyne is made from calcium carbide and water. Terminal alkynes are weakly acidic and give a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate.
- Benzene has six equal C–C bonds and a delocalised π cloud, so it prefers substitution to addition. Nitration uses concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ (electrophile NO₂⁺); halogenation needs FeBr₃ or AlCl₃.
- Groups such as –OH, –NH₂ and –CH₃ direct new groups to the ortho and para positions; –NO₂, –CHO and –COOH direct to meta.
> Example 2. Give the main product when HBr adds to propene, CH₃CH=CH₂.
> H goes to the end CH₂ carbon (it already has more H); Br goes to the middle carbon. The product is 2-bromopropane, CH₃CHBrCH₃.
## Functional group chemistry
- Alkyl halides: aqueous KOH substitutes to give an alcohol; alcoholic KOH eliminates to give an alkene. SN1 suits tertiary halides, SN2 primary ones.
- Alcohols: primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes and then acids; secondary to ketones; tertiary resist oxidation. Phenol is more acidic than ethanol and gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl₃.
- Aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent (silver mirror) and Fehling's solution (red precipitate); ketones do not. Both give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH.
- The iodoform test (yellow CHI₃) is positive for methyl ketones, ethanal, ethanol and propan-2-ol.
- Carboxylic acids fizz with NaHCO₃, releasing CO₂, and react with alcohols to give esters. Esters smell fruity; alkaline hydrolysis of fats is saponification.
- Amines are weak bases; aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia, and phenylamine is weaker.
> Example 3. Which test distinguishes ethanal from propanone?
> Tollens' reagent: ethanal gives a silver mirror, propanone does not. The iodoform test fails here, because both compounds give it.
## Biomolecules
- Carbohydrates: glucose (an aldohexose) and fructose (a ketohexose) are both C₆H₁₂O₆. Sucrose is glucose + fructose and is non-reducing. Starch and cellulose are polymers of glucose.
- Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds (–CO–NH–). Amino acids exist as zwitterions; glycine is the only common one without a chiral carbon.
- Lipids: fats and oils are esters of glycerol with fatty acids (triglycerides). Oils are hydrogenated with a nickel catalyst to make ghee.
- Nucleic acids: DNA bases pair A with T and G with C; RNA has uracil in place of thymine. Enzymes are protein catalysts denatured by heat.
## Polymers
- Addition polymers form from alkene monomers with nothing lost: polythene (ethene), PVC (chloroethene), Teflon (tetrafluoroethene), polystyrene (phenylethene).
- Condensation polymers lose a small molecule such as water at each link: nylon-6,6 (from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid) and terylene (a polyester).
- Natural rubber is a polymer of isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene).
> Example 4. A sample of polythene has a molar mass of 28,000 g/mol. How many ethene units does each chain contain?
> Ethene C₂H₄ has M = 28, so the number of units = 28,000 ÷ 28 = 1,000.
! Ester names start with the alcohol part: CH₃COOC₂H₅ is ethyl ethanoate, not ethanoyl ethyl or ethyl methanoate.
! A tertiary alcohol is not oxidised by acidified dichromate; the orange colour stays.
! Cis-trans isomerism is impossible if one carbon of the C=C carries two identical groups, as in propene.
## Quick check
- General formula of alkynes? (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂)
- Reaction type of benzene with nitric acid? (electrophilic substitution)
- Monomer of PVC? (chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl)
- Which gives a silver mirror, an aldehyde or a ketone? (an aldehyde)
- Bond joining amino acids in a protein? (peptide bond)

title: Physical Chemistry
lines: Physical chemistry questions in USAT mix concepts and short calculations: shapes of molecules and hybridisation, enthalpy changes and Hess's law, equilibrium constants and Le Chatelier's principle, pH, rate laws and half-lives, cell potentials and electrolysis, and the properties of solutions. Learn the rules in each area and the few formulas that go with them.
## Chemical bonding

- Ionic bonds form by electron transfer, usually when the electronegativity difference is about 1.7 or more. Covalent bonds share electron pairs. In a coordinate bond both shared electrons come from one atom (NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺).
- Electronegativity: F (4.0) > O > N ≈ Cl > C > H.
- VSEPR: electron pairs repel and spread out; lone pairs repel more than bond pairs, squeezing the bond angles.
| Molecule | Pairs (bond, lone) | Shape, angle
| BeCl₂, CO₂ | 2, 0 | linear, 180°
| BF₃ | 3, 0 | trigonal planar, 120°
| CH₄ | 4, 0 | tetrahedral, 109.5°
| NH₃ | 3, 1 | pyramidal, about 107°
- Hybridisation: sp (linear), sp² (trigonal planar), sp³ (tetrahedral). A single bond is one σ bond; a double bond is σ + π; a triple bond is σ + 2π.
- A molecule with polar bonds can have zero dipole moment if it is symmetrical (CO₂, BF₃, CCl₄).
## Thermochemistry
- Exothermic: ΔH negative. Endothermic: ΔH positive. Standard conditions: 298 K and 1 atm.

- The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is zero. Enthalpy of combustion is always negative. Neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base gives about −57 kJ per mole of water.
- Hess's law: the total enthalpy change is the same whatever route is taken. ΔH(reaction) = ΣΔH(f, products) − ΣΔH(f, reactants).
> Example 1. C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −394 kJ/mol. CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283 kJ/mol. Find ΔH for C + ½O₂ → CO.
> Take the first equation and subtract the second: ΔH = −394 − (−283) = −111 kJ/mol.
## Chemical equilibrium
- At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stay constant (not necessarily equal).
- For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ ÷ [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ. Pure solids and liquids are left out. Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is the change in moles of gas.
- K changes only with temperature. Reversing the equation gives 1/K.

- Le Chatelier: a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose any change. Adding a reactant shifts it forward; raising pressure favours fewer gas moles; heating favours the endothermic direction. A catalyst does not shift the position; it only brings equilibrium sooner.
## Acids, bases and pH
- Arrhenius acids give H⁺ in water. Brønsted-Lowry acids donate protons; bases accept them. Lewis acids accept an electron pair (BF₃, AlCl₃); Lewis bases donate one (NH₃).
- pH = −log[H⁺]. At 25 °C, Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ and pH + pOH = 14.
- A buffer (a weak acid with its salt, or a weak base with its salt) resists changes in pH. pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]).
- Salts of a strong acid and a weak base (NH₄Cl) are acidic; salts of a weak acid and a strong base (CH₃COONa) are basic.
- Solubility product: a precipitate forms when the ionic product exceeds Ksp. For AgCl, Ksp = s².
> Example 2. Find the pH of 0.005 M H₂SO₄, assuming complete ionisation.
> Each H₂SO₄ gives 2 H⁺, so [H⁺] = 0.010 M = 10⁻² M and pH = 2.
## Chemical kinetics
- Rate = change in concentration per unit time. Rate law: rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ; the overall order is x + y and comes from experiment, not from the balanced equation.
- Units of k: zero order mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, first order s⁻¹, second order dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
- First-order half-life t½ = 0.693/k does not depend on the starting concentration. Radioactive decay is first order.
- Rate rises with concentration, temperature, surface area and a catalyst. A catalyst lowers the activation energy by giving a new path; it does not change ΔH or K.
> Example 3. A first-order reaction has k = 0.0693 min⁻¹. Find its half-life and the fraction left after 30 minutes.
> t½ = 0.693 ÷ 0.0693 = 10 min. 30 minutes is 3 half-lives, so (½)³ = ⅛ remains.
## Electrochemistry
- Oxidation is loss of electrons (oxidation number rises); reduction is gain of electrons. The oxidising agent is itself reduced.
- Oxidation number rules: elements 0; O usually −2 (−1 in peroxides); H usually +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); the sum equals the charge.

- In a galvanic cell chemical energy becomes electrical energy; the anode (oxidation) is negative. E°(cell) = E°(cathode) − E°(anode); a positive value means the reaction is feasible. Daniell cell: E° = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.
- In electrolysis the cathode is negative and reduction happens there. Faraday's laws: 1 F = 96,500 C is the charge on one mole of electrons; mass deposited = (M × Q) ÷ (n × F).
> Example 4. A charge of 0.5 F is passed through CuSO₄ solution. What mass of copper is deposited (Cu = 63.5)?
> Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so 0.5 F deposits 0.25 mol = 0.25 × 63.5 ≈ 15.9 g.
## Solutions
- Molarity = moles of solute per dm³ of solution; molality = moles of solute per kg of solvent; mole fraction = moles of one component ÷ total moles.
- Raoult's law: the vapour pressure of a solvent is proportional to its mole fraction. A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure.

- Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles, not their nature: lowering of vapour pressure, rise in boiling point (ΔT = Kb m), fall in freezing point (ΔT = Kf m) and osmotic pressure. NaCl counts as two particles per formula.
! A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally; it never changes the equilibrium yield.
! Order cannot be read from the coefficients of the balanced equation.
! The anode is negative in a galvanic cell but positive in an electrolytic cell; oxidation happens at the anode in both.
## Quick check
- Shape and bond angle of BF₃? (trigonal planar, 120°)
- pH of 0.001 M NaOH? (11)
- Effect of a catalyst on ΔH? (none)
- Charge on one mole of electrons? (96,500 C)
- Which has the larger freezing-point depression, 0.1 molal glucose or 0.1 molal NaCl? (NaCl)

title: Banking, Insurance and Transport
lines: This topic gives USAT-COM a steady supply of questions: bank functions and accounts, the central bank, cheques and their crossings, bills and notes under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Islamic modes of finance, the principles of insurance, and the merits of each mode of transport and kind of warehouse. Learn the definitions precisely; the distractors are usually the neighbouring term.
## Commercial banks

Primary functions: accepting deposits and advancing loans. Secondary functions are agency services (collecting cheques and dividends, paying bills on standing instructions, buying shares for customers) and general utility services (lockers, letters of credit, drafts, travellers' cheques).
| Account | Who uses it | Key point
| current | traders | unlimited cheque withdrawals; usually no return
| savings | individuals | encourages thrift; some limits on withdrawals
| fixed (term) | savers with spare funds | higher return; locked for a period
An overdraft lets a current-account holder draw beyond his balance up to a limit. When a bank lends, the money returns to banks as new deposits, so banks create credit.
## The central bank

The State Bank of Pakistan began working on 1 July 1948. It issues currency notes, is banker to the government and to the banks, acts as lender of last resort, keeps foreign exchange reserves and controls credit.
- To contract credit: raise the policy rate, sell securities in the open market, raise the cash reserve ratio.
- To expand credit: do the opposite.
## Negotiable instruments
| Instrument | Nature | Parties
| promissory note | promise to pay | maker, payee
| bill of exchange | order to pay | drawer, drawee, payee
| cheque | bill on a specified banker, payable on demand | drawer, bank, payee
A bill or note payable otherwise than on demand gets three days of grace. A holder in due course takes the instrument for value, in good faith and before maturity, and gets a good title.
Cheques: a bearer cheque is paid to whoever presents it; an order cheque to the named payee or his order. A post-dated cheque bears a future date; a stale cheque is presented too long after its date.
- General crossing: two parallel lines; payment only through a bank account.
- Special crossing: a bank's name in the crossing; payment only through that bank.
- "Not Negotiable": transferable, but the transferee gets no better title than the transferor.
- "Account Payee": collect only for the payee's own account.
Endorsements: blank (signature only, becomes bearer), special or full (names the endorsee), restrictive ("Pay Ali only"), sans recourse (endorser not liable).
