## Islamic modes of finance
- Mudarabah: one party gives capital, the other skill; profit by agreed ratio, financial loss on the capital provider.
- Musharakah: all partners give capital; profit by agreement, loss by capital ratio.
- Murabahah: cost-plus sale with the profit disclosed.
- Ijarah: leasing; the bank keeps ownership.
- Salam: full price in advance, goods later. Istisna: order to manufacture.
## Insurance
Insurance spreads the loss of a few over many. The insured pays a premium; the policy is the contract.
- Utmost good faith: disclose all material facts.
- Insurable interest: you must stand to lose money from the loss.
- Indemnity: restore the insured to his position before the loss, no profit; it does not apply to life insurance.
- Contribution: with double insurance, insurers share the loss in proportion to their sums insured.
- Subrogation: after paying, the insurer takes over the insured's rights against others.
- Proximate cause: the nearest effective cause must be an insured risk.

Life policies: whole life (pays on death), endowment (pays at maturity or on earlier death), term (pays only if death occurs within the term). Reinsurance is an insurer insuring part of its risk with another insurer. In marine insurance, a sacrifice for the common safety is a general average loss shared by all; accidental partial damage is particular average, borne by its owner.
## Transport and warehousing
| Mode | Best for
| road | short distances, door-to-door, flexible
| rail | heavy goods over long distances on land
| water | cheapest for bulky goods; slow
| air | fastest; perishable or valuable goods
| pipeline | oil and gas

Liners keep fixed routes and timetables; tramps go wherever cargo is. Warehouses remove the hindrance of time, steady prices and help finance. A bonded warehouse holds imported goods before duty is paid; cold storage keeps perishables. A warehouse warrant is a document of title; a warehouse keeper's receipt is only an acknowledgement.
## Worked examples
> A bill dated 20 March is payable one month after date.
> One month after date: 20 April. Add 3 days of grace: maturity 23 April.
> Sara insures goods for Rs. 300,000 with A and Rs. 200,000 with B; loss Rs. 100,000.
> Ratio 3 : 2, so A pays Rs. 60,000 and B pays Rs. 40,000. Sara receives only her actual loss.
> A cheque crossed with "Meezan Bank" between the lines.
> This is a special crossing: the paying bank pays only through Meezan Bank.
## Traps
! "Not Negotiable" does not stop transfer; it removes protection of title.
! Indemnity does not apply to life insurance.
! An overdraft is for current-account holders, not a loan on a fixed deposit.
! Cheques get no days of grace: they are payable on demand.
## Quick check
- Which crossing names a bank? (special crossing)
- Who are the parties to a promissory note? (maker and payee)
- Which principle lets an insurer recover from the wrongdoer? (subrogation)
- Which warehouse stores goods before customs duty is paid? (bonded warehouse)

title: Marketing, Office and Communication
lines: The last Commerce topic mixes four areas: marketing and advertising, the stock exchange, office work and filing, and business communication. USAT-COM questions here are mostly about terms: the four Ps, stages of the product life cycle, bulls and bears, methods of filing, and the parts and kinds of business letters. One clear definition per term is enough to answer most of them.
## Marketing

Marketing is every activity that moves goods from producer to consumer and satisfies the buyer's needs at a profit. Its functions include buying, selling, transport, storage, standardisation and grading, financing, risk bearing and market information.
The marketing mix (the four Ps):
- Product: design, quality, brand and packaging.
- Price: the pricing policy.
- Place: channels of distribution through wholesalers and retailers.
- Promotion: advertising, personal selling, sales promotion and publicity.

A brand is a name, sign or symbol that identifies a product; a registered brand is a trademark. Grading sorts goods into classes of similar quality. Market research collects and studies information about buyers and rivals.
Pricing: skimming starts high for buyers willing to pay more, then lowers; penetration starts low to win market share fast.
| Life-cycle stage | Sales | Typical action
| introduction | low, slow growth | heavy promotion; profits low or negative
| growth | rising fast | profits rise; rivals enter
| maturity | at peak | strong competition; price pressure
| decline | falling | cut costs or withdraw
## Advertising and promotion

Advertising is paid, non-personal communication that informs and persuades. Publicity is unpaid and not controlled by the firm. Media include the press, radio, television, outdoor (billboards), direct mail and the internet. Sales promotion uses short-term incentives: free samples, coupons, contests, discounts.
A good advertisement follows AIDA: attention, interest, desire, action.
## The stock exchange

A stock exchange is an organised market for buying and selling existing securities. It gives investors liquidity, helps value securities and channels savings into industry. The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) was formed in January 2016 by merging the Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad exchanges; the SECP regulates it.
- Primary market: new issues sold by the company itself (for example an IPO).
- Secondary market: existing securities traded between investors.
- Listed securities are admitted to trading on the exchange. A broker trades for clients on commission.
| Speculator | Expects | Does
| bull | prices to rise | buys now, sells later
| bear | prices to fall | sells now, buys back later
| stag | quick premium on new issues | applies for new shares to sell soon
| lame duck | (a bear in trouble) | cannot meet his commitments
Market value is the price on the exchange; face value is printed on the share.
## The office and filing

An office receives, records, arranges and supplies information, and safeguards records. Incoming letters go in the inward mail register, letters sent in the outward mail register; letters delivered by hand are signed for in the peon book. A franking machine prints postage; a shredder destroys confidential papers.
Filing keeps records so they can be found quickly.
- Alphabetical: by first letters of names; simplest and most common.
- Numerical: each correspondent has a number; needs a card index.
- Geographical: by area, such as province then city.
- Subject: by topic. Chronological: by date.

Centralised filing keeps all records in one department; decentralised filing leaves them with each department. An index guides the user to the right file. Microfilm or scanning saves space while keeping records available.
## Business communication

Communication can be oral, written or non-verbal (gestures, expressions). In direction it is downward (orders), upward (reports, suggestions) or horizontal (between equals). The grapevine is the informal rumour network. Barriers include jargon, noise, poor listening and emotional states. A good message is clear, concise, complete, correct and courteous.

Parts of a business letter: letterhead, date, reference, inside address, salutation, subject line, body, complimentary close, signature and enclosures. In British usage, "Dear Sir" pairs with "Yours faithfully", while "Dear Mr Raza" pairs with "Yours sincerely".
| Letter | Purpose
| enquiry | ask for prices, terms or samples
| order | ask for goods on stated terms
| complaint | report a problem with goods or service
| adjustment | reply to a complaint and settle it
| collection | ask for payment of an overdue account
| status enquiry | ask about a customer's creditworthiness
| circular | one message to many readers
Inside a firm, a memo replaces a letter. For meetings, the notice gives date, time and place; the agenda lists the business; the minutes record what was decided.
## Worked examples
> A trader thinks share prices will fall next week, so he sells shares now.
> He is a bear. If prices rise instead and he cannot deliver, he becomes a lame duck.
> A company with branches in every province arranges files first by province, then by city.
> This is geographical filing; within each city, files may be alphabetical.
> A letter begins "Dear Sir" and ends "Yours sincerely".
> In British usage the close should be "Yours faithfully"; "Yours sincerely" follows a named salutation.
## Traps
! Publicity is free; advertising is paid. Do not confuse the two.
! A stag deals in new issues, not existing shares.
! Numerical filing needs an index; alphabetical filing usually does not.
! The agenda comes before a meeting, the minutes after it.
## Quick check
- What does AIDA stand for? (attention, interest, desire, action)
- In which life-cycle stage are sales at their peak? (maturity)
- Who expects prices to rise? (a bull)
- Which letter answers a complaint? (letter of adjustment)

title: Forms of Business Organisation
lines: USAT-COM questions on business organisation test whether you can tell the forms apart: who owns, who controls, how far the owners are liable, and which document governs the business. Expect questions on kinds of partners, company documents, kinds of shares and capital, cooperative principles and types of public enterprise. Most wrong options are true of a different form of business, so compare the forms side by side.
## Sole proprietorship

One person supplies the capital, manages, takes all the profit and bears all the loss. It is easy to start, decisions are quick, the owner keeps personal contact with customers and business secrets stay private.
- Liability is unlimited: the owner's private property can be taken to pay business debts.
- Capital and managing ability are limited to one person.
- The business has no separate legal existence; it may end with the owner's death or illness.
## Partnership

In Pakistan partnerships are governed by the Partnership Act, 1932. A partnership is the relation between persons who agree to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. So at least two persons are needed, and each partner is an agent of the firm and of the others (mutual agency).
- The partnership deed records capital, profit-sharing ratio, salaries, interest and duties.
- If the deed is silent, profits and losses are shared equally.
- Liability is unlimited and joint and several: a creditor can recover the whole debt from any partner.
- Registration is optional, but an unregistered firm cannot sue outsiders to enforce its contracts.
- A new partner can be admitted only with the consent of all partners.
| Kind of partner | Capital | Manages | Known to public
| active (working) | yes | yes | yes
| sleeping (dormant) | yes | no | usually not
| nominal | no | no | yes, lends his name
| secret | yes | yes | no

A minor cannot be a full partner, but with all partners' consent he can be admitted to the benefits of partnership; his liability is limited to his share in the firm. A partnership at will has no fixed period and can be dissolved by notice. Dissolution is compulsory when all, or all but one, partners become insolvent or the business becomes unlawful.
## Joint stock company

A company is an artificial person created by registration under the companies law; in Pakistan, the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) registers and regulates companies. Its features:
- separate legal entity: it owns property, sues and is sued in its own name;
- perpetual succession: members may change or die, the company continues;
- limited liability: a shareholder can lose at most the unpaid amount on his shares;
- management by elected directors, not by all members;
- transferable shares in a public company.
A private company restricts the transfer of its shares and cannot invite the public to buy them; a public company can, through a prospectus.
## Company documents and doctrines
| Document | Purpose
| memorandum of association | charter: name, registered office, objects, liability, capital; relations with outsiders
| articles of association | internal rules: meetings, directors, voting, transfer of shares
| certificate of incorporation | the company is born on its date
| prospectus | invites the public to buy shares or debentures
- Ultra vires: an act beyond the objects in the memorandum is void and cannot be ratified even by all members.
- Constructive notice: outsiders are presumed to know the memorandum and articles.
- Indoor management: outsiders acting in good faith may assume internal procedures were followed.
## Shares, debentures and capital
- Ordinary shareholders own the company, vote, and receive a dividend that varies with profit.
- Preference shareholders receive a fixed dividend before ordinary shareholders and are repaid capital first on winding up. Cumulative preference dividends unpaid in a bad year are carried forward.
- Debenture holders are creditors who receive fixed interest whether or not there is a profit.
- Bonus shares are free, issued from reserves. Right shares are offered first to existing members and paid for.
Capital: authorised (maximum in the memorandum) → issued → subscribed → called-up → paid-up (called-up less calls in arrears). Reserve capital can be called only on winding up.
An ordinary resolution needs a simple majority; a special resolution needs at least three-fourths of the votes cast.
## Cooperatives and public enterprises

A cooperative society is a voluntary association for mutual service. Principles: open membership, one member one vote, democratic management by an elected committee, limited return on capital, and surplus shared by patronage. Types include consumers', producers', credit, marketing and housing societies.

Public enterprises are owned by the state: a departmental undertaking is run by a ministry and financed by the budget; a statutory (public) corporation is created by a special Act and is a separate legal person; a government company is registered under the companies law with the state holding a majority of shares.
## Worked examples
> A company issues 50,000 shares of Rs. 10, calls Rs. 7, and Rs. 3 is unpaid on 2,000 shares.
> Called-up = 50,000 × 7 = Rs. 350,000. Calls in arrears = 2,000 × 3 = Rs. 6,000.
> Paid-up = Rs. 344,000.
> Asad invests in a firm but never visits the office.
> He is a sleeping partner and still has unlimited liability for the firm's debts.
## Traps
! Sharing profits in the capital ratio applies only if agreed; the default is equal sharing.
! Mutual agency is a feature of partnership, not of a company.
! A debenture holder is a creditor, not an owner.
! "One share, one vote" is the company rule; cooperatives use one member, one vote.
## Quick check
- Which document governs a company's internal management? (articles of association)
- Which partner lends only his name? (nominal partner)
- What majority does a special resolution need? (three-fourths of votes cast)
- Which public enterprise is created by its own Act? (statutory corporation)

title: Commerce and Trade
lines: USAT-COM asks about 10 Commerce questions in all, and several come from this topic. Expect short definition questions (what is entrepot trade, what does a debit note do), questions that match an aid to trade with the hindrance it removes, and one or two small discount calculations. Learn the exact meaning of each term: wrong options are usually real terms used in the wrong place.
## Commerce, trade and industry
Industry makes goods; commerce gets them to the people who want them. Commerce has two parts: trade (buying and selling) and the aids to trade that make trade possible.
- Extractive industry takes wealth from nature: mining, fishing, quarrying.
- Genetic industry breeds and rears living things: poultry farms, cattle breeding, plant nurseries.
- Manufacturing turns raw materials into finished goods: a Faisalabad mill making cloth from cotton.
- Construction builds roads, bridges, dams and buildings.

Before money, people used barter: goods exchanged directly for goods. Its main weakness was the lack of double coincidence of wants, since each side must want exactly what the other has. Money removed this problem.
## Hindrances and aids to trade
Each aid to trade removes one hindrance. This table is asked again and again.
| Hindrance | Removed by
| persons (producer and consumer do not meet) | trade: wholesalers and retailers
| place (distance) | transport
| time (produced now, used later) | warehousing
| risk (fire, theft, loss at sea) | insurance
| finance (shortage of money) | banking
| knowledge (buyers do not know about goods) | advertising and communication
! Insurance does not remove risk; it spreads the financial loss of a few among the many who pay premiums.
## Home trade and foreign trade
Home trade happens inside one country. It is divided into wholesale and retail trade.
- The wholesaler buys in bulk from producers, stores goods, breaks bulk and sells to retailers, often on credit. He relieves producers of storage and finding many small buyers.
- The retailer is the last link: he sells small quantities to consumers.

- Itinerant retailers (hawkers, pedlars) have no fixed shop. Fixed-shop retailers include general stores, single-line stores, departmental stores (many departments, one building, one management), multiple or chain shops (many branches, one owner, uniform goods and prices), supermarkets (self-service) and mail-order houses (catalogue or online orders, goods delivered).

Foreign trade crosses national borders: import trade (buying from abroad), export trade (selling abroad) and entrepot trade (importing in order to re-export to a third country). The balance of trade compares exports and imports of goods only; the balance of payments includes services, remittances and capital flows too.
## Middlemen
- A broker brings buyer and seller together but never holds the goods.
- A factor holds the goods and may sell them in his own name.
- A commission agent is paid a percentage of the business he arranges.
- A del credere agent guarantees that the buyers he finds will pay, for an extra commission.
- An auctioneer sells to the highest bidder in public.
## Documents of trade
| Document | Sent by and purpose
| enquiry | buyer asks for prices and terms
| quotation | seller states prices and terms
| order | buyer asks for goods on stated terms
| invoice | seller lists goods sent and amount due
| pro forma invoice | seller, before a sale; demands no payment
| debit note | seller, to increase the buyer's debt (undercharge)
| credit note | seller, to reduce the buyer's debt (returns, overcharge)
| statement of account | seller, periodic summary and balance due
"E. & O.E." on an invoice means errors and omissions excepted. Trade discount is deducted from list price for traders; cash discount is for prompt payment and is calculated after trade discount.

In foreign trade: an indent is an import order through an agent (open indent: agent chooses the supplier; closed indent: supplier named). The mate's receipt is given on loading and exchanged for the bill of lading, which is the receipt, contract of carriage and document of title for goods sent by sea. A charter party hires a whole ship. A letter of credit is a bank's undertaking to pay the exporter against documents. A certificate of origin shows where goods were made; a consular invoice is certified by the importing country's consul. The importer clears goods with a bill of entry, the exporter with a shipping bill.
## Price terms
- Loco price: at the seller's premises; the buyer pays all carriage.
- F.O.B.: the seller pays costs until goods are on board the ship.
- C.I.F.: cost, insurance and freight to the port of destination.
- Franco price: all costs up to the buyer's premises.
## Worked examples
> List price Rs. 50,000, trade discount 20 %, cash discount 2 %. Buyer pays promptly.
> After trade discount: 50,000 × 0.80 = 40,000.
> Cash discount: 2 % of 40,000 = 800.
> A Karachi trader imports tea from Kenya and sells it to Afghanistan.
> The goods enter and leave Pakistan without being produced here, so this is entrepot (re-export) trade, not export trade.
> A seller charged Rs. 1,000 too little on an invoice.
> The buyer must pay more, so the seller sends a debit note. If he had charged too much, he would send a credit note.
## Traps
! The quotation comes from the seller and the order from the buyer; do not swap them.
! The mate's receipt is not a document of title; the bill of lading is.
! Successive discounts are not added: 10 % and 5 % make 14.5 %, not 15 %.
## Quick check
- Which aid to trade removes the hindrance of time? (warehousing)
- Who keeps the goods: a broker or a factor? (factor)
- What does a C.I.F. price include? (cost, insurance and freight to the destination port)
- Which document is exchanged for the bill of lading? (mate's receipt)

title: Database Fundamentals
lines: USAT-CS database questions test terms (table, record, field, keys), relationships, normal forms and basic SQL. A common type gives a small table and a query and asks what the query returns, so practise reading SELECT statements row by row.
## Why a database?

A database is an organised collection of related data. A database management system (DBMS), such as MySQL, Oracle or MS Access, stores, retrieves and protects it. Compared with separate files, a DBMS reduces duplicated data (redundancy) and inconsistency, allows sharing, and gives better security and data independence: programs keep working when the storage details change.
## Terms
| Term | Meaning
| Table (relation) | data about one kind of thing, in rows and columns
| Record (row, tuple) | all the data about one item
| Field (column, attribute) | one property, such as Name or City
| Entity | a thing data is kept about, such as Student or Course
| Degree | number of columns in a table
| Cardinality (of a table) | number of rows
| Domain | the set of allowed values for a field
- The relational model, proposed by E. F. Codd, stores data in tables. Other models are hierarchical (tree), network and object-oriented.
- In an ER diagram an entity is a rectangle, an attribute an ellipse and a relationship a diamond.
## Keys
| Key | Meaning
| Super key | any set of fields that identifies each row uniquely
| Candidate key | a minimal super key: no field can be removed
| Primary key | the candidate key chosen; unique and never NULL
| Alternate key | a candidate key that was not chosen
| Composite key | a key made of two or more fields together
| Foreign key | a field that matches the primary key of another table
- Entity integrity: a primary key value can never be NULL.
- Referential integrity: every foreign key value must match an existing primary key value (or be NULL).
! Name is a poor key because two people can share a name. A foreign key value may repeat; a primary key value may not.
## Relationships
- One-to-one (1:1): one person has one CNIC number.
- One-to-many (1:M): one department has many employees, but each employee is in one department. The foreign key goes in the "many" table (Employee holds DeptID).

- Many-to-many (M:N): a student takes many courses and a course has many students. It is built with a linking table, such as Enrolment(StudentID, CourseID, Grade), whose primary key is the composite (StudentID, CourseID).
## Normalisation
Normalisation splits tables to remove redundancy and the insertion, update and deletion anomalies it causes.
| Normal form | Rule
| 1NF | every cell holds one atomic value; no repeating groups
| 2NF | 1NF, and no non-key field depends on only part of a composite key
| 3NF | 2NF, and no non-key field depends on another non-key field (no transitive dependency)
> Enrolment(StudentID, CourseID, CourseTitle, Grade) has the key (StudentID, CourseID). Which normal form does it break, and how is it fixed?
> CourseTitle depends on CourseID alone, which is only part of the key: a partial dependency.
> The table breaks 2NF. Fix: move CourseTitle into Course(CourseID, CourseTitle) and keep Enrolment(StudentID, CourseID, Grade).
> Student(RollNo, Name, DeptID, DeptName) has the key RollNo. What is wrong?
> DeptName depends on DeptID, which is not a key: RollNo → DeptID → DeptName is a transitive dependency.
> The table breaks 3NF. Fix: Department(DeptID, DeptName) and Student(RollNo, Name, DeptID).
- A functional dependency X → Y means one value of X fixes one value of Y, as in RollNo → Name.
## SQL basics
| Group | Commands
| DDL (definition) | CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
| DML (manipulation) | SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
| DCL (control) | GRANT, REVOKE
- SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY column; ORDER BY sorts ascending unless DESC is written.
- Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(column) and AVG skip NULL values.
- GROUP BY makes one result row per group. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping.
- BETWEEN 60 AND 80 includes both 60 and 80. IN ('Lahore', 'Multan') matches any value in the list. IS NULL finds empty fields; = NULL does not work.
- LIKE patterns: % matches any number of characters and _ matches exactly one. LIKE 'S%' finds names starting with S; LIKE '_a%' finds names whose second letter is a.
- INSERT INTO Student VALUES (6, 'Iqra', 'Sialkot', 77); adds a row. UPDATE Student SET Marks = 80 WHERE RollNo = 2; changes a row. DELETE FROM Student WHERE RollNo = 4; removes a row.
- DELETE removes rows but keeps the table; DROP TABLE removes the table and its structure.
- A join combines tables on a matching key: SELECT EName, DName FROM Emp, Dept WHERE Emp.DID = Dept.DID;
Use this table for the examples. Student(RollNo, Name, City, Marks):
| RollNo | Name | City | Marks
| 1 | Hina | Multan | 72
| 2 | Usman | Lahore | 58
| 3 | Sana | Lahore | 85
| 4 | Ali | Quetta | 64
| 5 | Fahad | Multan | 91
> SELECT Name FROM Student WHERE City = 'Lahore' AND Marks > 60;
> Lahore rows: Usman (58) and Sana (85). Only Sana has Marks above 60.
> Result: Sana
> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Student WHERE Marks BETWEEN 64 AND 85;
> 72, 85 and 64 fall in the range; BETWEEN includes both ends.
> Result: 3
> SELECT City, AVG(Marks) FROM Student GROUP BY City HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
> Groups: Multan (72, 91), Lahore (58, 85), Quetta (64). Quetta has only one row and is dropped by HAVING.
> Result: Multan 81.5 and Lahore 71.5
! WHERE cannot use an aggregate such as AVG(Marks) > 70; that condition belongs in HAVING, after GROUP BY.
## Quick check
- Which key links a table to another table's primary key? (foreign key)
- Which normal form removes transitive dependencies? (3NF)
- Is SELECT a DDL or a DML command? (DML)
- Which wildcard matches exactly one character in SQL? (_)
- Which clause filters groups? (HAVING)
- Number of columns in a table is its…? (degree)

title: Computer Fundamentals
lines: This is the largest topic in USAT-CS. Expect questions on the parts of a computer and what each does, types of memory, number conversions (binary, octal, hexadecimal), two's complement, character codes, kinds of software and translators, operating system jobs, and everyday office tasks such as copying spreadsheet formulas.
## Hardware and the processing cycle
- Input devices: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, webcam, barcode reader. Output devices: monitor, printer, speaker, plotter (large drawings). A touchscreen is both input and output.
- The CPU has an arithmetic logic unit (ALU), which does arithmetic and comparisons, and a control unit (CU), which fetches and decodes instructions and sends control signals.

- Registers are tiny, very fast stores inside the CPU: the program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction; the instruction register (IR) holds the current one; MAR and MDR hold a memory address and the data moving to or from it.
- The machine (instruction) cycle is fetch → decode → execute.
- Buses: the address bus carries addresses from the CPU to memory (one way); the data bus carries data both ways; the control bus carries signals such as read, write and clock.
- An n-bit address bus can reach 2ⁿ memory locations. Clock speed is measured in hertz (GHz for modern processors).
## Memory and storage
| Type | Volatile? | Notes
| RAM | yes | main memory for running programs; read and write
| ROM | no | holds the start-up (boot) program; normally read only
| Cache | yes | small, fast SRAM between the CPU and RAM
| Secondary storage | no | hard disk, SSD, USB flash drive, CD/DVD, magnetic tape
- Speed from fastest to slowest: registers → cache → RAM → secondary storage. Cost per byte falls in the same order.
- PROM can be written once; EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light; EEPROM and flash memory are erased electrically.
- Magnetic tape allows only sequential access, so finding one record in the middle is slow; disks allow direct (random) access.
- Units: 1 nibble = 4 bits; 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KB = 1,024 bytes; 1 MB = 1,024 KB; then GB, TB.
## Number systems
| System | Base | Digits
| Binary | 2 | 0, 1
| Octal | 8 | 0-7
| Decimal | 10 | 0-9
| Hexadecimal | 16 | 0-9 and A-F (A = 10 … F = 15)
- Binary to decimal: add the place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 under each 1.
- Decimal to binary: divide by 2 repeatedly and read the remainders from bottom to top.
- Binary to octal: group bits in threes from the right. Binary to hexadecimal: group bits in fours from the right.
> Convert decimal 58 to binary, octal and hexadecimal.
> Hexadecimal: 0011 | 1010 → 3 A, so (3A)₁₆. Check: 3 × 16 + 10 = 58.
## Negative numbers and characters
- In two's complement, a negative number is made by inverting all bits of the positive number and adding 1. The leftmost bit is the sign bit: 1 means negative.
- An 8-bit two's complement number ranges from −128 to +127.
> Write −6 in 8-bit two's complement.
> Invert every bit: 11111001.
- ASCII is a 7-bit code with 128 characters: 'A' = 65, 'a' = 97, '0' = 48. Extended ASCII uses 8 bits (256 characters). Unicode gives codes to the characters of nearly all languages, including Urdu.
! Group bits from the right, not the left, and pad the leftmost group with 0s. 1101 is (D)₁₆, but 11010 is 0001 1010 = (1A)₁₆.
## Software
- System software runs the computer: the operating system, utility programs (antivirus, disk defragmenter, backup, file compression) and language translators.
- Application software does a user's task: word processor, spreadsheet, web browser, accounting package.

- Translators: an assembler turns assembly language into machine code; a compiler translates the whole high-level program at once and lists errors at the end; an interpreter translates and runs one line at a time and stops at the first error.
- Levels of language: machine language (binary) and assembly language are low level; C, C++, Java and Python are high level.
## Operating systems

- Jobs of the OS: process management (which program gets the CPU), memory management, file management, device management through drivers, security (user accounts and permissions), and the user interface (GUI or command line).
- Types: single-user, multi-user, batch, real-time (controls machines that must respond at once), and time-sharing.
- In Windows, files deleted from the hard disk go to the Recycle Bin and can be restored until it is emptied. Files deleted from a USB flash drive are normally removed for good.
- Cut and Paste moves a file; Copy and Paste duplicates it.
## Office basics

- Word processor: Find and Replace changes words throughout a document; Mail Merge combines one letter with a data list to make a copy for each person; a page break starts a new page; justified alignment lines text up with both margins.
- Spreadsheet: formulas start with =. When a formula is copied, relative references shift by the same rows and columns; a $ sign fixes the column or row written after it.
> Cell C1 holds =A1*B$1. It is copied to D3. What formula appears in D3?
> The move is 1 column right and 2 rows down.
> A1 becomes B3. In B$1 the column shifts (B → C) but the row is fixed, giving C$1.
> D3 holds =B3*C$1.
! A $ fixes only what directly follows it: $A1 fixes column A, A$1 fixes row 1, $A$1 fixes both.
## Quick check
- Which register holds the address of the next instruction? (program counter)
- Which memory loses its data when power is off? (RAM)
- (101101)₂ in decimal? (45)
- (2F)₁₆ in decimal? (47)
- How many locations can a 16-bit address bus reach? (65,536)
- Which translator runs a program line by line? (interpreter)

title: Networks, Internet and Security
lines: USAT-CS asks about network types and topologies, devices and the OSI layer each works at, protocols and addresses, transmission media and modes, how the internet and web work, and computer security and ethics. Many questions are definitions; a few ask you to count links, name an IP class or apply a simple cipher.
## Network types and topologies
- PAN: a few metres around one person (Bluetooth). LAN: a room, building or campus. MAN: a city. WAN: a country or the world; the internet is the largest WAN.
- Client-server: a central server provides files, mail or web pages to clients. Peer-to-peer: all computers are equal and share directly.
| Topology | Layout | Weak point
| Bus | all nodes on one backbone cable with terminators | a backbone break stops the network
| Star | every node joined to a central switch or hub | if the centre fails, all fail
| Ring | each node joined to two neighbours in a loop | one break can stop the ring
| Mesh | every node joined to every other | costly; uses the most cable
| Tree | star networks joined in a hierarchy | a fault high up cuts off a branch
> How many cables does a full mesh of 8 computers need?
> Each pair needs one link: n(n − 1) ÷ 2.
## Devices
| Device | Job | OSI layer
| Repeater | regenerates a weak signal on a long cable | 1 Physical
| Hub | sends incoming data to every port | 1 Physical
| Switch | sends a frame only to the port of the destination MAC address | 2 Data link
| Bridge | joins two LAN segments | 2 Data link
| Router | joins different networks and chooses a path by IP address | 3 Network
| Gateway | joins networks that use different protocols | up to 7
- A network interface card (NIC) connects a computer to a network and has a unique 48-bit MAC address.
- A modem converts digital signals to analogue (modulation) and back (demodulation).
## The OSI and TCP/IP models

The OSI reference model has 7 layers, from 1 to 7: Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. On the sending computer data moves down from layer 7 to layer 1; on the receiving computer it moves up.

- Physical: bits on the medium. Data link: frames and MAC addresses. Network: IP addresses and routing. Transport: end-to-end delivery (TCP, UDP). Session: opens and closes a conversation. Presentation: format, encryption, compression. Application: services for the user.
- TCP/IP, the model the internet uses, has 4 layers: application, transport, internet, network access (link).
- TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: it numbers packets and resends lost ones. UDP is faster but does not guarantee delivery; it suits live video and voice.
| Protocol | Use | Usual port
| HTTP / HTTPS | web pages / secure web pages | 80 / 443
| FTP | file transfer | 20, 21
| SMTP | sending e-mail | 25
| POP3 / IMAP | receiving e-mail | 110 / 143
| DNS | turns a domain name into an IP address | 53
| DHCP | gives a device an IP address automatically | 67, 68
## Addresses

- IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers from 0 to 255, such as 192.168.1.20. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written in hexadecimal groups, and were introduced because IPv4 addresses were running out.
- IPv4 classes by first octet: A 1-126, B 128-191, C 192-223, D 224-239 (multicast), E 240-255 (experimental). 127 is kept for loopback testing.
> To which class does the address 172.16.5.4 belong?
> The first octet is 172, which lies in 128-191.
> It is a class B address.
## Transmission
- Simplex: one way only (TV broadcast). Half duplex: both ways but one at a time (walkie-talkie). Full duplex: both ways at once (telephone call).

- Twisted pair cable is cheap and used in LANs; coaxial cable is shielded and used for cable TV; fibre-optic cable carries light, has the highest bandwidth and is not affected by electrical interference.
- Wireless media: radio waves (Wi-Fi), microwaves (line of sight), infrared (short range), satellites.
- Modulation changes a carrier wave's amplitude (AM), frequency (FM) or phase (PM) to carry data.
- Bandwidth is the data rate a channel can carry, in bits per second. Frequency is 1 ÷ time period, in hertz.
- Circuit switching keeps a dedicated path for the whole call (old telephone). Packet switching splits data into packets that may take different routes (the internet).
## The internet and the web
- The internet is a worldwide network of networks. The World Wide Web, invented by Tim Berners-Lee, is a service on it: pages written in HTML and linked by hyperlinks.
- A URL gives a resource's full address: in https://www.example.com/admissions/form.html, https is the protocol, www.example.com the domain name and /admissions/form.html the path.
- A browser displays web pages; a search engine finds them; an internet service provider (ISP) gives you the connection. "https" means the link is encrypted.
## Security
| Threat | What it does
| Virus | attaches to a file and spreads when that file runs
| Worm | copies itself across a network without a host file
| Trojan horse | looks useful but hides harm; does not copy itself
| Spyware | secretly records what the user does
| Ransomware | encrypts files and demands payment
| Phishing | fake messages trick users into giving passwords or card details
- Protection: antivirus software, a firewall (filters traffic by rules), strong passwords, two-factor authentication, updates and regular backups.
- Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext using a key. In symmetric encryption one key locks and unlocks; in public-key (asymmetric) encryption a public key encrypts and a private key decrypts.
> A Caesar cipher shifts every letter 3 places forward (A → D). Encrypt the word CAB.
> C → F, A → D, B → E.
> The ciphertext is FDE. To decrypt, shift each letter 3 places back.
## Ethics and software licences

- Copyright protects original work such as programs, books and music. Software piracy is copying or selling software without a licence. Plagiarism is passing off someone else's work as your own. Hacking is entering a system without permission.

- Freeware is free to use but its code is not open; shareware is free for a trial period, then must be paid for; open-source software lets anyone read and change the code; proprietary software is owned and licensed by a company.
- Netiquette: be polite, do not type whole sentences in capitals (it reads as shouting), and respect others' privacy.
! A hub sends data to every port; a switch sends it only to the destination. A router, not a switch, joins different networks.
! A virus needs a host file; a worm does not. A Trojan does not replicate itself.
## Quick check
- How many layers does the OSI model have? (7)
- At which layer does a router work? (network, layer 3)
- How many bits in an IPv4 address? (32)
- Which protocol sends e-mail? (SMTP)
- A walkie-talkie uses which mode? (half duplex)
- Software free for a trial and then paid for? (shareware)

title: Programming Fundamentals
lines: USAT-CS programming questions are mostly short C or C++ fragments: "What is the output?" Others ask about data types, operators, loops, arrays, functions, flowchart symbols and kinds of error. The key skill is tracing: follow the code line by line and write down every variable's value as it changes, exactly as the computer would.
## Algorithms and flowcharts
An algorithm is a finite, ordered list of clear steps that solves a problem. It can be written as pseudocode or drawn as a flowchart.
| Flowchart symbol | Meaning
| Oval (terminal) | start or stop
| Parallelogram | input or output
| Rectangle | process, such as a calculation
| Diamond | decision with yes/no branches
| Arrow (flow line) | order of steps
## Structure of a C/C++ program
- #include <stdio.h> brings in printf and scanf in C; #include <iostream> brings in cin and cout in C++.
- Every program starts running from main(). Each statement ends with a semicolon; a block is enclosed in braces { }.
- Comments: // to the end of the line, or /* … */ over several lines.
- Identifiers (names) use letters, digits and the underscore, must not start with a digit, must not be a keyword such as int or while, and are case sensitive: total and Total are different.
| Type | Holds | Example
| int | whole numbers | int n = 25;
| float | real numbers, single precision | float r = 2.5;
| double | real numbers, double precision | double d = 3.14159;
| char | one character, in single quotes | char g = 'A';
| bool (C++) | true or false | bool ok = true;
A char takes 1 byte. The size of int depends on the compiler: 2 bytes in old Turbo C, 4 bytes in modern compilers.
## Input and output
- C: printf("%d", n); prints an int; %f a float; %c a char; %s a string; \n starts a new line. scanf("%d", &n); reads an int; the & gives the variable's address.
- C++: cout << n << endl; prints; cin >> n; reads.
## Operators
- Arithmetic: + − * / %. When both operands are integers, / drops the fraction: 7 / 2 is 3. The % operator gives the remainder: 7 % 2 is 1.
- Relational: < <= > >= == !=. Logical: && (and), || (or), ! (not). A true condition has the value 1, false is 0, and any non-zero value counts as true.
- Assignment: =, +=, −=, *=, /=. x += 3 means x = x + 3.
- Precedence, high to low: ( ), unary (! ++ --), * / %, + −, relational, == !=, &&, ||, assignment. Operators of equal rank, such as * and /, are worked left to right.
- ++x increases x first and then uses it (pre-increment); x++ uses the old value and then increases x (post-increment).
> int a = 7, b = 2;
> printf("%d %d", a / b, a % b);
> Both are int, so 7 / 2 = 3 (fraction dropped) and 7 % 2 = 1.
> Output: 3 1
> int x = 5;
> int y = x++ * 2;
> printf("%d %d", x, y);
> x++ gives the old value 5 to the expression, so y = 5 × 2 = 10; then x becomes 6.
> Output: 6 10
! 5 / 2 * 2.0 gives 4.0, not 5.0: 5 / 2 is worked first as integer division (2), and only then multiplied by 2.0.
## Decisions
- if (condition) { … } else { … }. An else pairs with the nearest unmatched if.
- if (x = 5) assigns 5 to x and is always true; the comparison is written if (x == 5).
- switch (n) jumps to the matching case label; without break, execution falls through into the following cases. case labels must be integer or character constants.
- The conditional operator: big = (a > b) ? a : b; is a short if-else.
> int k = 1;
> switch (k) {
>     case 1: cout << "A";
>     case 2: cout << "B"; break;
>     case 3: cout << "C";
> k is 1, so execution starts at case 1 and prints A. There is no break, so it falls into case 2 and prints B; the break then leaves the switch.
> Output: AB
## Loops
- for (start; condition; update) { … } is best when the number of repetitions is known. for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) runs n times.
- while (condition) { … } tests first, so the body may run zero times.
- do { … } while (condition); tests last, so the body runs at least once. Note the semicolon after while( ).
- break leaves the loop at once; continue skips the rest of this round and goes to the next.
> int s = 0, i;
> printf("%d %d", s, i);
> After 7, i becomes 9, the test 9 <= 7 fails and the loop ends.
> Output: 16 9
! A semicolon straight after for ( … ); makes an empty loop body. The loop runs on its own, and the next statement runs only once, afterwards.
## Arrays and strings
- int a[5]; reserves 5 ints with indexes 0 to 4. a[5] is outside the array; C does not check this, so the result is unpredictable.
- An array can be set when declared: int a[4] = {2, 4, 6, 8};
- A string in C is a char array ending in the null character '\0'. char s[] = "pak"; uses 4 bytes: p, a, k and '\0'.
> int i, t = 0;
> printf("%d", t);
> Output: 12
## Functions
- A function is a named block that does one job. Its prototype, such as int sq(int);, ends with a semicolon and tells the compiler its name, return type and parameter types.
- Parameters appear in the definition; arguments are the values passed in the call.

- C passes arguments by value: the function works on a copy, so changes inside it do not affect the caller's variable. To change the caller's variable, pass its address (a pointer) or, in C++, use a reference parameter (int &x).
- return sends one value back; a void function returns nothing.
- A local variable exists only inside its function; a global variable is declared outside all functions.
- A recursive function calls itself and needs a base case to stop.
> int sq(int n) {
>     return n * n;
> int main() {
>     printf("%d", sq(3) + sq(2));
> sq(3) returns 9 and sq(2) returns 4.
> Output: 13
- Pointers: &x is the address of x; if p = &x, then *p is the value stored at that address, and changing *p changes x.
## Errors
| Error | Found | Example
| Syntax | by the compiler, before the program runs | missing semicolon, misspelt keyword
| Runtime | while the program runs; it may crash | division by zero, file not found
| Logic | not reported; the output is simply wrong | writing < instead of <=
Logic errors are the hardest to find because no message appears. Debugging tools include dry runs with a trace table, extra print statements and breakpoints.
## How to trace output
- Make a table with one column per variable and one row per step.
- Apply operator rules exactly: integer division, precedence, pre- or post-increment.
- For loops, check the condition before each round and note the value of the counter when the loop ends.
- Watch the format: spaces, commas and \n in printf decide what the output looks like.
## Quick check
- Value of 17 / 4 with int operands? (4)
- Value of 17 % 4? (1)
- Which loop always runs at least once? (do-while)
- Valid indexes of int m[10]? (0 to 9)
- Which flowchart symbol shows a decision? (diamond)
- Which error gives no message but a wrong answer? (logic error)

title: National Income and Macroeconomics
lines: Macroeconomics looks at the economy as a whole. USAT questions here are mostly definitions (GDP, GNP, inflation types, unemployment types) plus quick sums with the national income identities, MPC and the multiplier. Learn the chain from GDP to disposable income and the multiplier formula by heart.
## National income accounting
GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year. Only final goods are counted, or the value added at each stage, to avoid double counting.
| Measure | How to get it
| GNP | GDP + net factor income from abroad
| NNP at market price | GNP − depreciation
| National income (NNP at factor cost) | NNP at market price − indirect taxes + subsidies
| Personal income | national income − undistributed profits and company tax − social security contributions + transfer payments
| Disposable income | personal income − personal direct taxes
- Three methods: output (value added), income (wages + rent + interest + profit) and expenditure, C + I + G + (X − M).
- Not counted: transfer payments (pensions, gifts, scholarships), second-hand sales, purely financial deals, unpaid household work.
- Real GDP is valued at base-year prices. Real GDP = nominal GDP × 100 ÷ GDP deflator.
- Per capita income = national income ÷ population.
> GDP = Rs 900 billion. Residents earn Rs 60 billion abroad; foreigners earn Rs 20 billion here.
> Net factor income from abroad = 60 − 20 = 40.
> GNP = 900 + 40 = Rs 940 billion.
! Wheat Rs 500, flour Rs 800, bread Rs 1,200: value added is Rs 1,200, not the Rs 2,500 sum of all sales.
## Consumption and saving
Keynes's psychological law: when income rises, consumption rises but by less. Every extra rupee is spent or saved.
- APC = C ÷ Y and APS = S ÷ Y; APC + APS = 1.
- MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY and MPS = ΔS ÷ ΔY; MPC + MPS = 1.
- For C = a + bY, b is the MPC. Saving is zero at the break-even income where C = Y, that is Y = a ÷ (1 − b).
- Paradox of thrift: if everyone tries to save more, income falls and total saving may not rise.
## Investment and the multiplier

Investment means spending on new capital goods, not buying existing shares or gold. Keynes: firms invest while the marginal efficiency of capital (expected return) exceeds the rate of interest. Autonomous investment does not depend on income; induced investment does. The accelerator says investment depends on the rate of change of output.
Multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPS, and ΔY = k × ΔI (or ΔG).
> MPC = 0.75 and investment rises by Rs 20 billion.
> ΔY = 4 × 20 = Rs 80 billion.
! 1 ÷ MPC (1.33 here) is the classic wrong answer. Always divide by the MPS.
- Higher MPC gives a bigger multiplier; saving, taxes and imports are leakages that shrink it.
- Balanced budget multiplier = 1: equal rises in G and taxes raise income by the amount of G.
- Equilibrium in a two-sector model: planned saving = planned investment.
## Employment and unemployment

Classical economists relied on Say's law, 'supply creates its own demand', and flexible wages, so lasting unemployment was impossible. Keynes argued employment depends on effective demand, so unemployment can persist.
| Type | Cause
| Frictional | moving between jobs, searching
| Structural | change in technology or demand makes skills obsolete
| Cyclical | fall in aggregate demand in a recession
| Seasonal | work only in certain seasons (sugar mills, harvest)
| Disguised | more people on a job than needed; MP of extra workers is zero
## Inflation
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, so the value of money falls. Deflation is a sustained fall; disinflation is a slower rate of inflation.
- Demand-pull: too much money chasing too few goods. Cost-push: rising costs such as oil or wages.
- Stagflation: inflation with high unemployment and slow growth. Hyperinflation: extremely rapid price rises.
- Losers: fixed-income earners, savers and lenders. Gainers: borrowers and holders of real goods.
- Inflation rate = (new index − old index) ÷ old index × 100.
> CPI rises from 160 to 176.
## Business cycles
Four phases repeat: recovery, boom (peak), recession, depression (trough). In a recession output falls, unemployment rises and profits fall.
## Fiscal policy

Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxes. Expansionary policy (more spending, lower taxes) fights recession; contractionary policy fights inflation. A budget deficit means spending exceeds revenue. Crowding out: government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment. Automatic stabilisers, such as progressive taxes and unemployment benefits, damp swings without new decisions.
! Fiscal policy belongs to the government's budget; interest rates and money supply belong to monetary policy and the central bank.
## Quick check
- GDP → GNP: add net factor income from abroad. GNP → NNP: subtract depreciation.
- MPC + MPS = 1; k = 1 ÷ MPS.
- Transfer payments are not part of GDP.
- Disguised unemployment: marginal product zero.

title: Demand, Supply and Consumer Behaviour
lines: USAT Economics questions on this topic test whether you know the basic definitions, can tell a shift of a curve from a movement along it, and can do quick elasticity, utility and consumer surplus sums by hand. Expect two or three of the ten Economics questions from here.
## The economic problem

Wants are unlimited but resources are scarce, so every society must choose what to produce, how to produce it and for whom. Choice means sacrifice: the opportunity cost of anything is the next best alternative given up.
- Robbins: economics studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means with alternative uses (scarcity definition).
- Adam Smith called it the science of wealth; Marshall stressed material welfare.
- Microeconomics studies individual units (a consumer, a firm, one market); macroeconomics studies aggregates (national income, the price level).
- Positive statements can be tested by facts; normative statements say what ought to be.

The production possibility curve (PPC) shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can make with its resources and technology. It is bowed outward because opportunity cost rises as more of one good is made. A point inside the curve means unemployed or wasted resources; a point outside is unattainable; better technology or more resources shift the whole curve outward.
## Demand
The law of demand: other things remaining the same (ceteris paribus), quantity demanded falls when price rises. The demand curve slopes downward.
| Change | Effect on the demand curve
| Good's own price | movement along the curve (extension or contraction)
| Income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, population | shift of the whole curve
- Substitutes (tea and coffee): dearer tea raises demand for coffee.
- Complements (cars and petrol): dearer petrol lowers demand for cars.
- Normal goods: demand rises with income. Inferior goods: demand falls as income rises.
- Exceptions to the law: Giffen goods (a staple inferior good where the income effect outweighs the substitution effect) and Veblen goods (status goods bought because they are dear).
- Derived demand: demand for bricks comes from demand for houses. Joint supply: wheat and straw come together.
## Supply and equilibrium

The law of supply: quantity supplied rises with price. Supply shifts with input costs, technology, taxes and subsidies, and the number of firms. Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Above it there is a surplus that pushes price down; below it, a shortage that pushes price up.
- Price ceiling (maximum price) below equilibrium causes a shortage.
- Price floor (minimum support price) above equilibrium causes a surplus.
> Qd = 100 − 4P and Qs = 20 + 4P. Find the equilibrium.
> Set 100 − 4P = 20 + 4P, so 80 = 8P and P = Rs 10.
! An increase in demand raises both price and quantity. An increase in supply lowers price but raises quantity. Do not mix them up.
## Elasticity
Price elasticity of demand (PED) = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price, quoted without the minus sign.
| Value | Name | Price cut does this to revenue
| above 1 | elastic | raises total revenue
| exactly 1 | unitary | leaves revenue unchanged
| below 1 | inelastic | lowers total revenue
- Total outlay method: if spending moves the opposite way to price, demand is elastic; the same way, inelastic; unchanged, unitary.
- Demand is more elastic when there are close substitutes, the good is a luxury, it takes a large share of income, or buyers have time to adjust.

- A horizontal demand curve is perfectly elastic; a vertical one is perfectly inelastic. On a straight downward line, elasticity is 1 at the midpoint, above 1 on the upper half and below 1 on the lower half.
- Income elasticity: positive for normal goods (above 1 for luxuries), negative for inferior goods.
- Cross elasticity: positive for substitutes, negative for complements, zero for unrelated goods.
- Elasticity of supply: a vertical supply curve has elasticity zero; farm supply is inelastic in the short run.
> Price rises from Rs 50 to Rs 60; quantity falls from 400 to 300.
> PED = 25 ÷ 20 = 1.25, so demand is elastic.
! Put the quantity change on top. Dividing price change by quantity change gives the inverse (0.8 here), and it is always one of the options.
## Utility and consumer equilibrium

Utility is the satisfaction a consumer gets from a good. Marginal utility (MU) is the change in total utility (TU) from one more unit. The law of diminishing marginal utility says MU falls as more units are consumed. TU is at its maximum when MU is zero and falls once MU is negative.
With two or more goods, the law of equi-marginal utility says satisfaction is greatest when MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py and all income is spent. If one good gives more utility per rupee, buy more of it.
> MUx = 30, Px = Rs 10; MUy = 40, Py = Rs 20.
> MU per rupee: X gives 3, Y gives 2.
> Shift spending towards X until the ratios are equal.

Indifference curve approach (ordinal): an indifference curve joins combinations giving equal satisfaction. It slopes down and is convex to the origin because the marginal rate of substitution diminishes. Curves never cross. The consumer is in equilibrium where the budget line touches the highest indifference curve.
## Consumer surplus
Consumer surplus = what a buyer is willing to pay − what she actually pays. Add the surplus on each unit bought.
> Willing to pay Rs 50, 40, 30, 20 for four units; price Rs 20.
! Do not confuse total willingness to pay (Rs 140) or total spending (Rs 80) with the surplus.
## Quick check
- Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, not the money price paid.
- Own price: movement along. Anything else: shift.
- PED above 1: cut price to raise revenue. PED below 1: raise price to raise revenue.
- Negative income elasticity means an inferior good; negative cross elasticity means complements.
- Consumer equilibrium: MU ÷ P equal for every good.

title: Money, Banking and Trade
lines: This topic covers money, banking, the central bank, taxes and foreign trade. USAT mostly checks definitions and functions, with a few short sums: the quantity theory, the credit multiplier, terms of trade, the current account and exchange-rate conversions.
## Money and its functions
Barter needs a double coincidence of wants: each trader must want what the other has. Money removes this problem.
| Function | Meaning
| Medium of exchange | accepted in payment for goods and services
| Unit of account | prices of all goods are stated in it
| Store of value | holds purchasing power over time
| Standard of deferred payments | future payments, such as loans, are stated in it
- Fiat money has value by government order, not by its material. Legal tender must be accepted in settlement of a debt; a cheque is optional money.
- Bank (credit) money is deposits transferable by cheque. Near money (savings deposits, treasury bills) is highly liquid but not itself spent.
- Gresham's law: bad money drives good money out of circulation.
- The value of money is its purchasing power; it moves inversely with the price level. If a price index goes from 100 to 250, a rupee buys 100 ÷ 250 = 40 % of what it did.
Fisher's quantity theory: MV = PT, where M is money supply, V velocity of circulation, P price level and T volume of transactions. With V and T constant, P changes in proportion to M.
> M = Rs 500 billion, V = 6, T = 1,000 billion.
## Commercial banks

Primary functions: accepting deposits (current, savings, fixed) and lending (loans, overdrafts, discounting bills). Secondary functions include remittances, lockers and acting as an agent for customers. A bank balances liquidity (meeting withdrawals) against profitability (earning from loans), since the most liquid assets earn least.
Credit creation: a bank keeps only a fraction of each deposit as reserve and lends the rest, which returns to the system as new deposits. Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio.
> New deposit Rs 10,000, reserve ratio 20 %.
> Multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5.
> Maximum total deposits = 5 × 10,000 = Rs 50,000.
! Rs 8,000 is only the first loan. Cash held by the public and idle reserves make the real multiplier smaller.
## The central bank

The State Bank of Pakistan is Pakistan's central bank. Its functions: sole issue of notes, banker to the government, banker to banks, lender of last resort, custodian of foreign exchange reserves, and controller of credit.
| Tool | Tight money (fight inflation)
| Policy (bank) rate | raise it
| Open market operations | sell government securities
| Cash reserve ratio | raise it
| Selective controls | raise margins on loans for chosen goods
| Moral suasion | advise banks to lend less
Expansionary (easy) monetary policy does the opposite: lower rates, buy securities, lower reserve ratios.
! Buying securities injects money; selling securities drains it. The central bank buys to expand and sells to contract.
## Public finance and taxes

- A direct tax (income tax, wealth tax) is borne by the person on whom it is imposed. An indirect tax (sales tax, excise, customs) can be shifted to buyers. Impact is on the first payer; incidence on whoever finally bears it.
- Progressive: rate rises with income. Proportional: same rate for all. Regressive: takes a larger share of a poor person's income, as a fixed sales tax amount does.
- Adam Smith's canons: equality (ability to pay), certainty (clear amount and time), convenience (suitable time and manner) and economy (low collection cost).
- Incidence and elasticity: with perfectly inelastic demand buyers bear the whole tax; with perfectly elastic demand sellers bear it.
- Public debt is internal (owed at home) or external (owed abroad, usually in foreign currency). Non-tax revenue includes profits of state enterprises, fees and fines.
## International trade

Absolute advantage (Adam Smith): a country produces more of a good with the same resources. Comparative advantage (Ricardo): a country produces a good at a lower opportunity cost. Trade benefits both sides when opportunity costs differ.
> A: one worker-day makes 10 m cloth or 5 kg rice. B: 6 m cloth or 4 kg rice.
> Cost of 1 kg rice: A gives up 2 m cloth, B gives up 1.5 m.
> B specialises in rice, A in cloth.
- Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. A rise means exports buy more imports.

- Protection: tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on quantity), subsidies. The infant industry argument supports temporary protection. Dumping is selling abroad below the home price or below cost.
## Balance of payments and exchange rates
The balance of trade covers goods only. The balance of payments records all transactions with the rest of the world by double entry, so in accounting terms it always balances.
- Current account: goods, services (invisibles such as tourism and shipping), primary income and current transfers such as workers' remittances.
- Capital and financial account: loans, investment flows, changes in reserves.
- A floating exchange rate is set by demand for and supply of the currency. Exports create demand for the rupee; imports supply rupees.
- Depreciation (market fall) or devaluation (official cut) makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home. Appreciation does the reverse.
- Purchasing power parity: in the long run exchange rates move so a currency buys the same basket everywhere.
> Rupee moves from Rs 200 to Rs 250 per dollar; cloth costs Rs 1,000.
> Dollar price falls from 1,000 ÷ 200 = 5 to 1,000 ÷ 250 = 4 dollars.
! A rise in the number of rupees per dollar is a fall in the rupee's value.
## Quick check
- Four functions of money: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, standard of deferred payments.
- Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio.
- To fight inflation: raise the policy rate, sell securities, raise reserve ratios.
- Remittances are in the current account; foreign loans are not.

title: Production, Costs and Markets
lines: USAT asks about the factors of production and their rewards, the laws of returns, the cost and revenue terms (with short sums), and how the main market forms differ. Learn the definitions exactly: many wrong options are the right idea attached to the wrong term.
## Factors of production
| Factor | Meaning | Reward
| Land | all gifts of nature; fixed in total supply, immobile | rent
| Labour | human effort, mental or physical | wages
| Capital | man-made goods used to produce more goods (machines, tools) | interest
| Entrepreneur | organises the other factors and bears uncertainty | profit

Production means the creation of utility, not of matter: changing a good's form, place, time or ownership. Division of labour raises skill and speed but brings monotony and the risk that a narrow skill becomes useless.
## Laws of returns
In the short run at least one factor is fixed. Adding more of a variable factor to it is governed by the law of variable proportions (diminishing returns).
- Total product (TP): total output. Average product (AP) = TP ÷ units of the variable factor. Marginal product (MP) = change in TP from one more unit.
- Stage I: AP rising. Stage II: from maximum AP to MP = 0, where a rational firm operates. Stage III: MP negative.
- TP is at its maximum when MP is zero. MP cuts AP at the highest point of AP.

Returns to scale are a long-run idea: all inputs change together. If output rises by a larger proportion than inputs, returns to scale are increasing; same proportion, constant; smaller proportion, decreasing.
> TP with 1, 2, 3, 4 workers: 10, 24, 33, 38 tonnes.
> MP of the 3rd worker = 33 − 24 = 9 tonnes.
> AP of 3 workers = 33 ÷ 3 = 11 tonnes.
## Costs
- Fixed cost (rent, insurance, loan interest) does not change with output and is paid even at zero output.
- Variable cost (raw materials, daily wages, power) rises with output. TC = TFC + TVC.
- AFC = TFC ÷ Q falls continuously. AVC = TVC ÷ Q. ATC = TC ÷ Q = AFC + AVC.
- MC = change in TC from one more unit. MC cuts AVC and ATC at their lowest points.

- Short-run AC is U-shaped because of the law of variable proportions; long-run AC is U-shaped because of economies and then diseconomies of scale. The long-run AC is an envelope of short-run AC curves.
- Internal economies belong to one growing firm (bulk buying, better machines, cheaper finance). External economies are shared by all firms when the industry grows in an area.
- Economists count implicit costs (the owner's own time and property) as well as explicit cash costs. Normal profit is part of cost.
> TFC = Rs 30,000, variable cost Rs 40 a unit, price Rs 100.
> Each unit covers 100 − 40 = Rs 60 of fixed cost.
> Break-even output = 30,000 ÷ 60 = 500 units.
## Revenue and profit
- TR = P × Q. AR = TR ÷ Q = price. MR = change in TR from selling one more unit.
- Profit is greatest where MR = MC (with MC rising).
- A firm stays open in the short run if price covers AVC; below minimum AVC it shuts down.
> 8 units sell at Rs 50 each, 9 units at Rs 48 each.
> TR rises from 400 to 432, so MR of the 9th unit = Rs 32, below the price of Rs 48.
! MR is below price whenever a firm must cut its price to sell more, because the cut applies to every unit sold.
## Market forms
| Form | Sellers | Product | Firm's demand curve
| Perfect competition | very many | identical | horizontal: P = AR = MR
| Monopolistic competition | many | differentiated (brands) | downward, fairly elastic
| Oligopoly | a few, interdependent | identical or differentiated | kinked in one model
| Monopoly | one | no close substitute | downward: MR below AR
- Perfect competition: free entry and exit and perfect knowledge, so in the long run firms earn only normal profit.

- Monopoly comes from barriers to entry such as patents, licences or control of a raw material. Compared with competition it charges a higher price and produces less. Price discrimination means charging different groups different prices for the same product.
- Oligopoly: in the kinked demand model rivals match price cuts but not rises, so prices are sticky. A cartel is an agreement to fix prices or output.
- Duopoly has two sellers; monopsony has one buyer.
! Monopoly is one seller; monopsony is one buyer. The two words are often swapped in the options.
## Factor pricing
- Marginal productivity theory: a firm hires labour until the wage equals the marginal revenue product. Demand for factors is derived demand.
- Real wage is what the money wage buys; if prices rise faster than money wages, the real wage falls.

- Ricardian rent arises from differences in land fertility and the scarcity of good land. Economic rent is earnings above transfer earnings (what is needed to keep a factor in its present use). Quasi-rent is a short-run surplus earned by machines.
- Keynes: interest is the reward for parting with liquidity. Classical view: reward for waiting or abstinence.
- Knight: profit is the reward for bearing uncertainty that cannot be insured.
! Transfer earnings are not the rent. Rent is only the part above them.
## Quick check
- MC = AC at minimum AC; MP = AP at maximum AP; TP is highest when MP = 0.
- AFC always falls; AVC, ATC and MC are U-shaped.
- Profit maximum: MR = MC. Shutdown: price below minimum AVC.
- Perfect competition: P = AR = MR; long-run normal profit only.

title: Ethics
lines: Candidates who are not Muslim take Ethics in place of Islamiat. USAT ethics questions test moral ideas and how to apply them: honesty, justice, duty, tolerance, citizenship, professional conduct, the main ideas of moral thinkers, and the moral teaching that world religions share. Many questions describe a situation and ask for the right action.
## Core virtues
| Virtue | Meaning | Opposite
| Honesty | telling the truth and not deceiving | lying, cheating
| Integrity | keeping to principles even when no one is watching | hypocrisy
| Justice | giving each person what is due by fair rules | favouritism, oppression
| Responsibility | doing one's duties and owning one's actions | negligence
| Tolerance | respecting people whose beliefs or ways differ | prejudice, bigotry
| Compassion | caring about others' suffering and helping | cruelty, indifference
| Empathy | understanding and sharing another's feelings | callousness
| Humility | not thinking oneself above others | arrogance
| Gratitude | thankfulness for what one receives | ingratitude
| Courage | doing right despite fear | cowardice
## Key ideas and terms
- Rights and duties go together: my right is someone else's duty, and others' rights are my duties.
- Equality treats everyone alike; equity gives each person what they need to have a fair chance.
- Merit means choosing people for jobs on ability and performance. Nepotism favours relatives; favouritism favours friends.
- Conflict of interest: a personal gain could affect a person's official judgement. The right step is to declare it and stand aside.
- Plagiarism: presenting another person's work as one's own. Corruption: misusing a trusted position for private gain; bribery is one form.
- Stereotyping judges a whole group by a few; prejudice is an opinion formed without facts; discrimination is unfair treatment because of group membership.
- Sustainability: meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
## Moral thinkers
| Thinker or theory | Main idea
| Socrates | the unexamined life is not worth living; knowledge leads to virtue
| Aristotle | virtue is a golden mean between two extremes (courage between cowardice and rashness)
| Confucius | ren (humaneness), respect for family and proper conduct
| Kant (duty ethics) | act only on rules you could want everyone to follow; treat people as ends, never merely as means
| Bentham and Mill (utilitarianism) | the right act produces the greatest good for the greatest number
## Shared teaching of world religions
| Tradition | Sacred text | Moral teaching often cited
| Judaism | Torah | Ten Commandments; tzedakah (charity as justice)
| Christianity | Bible | love your neighbour as yourself; forgiveness
| Hinduism | Vedas, Bhagavad Gita | dharma (duty), ahimsa (non-violence)
| Buddhism | Tripitaka | Four Noble Truths, Noble Eightfold Path, compassion
| Sikhism | Guru Granth Sahib | equality, honest work, sharing; langar, the free community kitchen
| Zoroastrianism | Avesta | good thoughts, good words, good deeds

Almost every tradition teaches some form of the Golden Rule: treat others as you would wish to be treated. All value truthfulness, care for the poor, respect for parents and justice. Ethics questions never ask which religion is best; they ask what traditions share.
## Applying ethics: worked examples
> A shopkeeper gives Daniel Rs 500 too much change. What should he do?
> (A) Keep it, since it was the shopkeeper's mistake  (B) Return it at once  (C) Give it to charity  (D) Keep it and buy something later at the shop
> B. The money belongs to the shopkeeper; honesty means returning it. Giving it to charity is still giving away what is not yours.
> Maria, a junior engineer, finds a safety flaw in a design her firm has approved. The most responsible step is to
> (A) stay silent to protect her job  (B) post about it on social media first  (C) report it promptly to her supervisor with the evidence  (D) fix the drawings quietly
> C. Professional duty puts public safety first and uses proper channels. Going public first skips those channels; quiet changes hide the problem.
## How to answer situation questions
- Choose the action that is honest, fair to everyone affected, and lawful.
- Prefer proper channels (report to the person responsible) over silence or public shaming.
- Beware of options that sound kind but break a duty, such as covering up a friend's cheating.
## Traps
! An action is not right because "everyone does it" or because no one will find out.
! Equality and equity are not the same; check which one the question describes.
! Utilitarianism judges results; Kant judges duty and intention. Do not swap them.
## Quick check
- Know the virtues and their opposites.
- Aristotle: golden mean. Kant: duty. Mill: greatest good. Confucius: ren.
- Match each faith with its text and a shared value.
- In cases, pick the honest, fair, responsible action through proper channels.

title: Economy and Civics
lines: This topic tests basic ideas of economics and government, common abbreviations, and international bodies. USAT asks for meanings of terms, the job of an institution, or what an abbreviation stands for. Numbers that change, such as growth rates or budgets, are not asked.
## Basic economics
| Term | Meaning
| GDP | Gross Domestic Product: value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year
| GNP | Gross National Product: GDP plus net income earned by citizens abroad
| Per capita income | national income divided by population
| Inflation | a general rise in prices, which lowers the buying power of money
| Deflation | a general fall in prices
| Fiscal policy | government taxing and spending, set through the budget
| Monetary policy | central bank control of money supply and interest rates
| Budget deficit | government spending greater than revenue
| Balance of trade | exports minus imports of goods
| Balance of payments | record of all transactions with the rest of the world
| Direct tax | paid by the person on whom it falls, e.g. income tax
| Indirect tax | passed on through prices, e.g. sales tax, customs duty
- Law of demand: when price rises, quantity demanded falls (other things equal). Law of supply: when price rises, quantity supplied rises.
- Devaluation lowers a currency's value against others, making exports cheaper and imports dearer.
## Government and the state
- Four elements of a state: population, territory, government and sovereignty.
- Three organs: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, and the judiciary interprets them and settles disputes. Montesquieu argued for separation of these powers.
| System | Feature | Example
| Federal | power divided between centre and provinces or states | Pakistan, USA
| Unitary | power held mainly by the centre | United Kingdom, France
| Parliamentary | government answers to the legislature; head of state and head of government are separate | Pakistan, UK
| Presidential | president is both head of state and government, elected separately | USA
- Democracy is rule by the people through elected representatives. A constitution is the basic law that sets up the state. Franchise is the right to vote.
## Abbreviations: Pakistan
| Abbreviation | Full form
| NADRA | National Database and Registration Authority
| HEC | Higher Education Commission
| WAPDA | Water and Power Development Authority
| FBR | Federal Board of Revenue
| SBP | State Bank of Pakistan
| SECP | Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan
| PEMRA | Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority
| PTA | Pakistan Telecommunication Authority
| NAB | National Accountability Bureau
| CPEC | China-Pakistan Economic Corridor
## Abbreviations: international
| Abbreviation | Full form
| UNO | United Nations Organisation
| UNESCO | United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization
| UNICEF | United Nations Children's Fund
| IMF | International Monetary Fund
| WTO | World Trade Organization
| OIC | Organisation of Islamic Cooperation
| SAARC | South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation
| ECO | Economic Cooperation Organization
| NATO | North Atlantic Treaty Organization
| OPEC | Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
| ASEAN | Association of Southeast Asian Nations
## International bodies and their roles
- IMF: short-term loans to countries with balance-of-payments problems. World Bank: long-term loans for development projects.
- WTO: rules for international trade and settling trade disputes.
- International Court of Justice: disputes between states, at The Hague.
> A government raises income tax and cuts its own spending to control inflation. This is an example of  (A) monetary policy  (B) fiscal policy  (C) trade policy  (D) devaluation
> B. Taxes and government spending are fiscal tools. Monetary policy works through interest rates and money supply, set by the central bank.
> Sales tax is an example of  (A) a direct tax  (B) an indirect tax  (C) a wealth tax  (D) a property tax
> B. The seller collects sales tax and passes it on to the buyer through the price.
## Traps
! Fiscal policy belongs to the government; monetary policy to the central bank (the State Bank in Pakistan).
! GDP counts production inside the country; GNP adds net income from abroad.
! The IMF lends for balance-of-payments support; the World Bank lends for projects. Do not swap them.
## Quick check
- GDP, inflation, fiscal versus monetary policy, direct versus indirect tax.
- Elements of a state; three organs; federal versus unitary; parliamentary versus presidential.
- NADRA, HEC, WAPDA, FBR, SECP, PEMRA.
- IMF, World Bank, WTO, ICJ: who does what.

title: World Geography
lines: World geography questions in USAT-A ask about continents and oceans, the largest and longest features, countries with their capitals and currencies, famous landmarks, straits and canals, and lines of latitude and longitude. These facts change very slowly, which makes them ideal for revision tables.
## Continents and oceans
- Seven continents, from largest to smallest: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia (Oceania).
- Asia is both the largest and the most populous continent. Australia is the smallest.
- Five oceans, from largest: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic. The Pacific is also the deepest; its Mariana Trench holds the deepest point on Earth.
## World records
| Feature | Answer
| Highest mountain | Mount Everest, about 8,849 m, on the Nepal-China border
| Second-highest mountain | K2, in Pakistan
| Longest river | the Nile (usually given); the Amazon carries the most water
| Largest hot desert | the Sahara
| Largest country by area | Russia
| Smallest country | Vatican City
| Largest island | Greenland
| Largest lake | Caspian Sea (salt water)
| Longest mountain range | the Andes
| Highest waterfall | Angel Falls, Venezuela
## Capitals and currencies
| Country | Capital | Currency
| Afghanistan | Kabul | afghani
| Bangladesh | Dhaka | taka
| China | Beijing | yuan (renminbi)
| India | New Delhi | rupee
| Iran | Tehran | rial
| Saudi Arabia | Riyadh | riyal
| Turkey (Türkiye) | Ankara | lira
| Japan | Tokyo | yen
| Nepal | Kathmandu | rupee
| United Kingdom | London | pound sterling
| United States | Washington, D.C. | dollar
