| Russia | Moscow | rouble
| France, Germany, Italy | Paris, Berlin, Rome | euro
| Australia | Canberra | Australian dollar
| Canada | Ottawa | Canadian dollar
| Brazil | Brasília | real
| Nigeria | Abuja | naira
| Kenya | Nairobi | shilling
! Many questions test the capital that is not the biggest city: Canberra not Sydney, Ottawa not Toronto, Ankara not Istanbul, Brasília not Rio de Janeiro, Abuja not Lagos.
## Landmarks
| Landmark | Place
| Eiffel Tower | Paris, France
| Great Wall | China
| Taj Mahal | Agra, India
| Pyramids of Giza | Egypt
| Colosseum | Rome, Italy
| Statue of Liberty | New York, USA
| Petra | Jordan
| Machu Picchu | Peru
| Big Ben | London, UK
## Straits and canals
| Waterway | Connects or separates
| Strait of Gibraltar | Spain and Morocco; Atlantic and Mediterranean
| Bosphorus | Europe and Asia at Istanbul; Black Sea and Sea of Marmara
| Strait of Hormuz | Iran and Oman; Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman
| Strait of Malacca | Malaysia and Sumatra; Indian Ocean and South China Sea
| Bab-el-Mandeb | Yemen and Djibouti; Red Sea and Gulf of Aden
| Bering Strait | Asia and North America
| Suez Canal (1869) | Mediterranean and Red Sea, in Egypt
| Panama Canal (1914) | Atlantic and Pacific
## Lines on the globe
- The Equator (0° latitude) divides north and south. The Tropic of Cancer (about 23.5° N) and Tropic of Capricorn (about 23.5° S) mark where the Sun can be directly overhead.
- The Prime Meridian (0° longitude) passes through Greenwich, London. The International Date Line runs roughly along 180°.
- The Earth turns 15° of longitude each hour, so places 15° apart differ by one hour of local time.
> Which strait links the Persian Gulf to the open sea?  (A) Malacca  (B) Hormuz  (C) Bosphorus  (D) Gibraltar
> B. Hormuz lies between Iran and Oman and is a key route for oil tankers.
> The currency of Bangladesh is the  (A) rupee  (B) taka  (C) rupiah  (D) riyal
> B. The rupiah is Indonesia's currency, a common confusion with the rupee.
## Traps
! The Sahara is the largest hot desert; Antarctica, a cold desert, is larger in area.
! The Caspian Sea is the largest lake, though it is salt water and called a sea.
! Mount Everest is the highest above sea level; K2 is second.
## Quick check
- Asia largest continent; Pacific largest and deepest ocean.
- Everest highest; Nile longest; Sahara largest hot desert; Russia largest country.
- Canberra, Ottawa, Ankara, Brasília, Abuja.
- Suez 1869 (Mediterranean–Red Sea); Panama 1914 (Atlantic–Pacific).

title: Everyday Science
lines: Everyday science questions in USAT-A test general awareness, not formulas. They ask who invented or discovered something, how the human body works, which vitamin prevents which disease, what causes common diseases, basic facts about the environment and space, and common technology terms.
## Inventions and discoveries
| Invention or discovery | Person
| Printing press with movable type | Johannes Gutenberg (about 1440)
| Laws of motion and gravitation | Isaac Newton
| Improved steam engine | James Watt
| Smallpox vaccine | Edward Jenner
| Telephone | Alexander Graham Bell (1876)
| Practical electric light bulb | Thomas Edison
| Radio communication | Guglielmo Marconi
| X-rays | Wilhelm Röntgen (1895)
| Radioactivity research, radium | Marie Curie
| Theory of relativity | Albert Einstein
| Penicillin | Alexander Fleming (1928)
| Aeroplane flight | the Wright brothers (1903)
| World Wide Web | Tim Berners-Lee (1989)
| Pasteurisation, rabies vaccine | Louis Pasteur
## The human body
| Fact | Answer
| Bones in an adult | 206
| Largest organ | skin
| Largest internal organ | liver (also stores bile in the gall bladder)
| Smallest bone | stapes, in the ear
| Normal body temperature | about 37 °C
| Oxygen carrier in blood | haemoglobin in red blood cells
| Fights infection | white blood cells
| Helps blood clot | platelets
| Insulin produced by | pancreas
| Universal donor blood group | O negative
## Vitamins and deficiency diseases
| Vitamin | Lack causes | Sources
| A | night blindness | carrots, milk, liver
| B1 | beriberi | whole grains
| C | scurvy (bleeding gums) | citrus fruit, guava
| D | rickets (soft bones) | sunlight, eggs, fish
| K | poor blood clotting | green leafy vegetables
- Iron deficiency causes anaemia; iodine deficiency causes goitre.
## Causes of disease
| Cause | Diseases
| Virus | polio, measles, influenza, hepatitis, dengue, rabies
| Bacterium | tuberculosis, typhoid, cholera, tetanus
| Protozoan | malaria (spread by the female Anopheles mosquito)
- Dengue is spread by the Aedes mosquito. Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses.
## Environment
- The ozone layer, in the stratosphere, absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays. CFCs damage it.
- Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trap heat and cause global warming.
- Acid rain is caused mainly by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Smog is smoke and fog mixed with pollutants.
## Space
- The Sun is a star; light from it takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.
- Eight planets in order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
- Mercury is nearest the Sun; Venus is the hottest; Mars is the Red Planet; Jupiter is the largest; Saturn is famous for its rings.
## Useful science facts
| Fact | Value
| Speed of light in vacuum | about 3 × 10⁸ m/s
| Speed of sound in air | about 340 m/s
| Water boils (sea level) | 100 °C
| Water freezes | 0 °C
| Most abundant gas in air | nitrogen, about 78 %
| Gas plants take in for photosynthesis | carbon dioxide
| Hardest natural substance | diamond
| Lightest element | hydrogen
- Lightning is seen before thunder is heard because light travels far faster than sound.
## Technology terms
| Term | Meaning
| CPU | Central Processing Unit, the processor
| RAM | Random Access Memory, temporary working memory
| ROM | Read-Only Memory
| URL | Uniform Resource Locator, a web address
| HTTP | HyperText Transfer Protocol
| GPS | Global Positioning System
| LED | Light-Emitting Diode
> Scurvy is caused by a lack of  (A) vitamin A  (B) vitamin C  (C) vitamin D  (D) vitamin K
> B. Vitamin D is the tempting choice for bone problems, but scurvy is bleeding gums from a lack of vitamin C.
> Which disease is caused by a virus?  (A) typhoid  (B) cholera  (C) polio  (D) malaria
> C. Typhoid and cholera are bacterial; malaria is caused by a protozoan.
## Traps
! The liver is the largest internal organ; the skin is the largest organ overall.
! Edison made the light bulb practical; Bell invented the telephone. Marconi is radio.
! Malaria is not a virus or a bacterium; it is a protozoan parasite carried by mosquitoes.
## Quick check
- 206 bones; 37 °C; insulin from the pancreas.
- A night blindness, C scurvy, D rickets, B1 beriberi.
- Penicillin Fleming 1928; telephone Bell 1876; WWW Berners-Lee.
- Eight planets; Jupiter largest, Mercury nearest, Venus hottest.

title: World Affairs and History
lines: General Knowledge in USAT-A uses stable facts only. For world affairs this means international organisations (founding year, headquarters, purpose), major treaties and events of world history, and famous firsts. Questions never ask about current leaders or the latest news, so learn facts that will stay true.
## The United Nations
- Founded on 24 October 1945 (United Nations Day), after the Second World War, replacing the League of Nations (1920, Geneva). Headquarters: New York. Pakistan joined on 30 September 1947.

- Six principal organs: General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council, Trusteeship Council (inactive since 1994), International Court of Justice (The Hague), and Secretariat, headed by the Secretary-General.
- The Security Council has 15 members: 5 permanent members with a veto (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States) and 10 elected for two-year terms.
## Organisations and headquarters
| Organisation | Founded | Headquarters
| UNESCO (education, science, culture) | 1945 | Paris
| WHO (health) | 1948 | Geneva
| FAO (food and agriculture) | 1945 | Rome
| UNICEF (children) | 1946 | New York
| ILO (labour) | 1919 | Geneva
| IAEA (atomic energy) | 1957 | Vienna
| IMF and World Bank | 1944 (Bretton Woods) | Washington, D.C.
| WTO (trade) | 1995 | Geneva
| OIC (Muslim countries) | 1969 | Jeddah
| Arab League | 1945 | Cairo
| NATO (defence alliance) | 1949 | Brussels
| European Union | 1993 (Maastricht Treaty) | Brussels
| ASEAN (South-East Asia) | 1967 | Jakarta
| SAARC (South Asia) | 1985 (Dhaka) | Kathmandu
| ECO (Economic Cooperation Organization) | 1985 | Tehran
| OPEC (oil exporters) | 1960 | Vienna
| Commonwealth | 1949 (modern form) | London
| Red Cross (ICRC) | 1863 | Geneva
## Turning points of world history
| Year | Event
| 1215 | Magna Carta sealed in England, limiting the king's power
| 1453 | Ottomans take Constantinople
| 1492 | Columbus reaches the Americas
| 1498 | Vasco da Gama reaches India by sea
| 1776 | American Declaration of Independence
| 1789 | French Revolution begins
| 1914–1918 | First World War; ended by the Treaty of Versailles (1919)
| 1917 | Russian Revolution
| 1939–1945 | Second World War; atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (1945)
| 1948 | Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted by the UN
| 1957 | Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite
| 1989 | Fall of the Berlin Wall
| 1991 | Break-up of the Soviet Union
## Treaties and agreements
| Treaty | Year | What it did
| Peace of Westphalia | 1648 | ended the Thirty Years' War; basis of the modern state system
| Treaty of Versailles | 1919 | peace terms with Germany after the First World War
| Geneva Conventions | 1949 | protect the wounded, prisoners and civilians in war
| Indus Waters Treaty | 1960 | shared the Indus rivers between Pakistan and India
| Tashkent Declaration | 1966 | Pakistan-India agreement after the 1965 war
| Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty | 1968 | limits the spread of nuclear weapons
| Simla Agreement | 1972 | Pakistan-India agreement after the 1971 war
| Kyoto Protocol | 1997 | first binding targets for greenhouse gases
| Paris Agreement | 2015 | climate pact to keep warming well below 2 °C
## Famous firsts
| First | Who and when
| Person in space | Yuri Gagarin (USSR), 1961
| Woman in space | Valentina Tereshkova (USSR), 1963
| People on the Moon | Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, Apollo 11, 1969
| Ascent of Mount Everest | Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, 1953
| Modern Olympic Games | Athens, 1896
| FIFA World Cup | Uruguay, 1930
| Cricket World Cup | England, 1975
- Pakistan won the Cricket World Cup in 1992 and the ICC T20 World Cup in 2009. These are historical facts and will stay true.
> The headquarters of the International Atomic Energy Agency is in  (A) Geneva  (B) Vienna  (C) Paris  (D) New York
> B. Geneva is the tempting choice because many UN bodies are there, but the IAEA, like OPEC, is in Vienna.
> Which country is NOT a permanent member of the Security Council?  (A) France  (B) China  (C) Germany  (D) Russia
> C. The five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the UK and the USA.
## Traps
! The League of Nations was based in Geneva; the UN is in New York.
! SAARC was founded at Dhaka, but its secretariat is in Kathmandu.
! The IMF and World Bank were planned at Bretton Woods in 1944 and are both in Washington, D.C.
## Quick check
- UN: 24 October 1945, New York, Security Council of 15 with 5 vetoes.
- Geneva: WHO, ILO, WTO, Red Cross. Vienna: IAEA, OPEC. Paris: UNESCO. Rome: FAO.
- OIC Jeddah 1969; SAARC 1985; ECO Tehran; ASEAN Jakarta.
- WWI 1914–18; WWII 1939–45; Moon landing 1969.

title: Beliefs and Pillars
lines: This is the largest Islamiat topic in USAT. Questions ask about the articles of faith (iman), the five pillars, and the details of prayer, fasting, zakat and Hajj: meanings of terms, numbers, months and places. Learn the tables below by heart and understand the reason behind each act.
## Articles of faith
| Article | Meaning
| Tawhid | belief in the oneness of Allah, without partner; its opposite, shirk, is the gravest sin
| Angels (malaikah) | created from light; obey Allah and carry out His commands
| Revealed books | Tawrat, Zabur, Injil and the Quran, the final and preserved book
| Prophets (risalah) | sent to every nation; Muhammad (PBUH) is the last (khatm an-nubuwwah)
| The Last Day (akhirah) | resurrection, judgement, Paradise (jannah) and Hell (jahannam)
| Qadar | Allah knows all things and has decreed what will happen; people remain responsible for their choices

The Kalimah Tayyibah declares that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad (PBUH) is His Messenger. Tawhid means that Allah is one in His being and His attributes, that He alone created and sustains everything, and that He alone deserves worship. Surah Al-Ikhlas sums this up.
## Angels and their duties
| Angel | Duty
| Jibreel (AS) | brings revelation to the prophets; called Ruh al-Amin
| Mikail (AS) | in charge of rain and provision
| Israfil (AS) | will blow the trumpet on the Last Day
| Malak al-Mawt | takes souls at death
| Kiraman Katibin | record each person's deeds
| Munkar and Nakir | question the dead in the grave
Life after death passes through Barzakh, the stage between death and resurrection, then the Day of Judgement, when deeds are weighed.
## The five pillars
| Pillar | Key facts
| Shahadah | declaring faith in Allah's oneness and the prophethood of Muhammad (PBUH)
| Salah | five daily prayers, made obligatory on the night of the Mi'raj
| Zakat | 2.5 % of savings above the nisab held for one lunar year; made obligatory in 2 AH
| Sawm | fasting from dawn to sunset in Ramadan; made obligatory in 2 AH
| Hajj | pilgrimage to Makkah in Dhul Hijjah, once in a lifetime for those able
## Salah
| Prayer | Fard rakats
| Fajr | 2
| Zuhr | 4
| Asr | 4
| Maghrib | 3
| Isha | 4
- That makes 17 fard rakats a day. Jumu'ah, 2 rakats with a khutbah, replaces Zuhr on Friday.
- Conditions before prayer include purity (wudu, or ghusl when required), clean clothes and place, facing the qibla (the Kaaba) and the right time.
- If water is not available or harmful, tayammum with clean earth replaces wudu.
- Positions: qiyam (standing), ruku (bowing), sujud (prostration) and qa'dah (sitting). The call to prayer is the adhan; the second call just before the prayer begins is the iqamah.
## Zakat and charity
- Zakat means purification and growth. It is due on savings, gold, silver, trade goods, crops and livestock, at set rates.
- The Quran (Surah At-Tawbah) lists eight groups who may receive zakat, including the poor, the needy, those in debt and travellers in need.
- Sadaqah is voluntary charity; sadaqah jariyah is continuing charity, such as a well or a school. Sadaqat al-Fitr is paid before the Eid al-Fitr prayer.
## Sawm
- The fast runs from dawn (suhur is eaten before it) to sunset (iftar). It teaches taqwa, God-consciousness.
- The sick and travellers may postpone fasts and make them up later. Laylat al-Qadr falls in the last ten nights of Ramadan. Eid al-Fitr is on 1 Shawwal.
## Hajj
| Day of Dhul Hijjah | Rite
| 8th | pilgrims in ihram go to Mina
| 9th | standing at Arafat, the central rite; night at Muzdalifah
| 10th | stoning at Jamarat, sacrifice, shaving or cutting hair, tawaf; Eid al-Adha
| 11th-13th | stoning the three pillars at Mina

- Tawaf is going seven times round the Kaaba; sa'i is walking seven times between Safa and Marwah, recalling Hajar (AS) searching for water. Umrah can be done at any time of year and does not include Arafat.
> How many fard rakats are offered in a day?  (A) 15  (B) 17  (C) 19  (D) 21
> The central rite of Hajj, without which Hajj is not complete, is  (A) tawaf  (B) sa'i  (C) standing at Arafat  (D) sacrifice
> C. The wuquf at Arafat on 9 Dhul Hijjah is the heart of Hajj. The other rites matter, but Arafat is the defining one.
## Traps
! Maghrib, not Fajr, has three fard rakats.
! Eid al-Adha is on 10 Dhul Hijjah, the day after Arafat; Eid al-Fitr is on 1 Shawwal.
! Zakat is 2.5 %, not 10 %. The higher rates you may read about apply to some crops, not savings.
## Quick check
- Six articles of faith; five pillars.
- 17 fard rakats a day; Maghrib has 3.
- Zakat 2.5 % after a lunar year above the nisab.
- Hajj: Mina 8th, Arafat 9th, Eid and Jamarat 10th Dhul Hijjah.

title: Hadith and Sunnah
lines: USAT questions on hadith ask what hadith and Sunnah mean, how a hadith is built and graded, who compiled the major collections, and what well-known hadith teach. Learn the terms and the compilers carefully; the teachings are best remembered by their meaning.
## Key terms
| Term | Meaning
| Hadith | a report of what the Holy Prophet (PBUH) said, did or approved
| Sunnah | the way or practice of the Prophet (PBUH); the second source of Islamic guidance after the Quran
| Qawli, fi'li, taqriri | saying, action, and silent approval (taqrir)
| Isnad (sanad) | the chain of narrators
| Matn | the text or content of the report
| Rawi | a narrator
| Sahabi | a companion who met the Prophet (PBUH) as a believer
| Tabi'i | a successor who met a companion
| Hadith Qudsi | a report in which the Prophet (PBUH) relates a meaning from Allah, in his own words
## Grades of hadith
- Sahih: sound. Every narrator is trustworthy with a strong memory, the chain is unbroken, and there is no hidden defect.
- Hasan: good. Like sahih but a narrator's memory is slightly less strong.
- Da'if: weak. A condition of acceptance is missing.
- Mawdu': fabricated, falsely attributed to the Prophet (PBUH), and rejected.
## Why hadith matter

The Quran commands Muslims to obey the Messenger (PBUH), and the Sunnah explains how its commands are carried out. For example, the Quran orders prayer and zakat; the Sunnah shows the number of rakats, the timings and the rates. Hadith also record the Prophet's (PBUH) character, which the Quran calls the best example.
## The six well-known collections
| Collection | Compiler | Note
| Sahih al-Bukhari | Imam Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari | regarded as the most authentic book after the Quran
| Sahih Muslim | Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj | with Bukhari, called the Sahihayn
| Sunan Abu Dawud | Imam Abu Dawud | focus on legal hadith
| Jami' at-Tirmidhi | Imam at-Tirmidhi | notes the grade of many hadith
| Sunan an-Nasa'i | Imam an-Nasa'i | known for strict standards
| Sunan Ibn Majah | Imam Ibn Majah | completes the six

Other well-known works: the Muwatta of Imam Malik, an early collection from Madinah; the Musnad of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, arranged by companion; and the Forty Hadith (Al-Arba'in) of Imam an-Nawawi, a short collection of core teachings. Abu Hurayrah (RA) narrated the largest number of hadith; Aisha (RA) is among the leading narrators.
## Collection in stages
- In the Prophet's (PBUH) time, companions memorised his words, and some wrote them down.
- Later generations travelled widely to hear hadith from those who had heard them, and recorded each chain of narrators.
- In the third century after the Hijrah, the great collections such as Bukhari and Muslim were completed, with careful checking of every chain.
## Well-known teachings (by meaning)
- Actions are judged by intentions. This hadith opens Sahih al-Bukhari.
- The strong person is not the one who wrestles others down, but the one who controls himself when angry.
- Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should speak good or keep silent.
- None of you truly believes until he wants for his brother what he wants for himself.
- A kind word is charity, and removing something harmful from the road is a branch of faith.
- The signs of a hypocrite include lying when speaking, breaking promises and betraying trust.
- Make things easy and do not make them difficult.
> A companion did something in front of the Holy Prophet (PBUH), who saw it and did not object. This kind of Sunnah is called
> (A) qawli  (B) fi'li  (C) taqriri  (D) qudsi
> C. Taqrir is silent approval. Qawli is a saying and fi'li an action of the Prophet (PBUH) himself; qudsi refers to a report of Allah's words.
> The chain of narrators of a hadith is called the  (A) matn  (B) isnad  (C) rawi  (D) sahih
> B. The matn is the text, a rawi is one narrator, and sahih is a grade.
## Traps
! Do not mix isnad and matn: the isnad comes first and lists the people; the matn is what was said.
! A Hadith Qudsi is not part of the Quran, although its meaning is from Allah.
! The Muwatta is by Imam Malik and the Musnad by Imam Ahmad; neither is one of the six.
## Quick check
- Hadith: saying, action or approval of the Prophet (PBUH).
- Isnad = chain; matn = text; grades sahih, hasan, da'if, mawdu'.
- Sahihayn = Bukhari and Muslim; then Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i, Ibn Majah.
- Most hadith narrated by Abu Hurayrah (RA).

title: Rightly Guided Caliphs and Islamic History
lines: USAT asks about the four Rightly Guided Caliphs (Khulafa ar-Rashidun), the main events of their rule, the later Muslim dynasties, and the Muslim scholars whose work shaped science and learning. Questions usually ask who did what, when, and where.
## The four caliphs at a glance
| Caliph | Rule | Title | Remembered for
| Abu Bakr (RA) | 632–634 CE (11–13 AH) | As-Siddiq | wars against false prophets and those who refused zakat; Quran gathered into one copy
| Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) | 634–644 CE (13–23 AH) | Al-Faruq | great expansion; Hijri calendar; organised government
| Uthman ibn Affan (RA) | 644–656 CE (23–35 AH) | Dhun-Nurayn | standard copies of the Quran; first Muslim navy
| Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) | 656–661 CE (35–40 AH) | Asadullah, Haidar | knowledge and justice; capital moved to Kufa
The Rashidun period lasted about 30 years. Each caliph was chosen through consultation (shura) or nomination accepted by the community, and each lived simply.
## Abu Bakr (RA)
- The Prophet's (PBUH) closest companion, first adult free man to accept Islam, and his companion in the Cave of Thawr.
- Sent the army of Usama ibn Zayd (RA), as the Prophet (PBUH) had planned.
- Fought the Wars of Apostasy (Riddah). Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA) defeated the false prophet Musaylimah at Yamamah.
- After Yamamah, had the Quran collected into one copy under Zayd ibn Thabit (RA). Nominated Umar (RA) before his death.
## Umar (RA)
- Defeated the Byzantines at Yarmuk (636 CE) and the Sasanian Persians at Qadisiyyah; Egypt was taken by Amr ibn al-As (RA).
- Jerusalem surrendered and Umar (RA) went there himself, giving its people a covenant of safety for their lives, property and churches.
- Adopted the Hijri calendar, counted from the Hijrah. Set up the diwan (registers), paid stipends, organised provinces under governors, and founded garrison cities such as Kufa, Basra and Fustat.
- Known for strict justice and accountability of officials. He was martyred while leading the dawn prayer, having named a council of six to choose his successor.
## Uthman (RA)
- Called Dhun-Nurayn, "possessor of two lights", because he married two daughters of the Prophet (PBUH): Ruqayyah and then Umm Kulthum (RA).
- Before his caliphate, he bought the well of Rumah for the people of Madinah and funded the army for Tabuk.
- Had standard copies of the Quran prepared and sent to the provinces. Under him the first Muslim navy was formed, and expansion continued in North Africa and Persia.
- He was martyred in his house in Madinah by rebels in 656 CE.
## Ali (RA)
- Cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet (PBUH), husband of Fatimah (RA), and among the first to accept Islam as a boy.
- Famous for knowledge, eloquence, bravery (he was called Asadullah, the Lion of Allah) and fair judgement.
- Moved the capital from Madinah to Kufa. His rule faced internal conflict. He was martyred in Kufa in 661 CE.
## Later dynasties: a timeline
| Date (CE) | Event
| 661–750 | Umayyad caliphate, capital Damascus
| 711 | Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses into Spain; Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq) named after him
| 712 | Muhammad bin Qasim conquers Sindh, beginning at Debal
| 750–1258 | Abbasid caliphate; Baghdad founded as capital in 762
| 756 | Umayyad rule set up in Spain with Cordoba as capital
| 9th century | House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikmah) in Baghdad: translation and research
| 1187 | Salahuddin Ayyubi recaptures Jerusalem after the Battle of Hattin
| 1258 | Mongols under Hulagu sack Baghdad, ending Abbasid rule there
| 1453 | Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II conquers Constantinople
## Muslim scholars and their fields
| Scholar | Field and work
| Al-Khwarizmi | mathematics; algebra takes its name from his book; spread the Hindu-Arabic numerals
| Ibn Sina (Avicenna) | medicine and philosophy; Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb
| Al-Razi (Rhazes) | medicine; distinguished smallpox from measles
| Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) | optics; showed that we see because light enters the eye
| Jabir ibn Hayyan | chemistry; laboratory methods
| Al-Biruni | astronomy, geography and a study of India (Kitab al-Hind)
| Al-Zahrawi | surgery; designed surgical instruments
| Ibn Khaldun | history and society; the Muqaddimah
| Ibn Battuta | travel; journeys across Africa and Asia
| Al-Idrisi | geography; a world map for Roger II of Sicily
> Which caliph adopted the Hijri calendar?  (A) Abu Bakr (RA)  (B) Umar (RA)  (C) Uthman (RA)  (D) Ali (RA)
> B. The calendar starts from the Hijrah of 622 CE but was adopted under Umar (RA), about 17 years later.
> Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb was written by  (A) Al-Biruni  (B) Ibn Khaldun  (C) Ibn Sina  (D) Al-Khwarizmi
> C. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was used as a textbook in Europe for centuries.
## Traps
! Gathering the Quran into one copy was under Abu Bakr (RA); standard copies were under Uthman (RA).
! Damascus was the Umayyad capital; Baghdad the Abbasid capital; Cordoba the capital in Spain.
! Muhammad bin Qasim (712) is linked with Sindh; Tariq ibn Ziyad (711) with Spain.
## Quick check
- Order: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali (RA); about 30 years in all.
- Umar (RA): Hijri calendar, diwan, Jerusalem. Uthman (RA): standard Quran, navy. Ali (RA): Kufa.
- Umayyads Damascus 661; Abbasids Baghdad 750; Baghdad falls 1258; Constantinople 1453.

title: The Holy Quran
lines: Islamiat questions on the Quran in USAT ask about how it was revealed and compiled, its structure, the names and themes of well-known surahs, the prophets it mentions, and its main teachings. The questions test stable facts, so a clear timeline and a few tables cover most of them.
## Revelation
- The Quran is the word of Allah, revealed to the Holy Prophet (PBUH) through the angel Jibreel (AS).

- The first revelation came in the Cave of Hira, on Jabal an-Nur near Makkah, in the month of Ramadan, when the Prophet (PBUH) was about 40 years old (610 CE). The first verses revealed were the opening verses of Surah Al-Alaq, which begin with the command to read.

- Revelation continued gradually for about 23 years: about 13 years in Makkah and 10 in Madinah. The Quran itself explains that gradual revelation strengthened the Prophet's heart and let believers learn step by step.
- The night on which revelation began is Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, described in Surah Al-Qadr as better than a thousand months.
- The Quran was revealed in Arabic. The word Quran means "recitation" or "that which is read". Other names used in the Quran include Al-Furqan (the Criterion) and Adh-Dhikr (the Reminder).
## Makki and Madani surahs
| Makki (before the Hijrah) | Madani (after the Hijrah)
| mostly shorter surahs and verses | mostly longer surahs and verses
| themes: Tawhid, the hereafter, prophethood, stories of earlier nations | themes: laws of worship, family, trade, community, war and peace
| examples: Al-Alaq, Al-Muddaththir, Yasin, Al-Kahf | examples: Al-Baqarah, Aal-Imran, An-Nisa, Al-Hujurat
## Compilation
- In the Prophet's (PBUH) lifetime, the Quran was memorised by many companions and written by scribes on parchment, bone, palm leaves and stones. Zayd ibn Thabit (RA) was a leading scribe.
- After many memorisers were martyred at the Battle of Yamamah (11-12 AH), Umar (RA) urged Abu Bakr (RA) to gather the Quran into one copy. Abu Bakr (RA) gave the task to Zayd ibn Thabit (RA).
- That copy stayed with Abu Bakr (RA), then Umar (RA), and then with Hafsa (RA), the daughter of Umar and a wife of the Prophet (PBUH).

- Uthman (RA) had standard copies prepared from Hafsa's copy and sent them to the main cities, so that all Muslims recited in one agreed form. For this he is called Jami' al-Quran (the gatherer of the Quran).
## Structure in numbers
| Fact | Value
| Surahs | 114
| Paras (juz) | 30
| Longest surah | Al-Baqarah, 286 verses
| Shortest surah | Al-Kawthar, 3 verses
| Opening surah | Al-Fatiha (Umm al-Kitab), 7 verses
| Surah without Bismillah at the start | At-Tawbah
| Bismillah occurring twice | An-Naml
| Surah named after a woman | Maryam
| Last two surahs (Al-Mu'awwidhatayn) | Al-Falaq and An-Nas
## Revealed books and prophets
| Book | Prophet
| Tawrat (Torah) | Musa (AS)
| Zabur (Psalms) | Dawud (AS)
| Injil (Gospel) | Isa (AS)
| Quran | Muhammad (PBUH)

The Quran also mentions scrolls (suhuf) given to Ibrahim (AS) and Musa (AS). It names 25 prophets, among them Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub, Yusuf, Musa, Harun, Dawud, Sulaiman, Yunus, Isa and Muhammad (peace be upon them).
## Stories and teachings often asked
- Nuh (AS) built the ark; Hud (AS) was sent to the people of Ad; Salih (AS) to Thamud; Shuaib (AS) to Madyan.
- Yusuf (AS): Surah Yusuf tells his story in one continuous narrative.
- Al-Kahf: the people of the cave, Musa (AS) and Khidr, and Dhul-Qarnayn.
- Ayat al-Kursi is in Surah Al-Baqarah; Surah Al-Ikhlas states the oneness of Allah.
- Al-Hujurat teaches manners: no mocking, backbiting or suspicion. Al-Asr says people are in loss except those who believe, do good and urge one another to truth and patience.
> Which statement about the compilation of the Quran is correct?
> (A) Uthman (RA) first wrote the Quran down  (B) Abu Bakr (RA) had it collected into one copy after Yamamah  (C) It was first compiled under the Umayyads  (D) Hafsa (RA) wrote the first copy herself
> B. The Quran was written down in the Prophet's (PBUH) lifetime; Abu Bakr (RA) gathered it into one volume, Hafsa (RA) kept that copy, and Uthman (RA) later had standard copies made.
> Which surah was revealed in Madinah?  (A) Al-Alaq  (B) Yasin  (C) Al-Baqarah  (D) Al-Kahf
> C. Al-Baqarah deals with laws and community life and is Madani; the others are Makki.
## Traps
! Uthman (RA) did not compose or first collect the Quran; he standardised copies of the collection made under Abu Bakr (RA).
! The first revelation was in Ramadan, but the Hijrah and the Islamic calendar came much later. Do not mix the two dates.
! Al-Fatiha is first in order, but it was not the first revelation; that was the start of Al-Alaq.
## Quick check
- 114 surahs, 30 paras, about 23 years of revelation.
- First revelation: Hira, Ramadan, Al-Alaq, age about 40.
- Compilation: Abu Bakr (RA) and Zayd ibn Thabit (RA); copy with Hafsa (RA); standard copies by Uthman (RA).
- Tawrat–Musa, Zabur–Dawud, Injil–Isa, Quran–Muhammad (PBUH).

title: Seerah of the Holy Prophet (PBUH)
lines: USAT Seerah questions ask about the life of the Holy Prophet (PBUH): his family, early life, the Makkan period, the Hijrah, the battles and treaties of Madinah, and his last days. Most questions ask for a name, a place or a year. A clear timeline is the best tool.
## Early life
- Born in Makkah in the Year of the Elephant (about 570 CE), into the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh tribe.
- His father Abdullah died before his birth. He spent early childhood with his wet nurse Halimah Sa'diyah among the Banu Sa'd.
- His mother Aminah bint Wahb died when he was about six. His grandfather Abdul Muttalib cared for him until his death about two years later; then his uncle Abu Talib.
- At about twelve he travelled with Abu Talib to Syria on a trade journey. Known for honesty, he was called Al-Amin (the Trustworthy) and As-Sadiq (the Truthful).
- He took part in Hilf al-Fudul, a pact to protect the wronged, and settled the dispute over placing the Black Stone when the Kaaba was rebuilt.
- At 25 he married Khadijah (RA), a respected merchant whose trade he had managed.
## The Makkan period (about 13 years)
| Year (approx.) | Event
| 610 CE, age 40 | first revelation in the Cave of Hira
| first 3 years | private call; early Muslims include Khadijah, Abu Bakr, Ali and Zayd ibn Haritha (RA); Dar al-Arqam used for teaching
| from about year 3 | public preaching; persecution of Bilal, Sumayyah and others
| 5th year | first migration to Abyssinia, where the Negus (Najashi) gave refuge
| 7th–10th year | boycott of Banu Hashim in Shi'b Abi Talib
| 10th year | Year of Sorrow: deaths of Khadijah (RA) and Abu Talib; journey to Ta'if
| before the Hijrah | Isra and Mi'raj; the five daily prayers prescribed
| 621 and 622 CE | first and second Pledges of Aqabah with people of Yathrib
## The Hijrah

- In 622 CE the Prophet (PBUH) migrated to Yathrib, later called Madinat an-Nabi (Madinah). Ali (RA) slept in his bed on the night he left; he and Abu Bakr (RA) hid for three nights in the Cave of Thawr.
- At Quba he built the first mosque, then the Prophet's Mosque (Masjid an-Nabawi) in Madinah.
- The migrants were the Muhajirun; the Muslims of Madinah who helped them were the Ansar. The Prophet (PBUH) joined them in brotherhood (mu'akhat).
- The Charter of Madinah set out the rights and duties of the Muslims, the Jewish tribes and others in the city.
- The Hijrah marks year 1 of the Islamic (Hijri) calendar, adopted later under Umar (RA).
## The Madinan period (10 years)
| Year | Event
| 2 AH | change of qibla to the Kaaba; fasting and zakat made obligatory; Battle of Badr (313 Muslims against about 1,000)
| 3 AH | Battle of Uhud; archers left their post
| 5 AH | Battle of the Trench (Khandaq), on Salman al-Farsi's (RA) advice
| 6 AH | Treaty of Hudaybiyyah; Bay'at ar-Ridwan
| 7 AH | Khaybar; letters (sent after Hudaybiyyah) inviting rulers to Islam
| 8 AH | Battle of Mu'tah; conquest of Makkah with a general amnesty; Battle of Hunayn
| 9 AH | Expedition of Tabuk; Year of Delegations
| 10 AH | Farewell Hajj and Farewell Sermon
| 11 AH (632 CE) | passing away in Madinah at age 63, buried in the room of Aisha (RA)
> In which year after the Hijrah was the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah signed?  (A) 4 AH  (B) 5 AH  (C) 6 AH  (D) 8 AH
> C. Remember the order Badr 2, Uhud 3, Trench 5, Hudaybiyyah 6, Makkah 8.
> The Farewell Sermon taught that  (A) Arabs are superior to non-Arabs  (B) no one is superior except by piety and good action  (C) wealth decides status  (D) tribes should keep old feuds
> B. The sermon declared human equality and cancelled feuds and interest from the days of ignorance.
## Family
- Wives include Khadijah, Sawdah, Aisha, Hafsa, Umm Salamah and Zaynab (RA). His son Ibrahim was born to Mariyah al-Qibtiyyah (RA) and died in infancy.
- Daughters: Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah (RA). Fatimah (RA) married Ali (RA); their sons were Hasan and Husain (RA).
## Traps
! The first mosque was Quba, not Masjid an-Nabawi.
! The Cave of Hira is linked with revelation; the Cave of Thawr with the Hijrah.
! The conquest of Makkah was in 8 AH, two years after Hudaybiyyah, not 10 AH.
## Quick check
- Born about 570 CE; revelation 610 CE at 40; Hijrah 622 CE; passed away 11 AH at 63.
- Badr 2, Uhud 3, Khandaq 5, Hudaybiyyah 6, Khaybar 7, Makkah 8, Tabuk 9, Farewell Hajj 10.
- Caves: Hira (revelation), Thawr (Hijrah). First mosque: Quba.

title: Algebra
lines: USAT Mathematics algebra questions are quick HSSC exercises: evaluate or invert a function, use the sum and product of roots, find a term or sum of a progression, multiply or invert a matrix, count arrangements, or pick out a term of a binomial expansion. There is no calculator, so the numbers are chosen to work out neatly; if your working gets messy, check your method.
## Functions
- A function gives exactly one output for each input. The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs.
- Domain rules: no division by zero, no square root of a negative number, logarithms only of positive numbers.
- Composition: (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)); apply g first. In general f∘g ≠ g∘f.
- Inverse: write y = f(x), swap x and y and solve for y. Only a one-one function has an inverse, and the graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in the line y = x.
- Even functions satisfy f(−x) = f(x) (symmetric about the y-axis); odd functions satisfy f(−x) = −f(x).
- Laws of logarithms: log(mn) = log m + log n, log(m/n) = log m − log n, log mⁿ = n log m, and logₐb = log b ÷ log a.
## Quadratic equations
For ax² + bx + c = 0, the roots are x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a.
- Sum of roots α + β = −b/a; product αβ = c/a. The equation with roots α, β is x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0.
- Useful forms: α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ and (α − β)² = (α + β)² − 4αβ.
| Discriminant b² − 4ac | Nature of roots
| positive perfect square | real, unequal, rational
| positive, not a square | real, unequal, irrational
| zero | real and equal
| negative | complex conjugates
- Cube roots of unity: 1, ω, ω², where ω³ = 1 and 1 + ω + ω² = 0.
> Example 1. If α and β are the roots of 2x² − 6x + 3 = 0, find α² + β².
## Sequences and series
- Arithmetic progression: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d; Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n − 1)d] = (n/2)(first + last). Arithmetic mean of a and b = (a + b)/2.
- Geometric progression: aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹; Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r); infinite sum a/(1 − r) when |r| < 1. Geometric mean of a and b = √(ab).
- Harmonic progression: the reciprocals form an AP. Harmonic mean of a and b = 2ab/(a + b).
- For positive unequal numbers, A > G > H and G² = AH.
> Example 2. The 5th term of an AP is 14 and the 10th term is 29. Find the sum of the first 20 terms.
## Matrices and determinants
- A product AB exists only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. In general AB ≠ BA.
- For A = [[a, b], [c, d]], |A| = ad − bc and A⁻¹ = (1/|A|)[[d, −b], [−c, a]]. A singular matrix (|A| = 0) has no inverse.
- (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ and (AB)ᵗ = BᵗAᵗ: the order reverses.
- Determinants: swapping two rows changes the sign; two equal rows give zero; for an n × n matrix, |kA| = kⁿ|A|.
- A system AX = B has a unique solution X = A⁻¹B when |A| ≠ 0 (Cramer's rule gives the same result).
## Permutations and combinations
- Fundamental principle: if one task can be done in m ways and another in n ways, both can be done in mn ways.
- Arrangements of r things from n: ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!. Selections: ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Remember 0! = 1.
- n things with p alike and q alike: n!/(p! q!). n people round a table: (n − 1)!.
- ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ, so ⁿCₓ = ⁿCᵧ means x = y or x + y = n.
- Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes; P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
> Example 3. A committee of 3 men and 2 women is chosen from 5 men and 4 women. In how many ways can it be formed?
> ⁵C₃ × ⁴C₂ = 10 × 6 = 60 ways.
## Binomial theorem
- (a + b)ⁿ has n + 1 terms; the general term is Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ.
- The sum of the coefficients is 2ⁿ (put a = b = 1).
- For n even there is one middle term, T(n/2 + 1); for n odd there are two.
- For any n and |x| < 1: (1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)x²/2! + …, an endless series when n is negative or a fraction.
> Example 4. Find the term independent of x in (x + 1/x)⁶.
> Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁶Cᵣ x⁶⁻ʳ x⁻ʳ = ⁶Cᵣ x⁶⁻²ʳ. The power is zero when r = 3, giving ⁶C₃ = 20.
! The rth term of a binomial expansion uses ⁿCᵣ₋₁, not ⁿCᵣ.
! f⁻¹(x) means the inverse function, not 1/f(x).
! Order matters for arrangements (permutations) but not for selections (combinations): a team is a combination.
## Quick check
- Sum of roots of 3x² + 6x − 1 = 0? (−2)
- Infinite sum of 1 + ½ + ¼ + …? (2)
- Number of terms in (x + y)¹⁰? (11)
- 3 × 3 matrix with |A| = 2: value of |3A|? (54)
- Ways to arrange the letters of LEVEL? (30)

title: Analytic Geometry and Vectors
lines: USAT analytic geometry questions use coordinates: distances and midpoints, slopes and equations of lines, the distance from a point to a line, circles from their equations, the focus and eccentricity of a conic, and vector products. Learn each standard form well enough to read off its key facts without working.
## Points
- Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂): √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Midpoint: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
- The point dividing the join in the ratio m : n internally is ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)).
- Centroid of a triangle: the average of the three vertices.
- Area of a triangle with vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃) = ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|. Zero area means the points are collinear.
## Straight lines
| Form | Equation
| Slope-intercept | y = mx + c
| Point-slope | y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
| Two-intercept | x/a + y/b = 1
| Normal | x cos α + y sin α = p
| General | ax + by + c = 0, slope −a/b
- Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = tan α, where α is the angle with the positive x-axis.
- Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have m₁m₂ = −1.
- Angle between two lines: tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.
- Distance from (x₁, y₁) to ax + by + c = 0: |ax₁ + by₁ + c| ÷ √(a² + b²). Between parallel lines ax + by + c₁ = 0 and ax + by + c₂ = 0: |c₁ − c₂| ÷ √(a² + b²).
> Example 1. Find the line through (2, 3) parallel to 3x − 4y + 5 = 0.
> A parallel line is 3x − 4y + k = 0. Substituting (2, 3): 6 − 12 + k = 0, so k = 6. The line is 3x − 4y + 6 = 0.
## Circles
- Centre (h, k), radius r: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².
- General form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: centre (−g, −f), radius √(g² + f² − c).
- Tangent to x² + y² = r² at (x₁, y₁): xx₁ + yy₁ = r². A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
- A line touches a circle when its distance from the centre equals the radius.
> Example 2. Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 8y = 0.
> 2g = −6 and 2f = 8, so g = −3, f = 4 and the centre is (3, −4). r = √(9 + 16 − 0) = 5. The circle passes through the origin.
## Conic sections
Each conic is the locus of points whose distance from a focus is e times the distance from a directrix: e = 1 parabola, e < 1 ellipse, e > 1 hyperbola.
| Conic | Standard form | Key facts
| Parabola | y² = 4ax | focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a, latus rectum 4a
| Ellipse (a > b) | x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 | c² = a² − b², foci (±c, 0), e = c/a
| Hyperbola | x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 | c² = a² + b², foci (±c, 0), asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x
- Parabolas x² = 4ay open upwards with focus (0, a).
- For an ellipse, the sum of the distances from any point to the two foci is 2a; for a hyperbola the difference is 2a.
- A rectangular hyperbola (a = b) has e = √2.
> Example 3. Find the foci and eccentricity of x²/169 + y²/144 = 1.
> a² = 169 and b² = 144, so c² = 25 and c = 5. Foci (±5, 0); e = c/a = 5/13.
## Vectors
- v = xi + yj + zk has magnitude |v| = √(x² + y² + z²); the unit vector is v/|v|. The vector from A to B is OB − OA.
- Direction cosines are x/|v|, y/|v|, z/|v|; the squares add up to 1.
- Dot product a·b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃, a scalar. a·b = 0 means the vectors are perpendicular.
- Projection of a on b = a·b ÷ |b|. Work done = F·d.
- Cross product a × b has size |a||b| sin θ and is perpendicular to both; a × b = −(b × a). i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j.
- Area of a parallelogram = |a × b|; of a triangle = ½|a × b|. Parallel vectors give a × b = 0.
- Scalar triple product a·(b × c) is the volume of a parallelepiped; it is zero when the vectors are coplanar.
> Example 4. Find the angle between a = i + j and b = j + k.
! From ax + by + c = 0 the slope is −a/b, not a/b. For 2x + 3y = 6 it is −2/3.
! In y² = 8x, 4a = 8 gives a = 2, so the focus is (2, 0), not (8, 0).
! Ellipse uses c² = a² − b²; hyperbola uses c² = a² + b². Mixing them is the commonest conic error.
## Quick check
- Distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6)? (5)
- Slope of a line perpendicular to y = 3x + 1? (−1/3)
- Radius of x² + y² = 49? (7)
- Eccentricity of any parabola? (1)
- Is i + 2j perpendicular to 2i − j? (yes, the dot product is 0)

title: Calculus
lines: Calculus questions in USAT ask you to evaluate a limit, differentiate with the product, quotient or chain rule, find a slope, a maximum or a rate, and evaluate an indefinite or definite integral or an area. They are standard HSSC exercises; the skill is recognising the right rule at once and avoiding sign slips.
## Limits
- If substituting gives a number, that is the limit. If it gives 0/0, factorise or rationalise, cancel, then substitute.
- Standard limits (x in radians): sin x/x → 1 and tan x/x → 1 as x → 0; (1 − cos x)/x² → ½; (eˣ − 1)/x → 1; (aˣ − 1)/x → ln a; (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e as n → ∞; (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) → naⁿ⁻¹ as x → a.
- Rational functions as x → ∞: compare the highest powers. Lower on top gives 0; equal powers give the ratio of leading coefficients; higher on top has no finite limit.
- f is continuous at a when f(a) exists and the left and right limits both equal f(a).
> Example 1. Find the limit of (x² − 9)/(x − 3) as x → 3, and of sin 3x / x as x → 0.
## Differentiation rules
- Definition: f′(x) = lim (h → 0) [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h, the slope of the tangent.
- Power rule: d/dx (xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹. Constants differentiate to zero.
- Product: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′. Quotient: (u/v)′ = (vu′ − uv′)/v². Chain: dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx).
- Implicit functions: differentiate every term with respect to x, writing dy/dx for each y term, then collect.
- Parametric form: dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt).
| sin x | cos x
| cos x | −sin x
| tan x | sec²x
| eˣ | eˣ
| aˣ | aˣ ln a
| ln x | 1/x
| sin⁻¹x | 1/√(1 − x²)
| tan⁻¹x | 1/(1 + x²)
> Example 2. Differentiate x² sin x and e³ˣ.
> Product rule: 2x sin x + x² cos x. Chain rule: e³ˣ × 3 = 3e³ˣ.
## Applications of derivatives
- The slope of the tangent at x = a is f′(a); the normal has slope −1/f′(a). Tangent line: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
- f is increasing where f′(x) > 0 and decreasing where f′(x) < 0.
- At a stationary point f′(x) = 0. If f″ < 0 there it is a maximum; if f″ > 0 it is a minimum.
- Rates: if s is displacement, velocity v = ds/dt and acceleration a = dv/dt.
- Small changes: δy ≈ f′(x) δx.
> Example 3. Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x) = x³ − 3x.
> f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = ±1. f″(x) = 6x: at x = −1, f″ < 0, a maximum, f(−1) = 2; at x = 1, f″ > 0, a minimum, f(1) = −2.
## Integration
Integration reverses differentiation; add a constant C to every indefinite integral.
| f(x) | ∫ f(x) dx
| 1/x | ln|x|
| eᵃˣ | eᵃˣ/a
| sin ax | −cos ax / a
| cos ax | sin ax / a
| sec²x | tan x
| 1/(1 + x²) | tan⁻¹x
| 1/√(1 − x²) | sin⁻¹x
- ∫ f′(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C, for example ∫ 2x/(x² + 1) dx = ln(x² + 1) + C.
- Substitution: replace an inner function by u and its derivative by du.
- By parts: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. Choose u in the order ILATE: inverse trig, logarithmic, algebraic, trigonometric, exponential. For example ∫ x eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1) + C.
- Partial fractions split rational functions: 1/(x(x + 1)) = 1/x − 1/(x + 1).
- Trigonometric powers: ∫ sin²x dx = x/2 − (sin 2x)/4 + C, using sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2.
## Definite integrals and area
- ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative. Swapping the limits changes the sign.
- For an odd function the integral from −a to a is 0; for an even function it is twice the integral from 0 to a.
- Area between a curve and the x-axis from a to b is ∫ |y| dx; area between two curves is ∫ (upper − lower) dx.
- Volume when y = f(x) turns about the x-axis: V = π ∫ y² dx.
- Differential equations: separate the variables and integrate both sides. dy/dx = ky gives y = Ae^(kx).
> Example 4. Evaluate the integral of 3x² + 2x from x = 0 to x = 1, and find the area between y = x² and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 3.
> [x³ + x²] from 0 to 1 = (1 + 1) − 0 = 2. Area = [x³/3] from 0 to 3 = 27/3 = 9 square units.
! In the quotient rule the order matters: bottom times derivative of the top comes first.
! ∫ 1/(1 + x²) dx is tan⁻¹x, not ln(1 + x²): the top must be the derivative of the bottom for the log rule.
! Area below the x-axis comes out negative; split the integral where the curve crosses the axis and add the sizes.
## Quick check
- Derivative of ln(3x)? (1/x)
- Limit of (1 − cos x)/x² as x → 0? (½)
- Slope of y = x³ at x = 2? (12)
- ∫ cos 2x dx? (½ sin 2x + C)
- Value of the integral of sin x from 0 to π? (2)

title: Trigonometry
lines: USAT trigonometry questions check standard values, signs in the four quadrants, identities, compound and double angles, periods, solutions of simple equations, and the principal values of inverse functions. Fast recall of the standard table and the main identities is the key; most answers need two lines.
## Angles and standard values
- π radians = 180°, so 1 rad ≈ 57.3°. Arc length l = rθ and sector area = ½r²θ, with θ in radians.
| θ | sin θ | cos θ | tan θ
| 90° (π/2) | 1 | 0 | undefined
- Memory aid: sin 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° = √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2; cos runs the list backwards.
## Signs and identities
- "All Students Take Coffee": in quadrant I all ratios are positive, in II sin (and cosec), in III tan (and cot), in IV cos (and sec).
- Pythagorean identities: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.
- Negative angles: sin(−θ) = −sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ, tan(−θ) = −tan θ.
- Allied angles: 90° ± θ and 270° ± θ change sin to cos and tan to cot; 180° ± θ and 360° − θ keep the same ratio. The sign comes from the quadrant.
## Compound and double angles
- sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B.
- cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B (the sign flips).
- tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B).
> Example 1. Find sin 75° exactly.
- sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A; tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 − tan²A).
> Example 2. sin A = 3/5 and A lies in quadrant II. Find cos A, tan A and sin 2A.
> cos A = −√(1 − 9/25) = −4/5 (cos is negative in quadrant II). tan A = −3/4. sin 2A = 2 × 3/5 × (−4/5) = −24/25.
- Half angles: sin²(A/2) = (1 − cos A)/2 and cos²(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2.
- Triple angles: sin 3A = 3 sin A − 4 sin³A and cos 3A = 4 cos³A − 3 cos A.
- Sum to product: sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2); cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2).
## Graphs and periods
| Function | Range | Period
| sin x, cos x | −1 to 1 | 2π
| tan x, cot x | all real numbers | π
| sec x, cosec x | ≤ −1 or ≥ 1 | 2π
- sin(ax + b) and cos(ax + b) have period 2π/|a|; tan(ax + b) has period π/|a|.
- a sin x + b cos x lies between −√(a² + b²) and +√(a² + b²); for example, 3 sin x + 4 cos x has a maximum of 5.
## Laws for any triangle
- Sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R, where R is the circumradius.
- Cosine rule: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.
- Area = ½bc sin A, or Hero's formula √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) with s = (a + b + c)/2.
## Trigonometric equations
- First find the principal solution, then all the angles in the required interval using the quadrant signs.
- General solutions (n any integer): sin θ = 0 gives θ = nπ; cos θ = 0 gives θ = (2n + 1)π/2; tan θ = k gives θ = α + nπ; cos θ = k gives θ = 2nπ ± α; sin θ = k gives θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿα.
- Quadratic equations in sin θ or cos θ: factorise, then reject any value outside −1 to 1.
> Example 3. Solve 2cos²θ − 3cos θ + 1 = 0 for 0 ≤ θ < 2π.
> (2cos θ − 1)(cos θ − 1) = 0, so cos θ = ½ or 1. cos θ = ½ gives π/3 and 5π/3; cos θ = 1 gives 0. The solutions are 0, π/3 and 5π/3.
## Inverse trigonometric functions
| Function | Domain | Principal values
| sin⁻¹x | −1 ≤ x ≤ 1 | −π/2 to π/2
| cos⁻¹x | −1 ≤ x ≤ 1 | 0 to π
| tan⁻¹x | all real x | between −π/2 and π/2
- sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 and tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2.
- tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)) when xy < 1.
- cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x, but sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹x.
> Example 4. Evaluate tan⁻¹(1/2) + tan⁻¹(1/3).
! sin⁻¹(sin θ) = θ only when θ lies between −π/2 and π/2. So sin⁻¹(sin 5π/6) = π/6.
! Never divide both sides of an equation by sin θ or cos θ: you lose the solutions where it is zero. Factorise instead.
! Use radians in l = rθ and in calculus; degrees give wrong answers.
## Quick check
- Value of cos 60° + sin 30°? (1)
- Period of sin 3x? (2π/3)
- Sign of tan 200°? (positive, quadrant III)
- Simplify 1 − 2sin²15°. (cos 30° = √3/2)
- Principal value of cos⁻¹(−½)? (2π/3)

title: Constitution and Government
lines: USAT asks how Pakistan's constitutions developed and how the state is organised under the 1973 Constitution: the houses of Parliament, the President and Prime Minister, the courts and the constitutional bodies. Questions use stable facts. They do not ask who holds office today, and numbers of seats change by amendment, so learn the structure rather than seat counts.
## Road to a constitution
- Until 1956 Pakistan was governed under the Government of India Act 1935, adapted, with the Governor-General as head of state.

- The Objectives Resolution was moved by Liaquat Ali Khan and passed by the first Constituent Assembly on 12 March 1949. It declared that sovereignty belongs to Allah, exercised by the people within limits He has set, and promised democracy, freedom, equality, tolerance, social justice and protection of minorities. It became the preamble of later constitutions and, in 1985, a substantive part of the 1973 Constitution.
- The first Constituent Assembly was dissolved in 1954. The One Unit scheme (1955) merged the provinces of West Pakistan into one province.
## Three constitutions compared
| Enforced | 23 March 1956 | 8 June 1962 | 14 August 1973
| System | parliamentary | presidential | federal parliamentary
| Legislature | one house | one house | two houses: National Assembly and Senate
| Election of President | by assemblies | through Basic Democracies (indirect) | electoral college of both houses and provincial assemblies
| Ended | martial law, October 1958 | abrogated, March 1969 | in force (with amendments)
- The 1956 Constitution named the country the Islamic Republic of Pakistan and was based on parity between East and West Pakistan. Iskander Mirza became the first President.
- The 1962 Constitution was given by Ayub Khan and made the President powerful. The first general elections on adult franchise came later, in December 1970.

- The 1973 Constitution was passed by the National Assembly on 10 April 1973 and enforced on 14 August 1973. It was framed by an assembly elected on adult franchise and was agreed by all the major parties.
## Structure under the 1973 Constitution
| Body | Key facts
| Majlis-e-Shoora (Parliament) | the President, the National Assembly and the Senate
| National Assembly | elected directly; term five years unless dissolved earlier; presided over by the Speaker; elects the Prime Minister
| Senate | equal representation of the provinces; members serve six years, half retiring every three years; never dissolved; presided over by the Chairman
| President | head of state; term five years; must be a Muslim of at least 45; Chairman of the Senate acts in his absence
| Prime Minister | head of government; leads the federal cabinet, which answers to the National Assembly
| Governor | appointed by the President for each province
| Chief Minister | head of a provincial government, elected by the provincial assembly
## Courts and constitutional bodies
- Supreme Court: highest court; High Courts in each province and Islamabad.
- Federal Shariat Court (1980): examines whether laws are repugnant to the injunctions of Islam.
- Council of Islamic Ideology: advises Parliament on bringing laws in line with Islam.
- Council of Common Interests: settles federal-provincial policy matters. National Finance Commission: shares federal revenue among provinces.
- Election Commission of Pakistan: conducts elections.
## Articles worth knowing
| Article | Subject
| 2 | Islam is the state religion
| 6 | high treason
| 8 | laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void
| 25 | equality of citizens
| 251 | Urdu is the national language
> Which feature belongs only to the 1973 Constitution?  (A) parliamentary system  (B) Islamic Republic as the name  (C) a two-house Parliament  (D) indirect election through Basic Democracies
> C. The 1956 Constitution was also parliamentary and used the name Islamic Republic; Basic Democracies belonged to 1962. Only 1973 created the Senate.

> A bill passed by the National Assembly is rejected by the Senate. Under the Constitution it may be referred to  (A) the Supreme Court  (B) a joint sitting of Parliament  (C) the President alone  (D) a referendum
> B. Disagreement between the houses is resolved in a joint sitting.
## Traps
! The Objectives Resolution was passed in 1949 but the first constitution only in 1956.
! The Senate is the house of equal provincial representation; the National Assembly seats follow population.
! The 18th Amendment (2010) increased provincial autonomy and renamed NWFP as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
## Quick check
- Constitutions: 1956 parliamentary, 1962 presidential, 1973 federal parliamentary.
- 1973: passed 10 April, enforced 14 August; two houses.
- NA five years; Senate six-year terms, half every three; President at least 45.

title: Culture and Economy
lines: This topic covers Pakistan's national symbols, languages, heritage sites, crops, minerals and industries. USAT asks short factual questions, so learn the tables. Figures such as output or population change from year to year; the test avoids them, and so should your revision.
## National symbols
| Symbol | Fact
| National language | Urdu (English is also used for official purposes)
| National anthem | lyrics by Hafeez Jalandhari, music by Ahmed G. Chagla; approved in 1954
| National flag | dark green with a white band at the hoist; crescent and star; adopted on 11 August 1947
| National poet | Allama Muhammad Iqbal
| National animal | markhor
| National bird | chukar partridge
| National tree | deodar
| National flower | jasmine (chambeli)
| National fruit | mango
| National dress | shalwar kameez
| Motto | Faith, Unity, Discipline (Iman, Ittehad, Nazm)
- On the flag, green stands for the Muslim majority and white for religious minorities. The crescent stands for progress and the star for light and knowledge.
## Languages
- Urdu is the national language and the main link language. Punjabi is the most widely spoken mother tongue.
- Other major languages: Pashto (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa), Sindhi (Sindh), Balochi and Brahui (Balochistan), Saraiki (southern Punjab), Hindko, Shina and Balti in the north.
## Heritage sites (UNESCO World Heritage)
| Site | Province | Note
| Mohenjo-daro | Sindh | Indus Valley city; the Great Bath
| Taxila | Punjab | Gandhara centre of Buddhist learning
| Takht-i-Bahi and Sahr-i-Bahlol | Khyber Pakhtunkhwa | Buddhist monastery ruins
| Makli monuments, Thatta | Sindh | one of the largest graveyards in the world
| Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens | Punjab | Mughal; the gardens built by Shah Jahan
| Rohtas Fort | Punjab | built by Sher Shah Suri near Jhelum
Other landmarks: Harappa (Punjab), Badshahi Mosque, Lahore (built by Aurangzeb), Faisal Mosque, Islamabad, Minar-e-Pakistan, Lahore, and the Mazar-e-Quaid, Karachi.
## Poets, saints and literature
| Figure | Language or place | Remember
| Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai | Sindhi | Shah Jo Risalo; shrine at Bhit Shah
| Waris Shah | Punjabi | the verse romance Heer
| Bulleh Shah | Punjabi | Sufi poet buried at Kasur
| Khushal Khan Khattak | Pashto | warrior-poet
| Rahman Baba | Pashto | Sufi poet of Peshawar
| Data Ganj Bakhsh (Ali Hujwiri) | Lahore | author of Kashf al-Mahjub
| Lal Shahbaz Qalandar | Sehwan, Sindh | famous Sufi shrine

- Cultural events include the Shandur Polo Festival, played on one of the world's highest polo grounds between Chitral and Gilgit teams. Lok Virsa in Islamabad preserves folk heritage, music and crafts.
## Agriculture
| Season | Sown | Crops
| Rabi | autumn and winter, harvested in spring | wheat, gram, barley, mustard
| Kharif | summer, harvested in autumn | rice, cotton, sugarcane, maize
- Wheat is the staple food. Cotton feeds the textile industry, the largest manufacturing sector and the main export earner.
- Sargodha is famous for citrus (kinnow); Multan and the Sindh belt for mangoes.
## Minerals and energy
| Resource | Where
| Natural gas | Sui, Balochistan (discovered 1952)
| Rock salt | Khewra, Salt Range
| Lignite coal | Thar, Sindh
| Copper and gold | Saindak and Reko Diq, Chagai, Balochistan
| Hydropower | Tarbela and Mangla dams
## Industries and cities
| City | Known for
| Faisalabad | textiles (the Manchester of Pakistan)
| Sialkot | sports goods and surgical instruments
| Gujranwala | metal and electrical goods
| Karachi | port, steel (Pakistan Steel Mills), finance
| Gujrat | ceramics and fans
| Hyderabad | bangles
- The State Bank of Pakistan is the central bank. It was inaugurated by Quaid-e-Azam on 1 July 1948.
> Which crop is sown in the rabi season?  (A) rice  (B) cotton  (C) wheat  (D) sugarcane
> C. Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in spring. The others are kharif crops.
> The Shalimar Gardens in Lahore were laid out by  (A) Akbar  (B) Shah Jahan  (C) Aurangzeb  (D) Jahangir
> B. Shah Jahan also built the Taj Mahal; Aurangzeb built the Badshahi Mosque.
## Traps
! White on the flag represents minorities, not peace.
! Rohtas Fort was built by Sher Shah Suri, not a Mughal emperor.
! Urdu is the national language; Punjabi has the most native speakers. The two facts are not in conflict.
## Quick check
- Markhor, chukar, deodar, jasmine, mango.
- Anthem: Hafeez Jalandhari (words), Ahmed G. Chagla (music).
- Six UNESCO sites: Mohenjo-daro, Taxila, Takht-i-Bahi, Makli, Lahore Fort with Shalimar, Rohtas.
- Rabi wheat; kharif rice, cotton, sugarcane, maize.

title: Geography of Pakistan
lines: USAT geography questions ask about Pakistan's provinces and capitals, neighbours, rivers and their dams and barrages, mountain ranges and peaks, passes, deserts, glaciers and lakes. These facts are stable and appear often, so tables are the best way to learn them.
## Location and neighbours
- Pakistan lies in South Asia, with the Arabian Sea to the south.
| Direction | Neighbour | Note
| East | India | the Radcliffe Line (1947) divided Punjab and Bengal
| North-east | China | linked by the Karakoram Highway through the Khunjerab Pass
| West and north-west | Afghanistan | the Durand Line (1893)
| South-west | Iran | border in Balochistan
- The narrow Wakhan Corridor of Afghanistan separates Pakistan from Tajikistan.
## Administrative units
| Unit | Capital | Remember
| Punjab | Lahore | most populous province
| Sindh | Karachi | largest city and main port
| Khyber Pakhtunkhwa | Peshawar | named NWFP until 2010
| Balochistan | Quetta | largest province by area, about 44 % of the country
| Islamabad Capital Territory | Islamabad | federal capital since the 1960s
| Gilgit-Baltistan | Gilgit | high mountains and glaciers
| Azad Jammu and Kashmir | Muzaffarabad | its own government
## Rivers
- The Indus rises in Tibet near Lake Mansarovar, flows through Gilgit-Baltistan, enters the plains and falls into the Arabian Sea near Keti Bandar in Sindh.
- Eastern tributaries: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Sutlej (and the Beas in India). They join to form the Panjnad, which meets the Indus near Mithankot.
- Western tributaries: Kabul (joins at Attock), Swat, Kurram, Gomal.
- Indus Waters Treaty (1960), arranged by the World Bank: the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) went to Pakistan; the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) to India.
## Dams and barrages
| Structure | River | Remember
| Tarbela Dam | Indus | one of the world's largest earth-filled dams
| Mangla Dam | Jhelum | in Azad Kashmir, near Mirpur
| Warsak Dam | Kabul | near Peshawar
| Sukkur Barrage | Indus | opened 1932; once called Lloyd Barrage
| Kotri, Guddu, Taunsa barrages | Indus | irrigation canals in Sindh and Punjab
## Mountains and peaks
| Range | Highest peak | Note
| Karakoram | K2 (8,611 m) | world's second-highest peak; Baltoro and Siachen glaciers
| Himalaya | Nanga Parbat (8,126 m) | the Killer Mountain
| Hindu Kush | Tirich Mir (7,708 m) | in Chitral
| Salt Range | Sakesar | Khewra salt mine
| Sulaiman and Kirthar ranges | — | western mountains of Balochistan and Sindh
## Passes
| Pass | Links
| Khyber | Peshawar and Afghanistan
| Bolan | Quetta with Sibi and the plains
| Khunjerab | Pakistan and China (Karakoram Highway)
| Lowari | Dir and Chitral
| Kohat, Gomal, Tochi | routes through the western hills
| Babusar | Kaghan valley and Chilas
## Climate
- Most of Pakistan is arid or semi-arid. The south and the plains have very hot summers; Jacobabad and Sibi are among the hottest places in the country.
- The summer monsoon (roughly July to September) brings most of the rain to the north-east, especially upper Punjab and Kashmir. Winter rain and snow come from western disturbances.
- The northern mountains are cold, with heavy snow, and feed the rivers through melting glaciers in summer. This is why river flows and floods peak in the hot months.
## Natural regions
- Northern mountains: Karakoram, Himalaya and Hindu Kush.
- Western mountains: Sulaiman, Kirthar and the ranges of Balochistan.
- Indus plain: the fertile, irrigated heartland of Punjab and Sindh.
- Plateaus and deserts: Potohar, Balochistan, Thar, Cholistan and Thal.
- Coastal areas: the Makran coast of Balochistan and the Indus delta with mangrove forests.
## Deserts, plateaus and lakes
- Deserts: Thar (Sindh), Cholistan (Punjab), Thal (between Indus and Jhelum), Kharan (Balochistan).
- Plateaus: Potohar (between the Indus and Jhelum) and the Balochistan plateau.
- Lakes: Manchar (largest freshwater lake, Sindh), Keenjhar or Kalri (water for Karachi), Saiful Muluk (Kaghan valley).
- Ports: Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar. Gwadar was bought from Oman in 1958.
> The Kabul River joins the Indus at  (A) Mithankot  (B) Attock  (C) Tarbela  (D) Sukkur
> B. Mithankot is where the Panjnad meets the Indus, a common mix-up.
> Under the Indus Waters Treaty, which river went to India?  (A) Jhelum  (B) Chenab  (C) Ravi  (D) Indus
> C. Remember "western to Pakistan": Indus, Jhelum, Chenab. The eastern rivers Ravi, Beas and Sutlej went to India.
## Traps
! Punjab is the most populous province, but Balochistan is the largest by area.
! K2 is in the Karakoram, not the Himalaya; Nanga Parbat is in the Himalaya.
! Mangla is on the Jhelum and Tarbela on the Indus. Do not swap them.
## Quick check
- Neighbours: India, China, Afghanistan, Iran.
- Capitals: Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar, Quetta; Gilgit; Muzaffarabad.
- K2 Karakoram; Nanga Parbat Himalaya; Tirich Mir Hindu Kush.
- Khyber–Peshawar; Bolan–Quetta; Khunjerab–China.

title: Pakistan Movement
lines: The Pakistan Movement is the biggest Pakistan Studies topic in USAT. Questions ask for the year of an event, the leader linked to a resolution or session, the aim of a reform, or the place where something happened. The span is 1857 to 1947. Learn the timeline in order; cause and effect then make the dates easy to remember.
## After 1857: Muslim revival
- The War of Independence (1857) failed; the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was exiled to Rangoon, and the British Crown took over from the East India Company (1858).

- Sir Syed Ahmad Khan wrote Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind on the causes of the revolt and urged Muslims to take up modern education. He founded the Scientific Society (1864) and the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental School at Aligarh (1875), which became a college in 1877. This was the Aligarh Movement.
- The Hindi-Urdu controversy (1867, Banaras) convinced Sir Syed that Hindus and Muslims were separate nations, an early form of the Two-Nation Theory.
- The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885. Sir Syed advised Muslims to stay away from it.
## Timeline 1905–1947
| Year | Event
| 1905 | Partition of Bengal by Lord Curzon; Muslims of East Bengal welcomed it
| 1906 | Simla Deputation under Sir Aga Khan III meets Lord Minto (1 October); All-India Muslim League founded at Dhaka (30 December)
| 1909 | Minto-Morley Reforms grant separate electorates
| 1911 | Partition of Bengal annulled
| 1913 | Jinnah joins the Muslim League
| 1916 | Lucknow Pact: Congress accepts separate electorates; Jinnah called Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity
| 1919 | Rowlatt Act; Jallianwala Bagh at Amritsar; Government of India Act introduces dyarchy
| 1919–1924 | Khilafat Movement led by Maulana Muhammad Ali Jauhar and Shaukat Ali
| 1927–1928 | Simon Commission (no Indian member); Nehru Report (1928) rejects separate electorates
| 1929 | Jinnah's Fourteen Points
| 1930 | Allama Iqbal's Allahabad Address calls for a Muslim state in north-west India
| 1930–1932 | Round Table Conferences in London
| 1933 | Chaudhry Rahmat Ali's pamphlet Now or Never proposes the name Pakistan
| 1935 | Government of India Act: provincial autonomy
| 1937 | Provincial elections; Congress ministries formed
| 1939 | Day of Deliverance (22 December) after Congress ministries resign
| 1940 | Lahore Resolution, moved on 23 March by A. K. Fazlul Huq at Minto Park, Lahore
| 1942 | Cripps Mission; Quit India Movement
| 1944 | Gandhi-Jinnah talks in Bombay
| 1945 | Simla Conference fails
| 1945–1946 | General elections: the League wins all Muslim seats in the Central Assembly
| 1946 | Cabinet Mission Plan; Direct Action Day (16 August)
| 1947 | 3 June Plan by Lord Mountbatten; Indian Independence Act (July); Pakistan comes into being on 14 August
## The Lahore Resolution

The Muslim League session at Lahore (22–24 March 1940) was presided over by Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The resolution, moved by Fazlul Huq on 23 March, demanded that the Muslim-majority areas in the north-west and east of India be grouped into independent states. The Hindu press called it the Pakistan Resolution, and the name stuck. Minar-e-Pakistan now stands at the site, in today's Iqbal Park.
## Key leaders
| Leader | Remember
| Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah | born Karachi, 25 December 1876; first Governor-General; died 11 September 1948
| Allama Muhammad Iqbal | born Sialkot, 1877; poet-philosopher; Allahabad Address 1930; died 1938
| Liaquat Ali Khan | first Prime Minister; moved the Objectives Resolution; assassinated in Rawalpindi, 1951
| Fatima Jinnah | Madar-e-Millat, the Mother of the Nation
| Sir Aga Khan III | led the Simla Deputation; first permanent president of the League
| Chaudhry Rahmat Ali | coined the name Pakistan (1933)
> Which reform first gave Muslims separate electorates?  (A) Lucknow Pact  (B) Minto-Morley Reforms  (C) Government of India Act 1935  (D) Nehru Report
> B. Separate electorates came with the 1909 reforms. Congress accepted them in the 1916 Lucknow Pact; the Nehru Report tried to remove them.
> Muslims celebrated the Day of Deliverance in 1939 because  (A) Pakistan was created  (B) the Congress ministries resigned  (C) the Simon Commission left  (D) Bengal was partitioned
> B. The League saw the end of the 1937–39 Congress ministries as relief from unfair rule.
## Traps
! The Lahore Resolution was moved by Fazlul Huq, but the session was presided over by Jinnah.
! The name Pakistan came from Rahmat Ali (1933), not from Iqbal's 1930 address, which did not use the word.
! The Muslim League was founded in Dhaka, not Lahore or Aligarh.
## Quick check
- 1857 revolt; 1875 Aligarh; 1885 Congress; 1906 League; 1909 separate electorates.
- 1916 Lucknow; 1928 Nehru Report; 1929 Fourteen Points; 1930 Allahabad; 1933 the name.
- 1940 Lahore Resolution; 1946 Cabinet Mission; 3 June 1947 Plan; 14 August 1947.

title: Electricity and Magnetism
lines: Electricity and magnetism is the second big physics topic in USAT. Expect Coulomb's law and field questions, capacitors in series and parallel, resistor networks, EMF and internal resistance, force on a current or a moving charge, Faraday's and Lenz's laws, transformers and a few AC ideas. Learn the units as well as the formulas: several questions simply ask for the SI unit of a quantity.
## Electrostatics
- Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r², with k = 1/4πε₀ ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻². In a medium of relative permittivity ε(r) the force falls to F/ε(r).
- Electric field E = F/q (N/C, the same as V/m). For a point charge E = kq/r²; between parallel plates E = V/d.
- Electric potential V = kq/r is a scalar, so potentials from several charges simply add with their signs. Work to move charge q through a p.d. V is W = qV.
- 1 electronvolt (eV) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, the energy an electron gains through 1 V.
- Gauss's law: the total flux through a closed surface = (charge enclosed)/ε₀. The field inside a charged hollow conductor is zero.
## Capacitors
- C = Q/V (farad). Parallel plates: C = ε(r)ε₀A/d, so a dielectric raises C.
- Energy stored: ½CV² = ½QV = Q²/2C.
- Parallel: C = C₁ + C₂ (same V). Series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (same Q).
- An RC circuit has time constant RC: in that time a capacitor charges to about 63 % of its final charge.
! Capacitors combine the opposite way to resistors: series capacitors give a smaller total.
## Current electricity
- Current I = Q/t (ampere). Ohm's law V = IR holds for a metal at constant temperature.
- Resistance R = ρL/A; resistivity ρ depends on the material and temperature, not on the wire's shape. Stretching a wire to n times its length (volume fixed) multiplies R by n².
- Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + … Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … n equal resistors R in parallel give R/n.
> Example 1. Three 6 Ω resistors are available. Find the total resistance when all three are in parallel, and when two in parallel are joined in series with the third.
> All in parallel: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 Ω. Two in parallel give 3 Ω; adding 6 Ω in series gives 9 Ω.
- Metals' resistance rises with temperature; semiconductors' and thermistors' falls.
- Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Energy = Pt, often in kWh.
- A cell of EMF E and internal resistance r drives I = E/(R + r). Terminal p.d. V = E − Ir; on open circuit V = E.
- Kirchhoff's first rule: currents into a junction = currents out (charge conserved). Second rule: in any closed loop, sum of EMFs = sum of IR drops (energy conserved).
- Wheatstone bridge: balanced (no current in the galvanometer) when P/Q = R/S.
> Example 2. A cell of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to a 5 Ω resistor. Find the current and the terminal p.d.
> I = E/(R + r) = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A. V = IR = 2 × 5 = 10 V; the other 2 V is "lost" inside the cell.
## Magnetism
- Force on a current-carrying wire in a field: F = BIL sin θ. The tesla is defined from this: 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ = 1 Wb/m².
- Force on a moving charge: F = qvB sin θ. It is always at right angles to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed stays constant.
- A charge moving at right angles to B follows a circle of radius r = mv/qB.
- Field of a long straight wire: B = μ₀I/2πr. Inside a long solenoid: B = μ₀nI, where n is turns per metre; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A.
- A galvanometer becomes an ammeter with a small shunt resistance in parallel, and a voltmeter with a large resistance in series.
- Magnetic flux Φ = BA cos θ (weber), where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the area.
## Electromagnetic induction
- Faraday's law: induced EMF ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt. A rod of length L moving at speed v across a field B: ε = BLv.
- Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change that causes it. This follows from conservation of energy.
- Self-inductance: ε = −L ΔI/Δt (henry). Energy stored in an inductor = ½LI².
- AC generator: peak EMF = NBAω. Its EMF is zero when the coil's plane is at right angles to the field and greatest when the plane is parallel to it.
- Ideal transformer: V(s)/V(p) = N(s)/N(p) = I(p)/I(s). It works only on alternating current. Power is sent at high voltage so that the current, and the I²R loss, is small.
> Example 3. A transformer steps 220 V down to 11 V. Its primary has 2,000 turns. How many turns does the secondary have?
## Alternating current
- V(rms) = V₀/√2 ≈ 0.707V₀. Pakistan's 220 V mains is an rms value; its peak is about 311 V.
- Inductive reactance X(L) = 2πfL rises with frequency; capacitive reactance X(C) = 1/(2πfC) falls with it.
- In a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by 90°; in a pure capacitor it leads by 90°. Neither uses power on average.
- Series RLC resonance at f = 1/(2π√(LC)): impedance is least (Z = R) and current greatest.
> Example 4. Two point charges are 10 cm apart and repel with a force of 8 N. What is the force when they are moved to 20 cm apart?
> F ∝ 1/r². Doubling r divides F by 4, so the new force is 2 N.
! A magnetic force on a moving charge never changes its speed or kinetic energy, only its direction.
! A transformer cannot step up steady DC: with no change of flux, no EMF is induced.
! Ammeters have very low resistance and go in series; voltmeters have very high resistance and go in parallel.
## Quick check
- SI unit of magnetic flux density? (tesla)
- Two 4 μF capacitors in series: total? (2 μF)
- Frequency of AC doubled: X(L) and X(C)? (X(L) doubles, X(C) halves)
- Which law expresses conservation of energy in induction? (Lenz's law)
- EMF across a cell on open circuit? (equal to its EMF; no current, no lost volts)

title: Heat and Thermodynamics
lines: USAT heat questions test the kinetic theory of gases, the first law of thermodynamics applied to gas processes, specific heats of gases, and heat engines (Carnot efficiency and the second law). Almost every numerical requires temperatures in kelvin, which is where most marks are lost.
## Temperature
- T(K) = t(°C) + 273. Absolute zero is 0 K ≈ −273 °C, where the molecular kinetic energy of an ideal gas would be zero.
- Thermal equilibrium (zeroth law): if A and B are each in equilibrium with C, they are in equilibrium with each other. This is what makes a thermometer work.
- Heat energy Q = mcΔT for a temperature change, and Q = mL for a change of state at constant temperature.
## Kinetic theory of gases

Assumptions: a gas consists of a very large number of tiny molecules in random motion, colliding elastically; their own volume is negligible and they do not attract each other except during collisions.
- Pressure: P = ⅓ρ⟨v²⟩, produced by molecules striking the walls.
- Ideal gas equation: PV = nRT = NkT, with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and Boltzmann's constant k = R/Nₐ = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
- Average translational kinetic energy of one molecule = (3/2)kT, which depends only on temperature.
- Root mean square speed v(rms) = √(3RT/M) = √(3kT/m).
> Example 1. A gas is heated from 27 °C to 927 °C. By what factor does its rms speed change?
> In kelvin: 300 K to 1,200 K, four times larger. Since v(rms) ∝ √T, the speed doubles.
- At the same temperature, all gases have the same average molecular kinetic energy, but lighter molecules move faster: hydrogen molecules are four times faster than oxygen molecules.
## Internal energy and the first law
The internal energy U of an ideal gas is the total kinetic energy of its molecules and depends only on temperature.
First law: Q = ΔU + W, where Q is the heat given to the gas and W is the work done by the gas. (Some books write ΔU = Q − W; it is the same law.)
| Process | Condition | First law becomes
| Isothermal | ΔT = 0 | ΔU = 0, so Q = W
| Adiabatic | Q = 0 | W = −ΔU; expansion cools the gas
| Isochoric | ΔV = 0 | W = 0, so Q = ΔU
| Isobaric | ΔP = 0 | Q = ΔU + PΔV
> Example 2. A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. Find the change in its internal energy.
> ΔU = Q − W = 500 − 200 = +300 J. The internal energy rises, so the gas gets hotter.
- Work done by a gas = area under its P-V graph; for a cycle it is the area enclosed.
- An adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal one through the same point (PV^γ = constant against PV = constant).
> Example 3. A gas expands at a constant pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Find the work done.
## Molar specific heats
- C(v) is the heat needed per mole per kelvin at constant volume, C(p) at constant pressure.
- C(p) − C(v) = R, and γ = C(p)/C(v).
- Monatomic gases (He, Ar): C(v) = (3/2)R, γ = 5/3. Diatomic gases (N₂, O₂, air): C(v) = (5/2)R, γ = 1.4.
