- C(p) is larger because at constant pressure part of the heat does work as the gas expands.
## Heat engines and the second law
A heat engine takes heat Q₁ from a hot source at T₁, does work W and rejects heat Q₂ to a cold sink at T₂.
- Efficiency η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁.
- The Carnot engine (two isothermal and two adiabatic steps) is the most efficient possible between two temperatures: η = 1 − T₂/T₁, with T in kelvin.
- Second law (Kelvin): no engine can turn all the heat it takes in into work. (Clausius): heat does not flow by itself from a cold body to a hot one.
- A refrigerator uses work to move heat from cold to hot. Its coefficient of performance is Q₂/W.
- Entropy change ΔS = ΔQ/T. In every real (irreversible) process the total entropy of the universe increases.
> Example 4. A Carnot engine works between 527 °C and 127 °C. Find its efficiency.
! Never put Celsius temperatures into η = 1 − T₂/T₁ or PV = nRT. 1 − 127/527 gives a wrong 76 %.
! Even a perfect Carnot engine cannot reach 100 % efficiency, because that would need a sink at 0 K.
! In an isothermal change the gas still takes in heat; it is the temperature, not the heat, that stays constant.
## Quick check
- Kelvin temperature doubled: average molecular kinetic energy? (doubled)
- Which process has no heat exchange? (adiabatic)
- Work done in an isochoric process? (zero)
- C(p) − C(v) for one mole of ideal gas? (R)
- Does Carnot efficiency depend on the working substance? (no, only on T₁ and T₂)

title: Mechanics
lines: Mechanics is the largest physics topic in USAT. Expect short numericals and one-line concept checks: resolve a vector, apply an equation of motion, find a centripetal force, compare kinetic energies or use Bernoulli's equation. Most questions need two or three lines of working once you know the right formula and keep every quantity in SI units.
## Vectors
A scalar has size only (mass, speed, work, energy, power). A vector has size and direction (displacement, velocity, force, momentum, torque).
- Components: Aₓ = A cos θ, Aᵧ = A sin θ, where θ is measured from the x-axis.
- Resultant: R = √(Rₓ² + Rᵧ²), direction tan θ = Rᵧ/Rₓ, read in the correct quadrant.
- Two forces A and B at angle θ: R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ. R is largest (A + B) at 0° and smallest (A − B) at 180°.
- Dot product A·B = AB cos θ is a scalar (work W = F·d). Cross product |A × B| = AB sin θ is a vector at right angles to both (torque τ = r × F).
## Kinematics
For constant acceleration, use the four equations of motion:
| Equation | Missing quantity
| v = u + at | distance
| s = ut + ½at² | final speed
| v² = u² + 2as | time
| s = ½(u + v)t | acceleration
- On a velocity-time graph the slope is acceleration and the area under the line is displacement.
- A body dropped from rest covers distances in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 in successive equal seconds.
- Projectile launched at speed u and angle θ: time of flight 2u sin θ/g, maximum height u² sin² θ/2g, range u² sin 2θ/g. The range is greatest at 45°, and angles θ and 90° − θ give equal ranges.
> Example 1. A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², find its greatest height and its time in the air.
> At the top v = 0, so 0 = 20² − 2 × 10 × h, giving h = 400 ÷ 20 = 20 m.
> Time to the top = u/g = 2 s. The fall takes the same time, so the ball is in the air for 4 s.
## Newton's laws and momentum
- First law: a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless a net force acts (inertia).
- Second law: F = ma, or more generally F = Δp/Δt, where momentum p = mv (unit kg m/s = N s).
- Third law: action and reaction are equal and opposite but act on different bodies, so they never cancel.
- Impulse = FΔt = change in momentum. A longer stopping time means a smaller force (crumple zones, bending the knees on landing).
- With no external force, total momentum is conserved: in all collisions and explosions, including a gun's recoil.
- Elastic collision: kinetic energy is conserved too. Inelastic: some kinetic energy turns into heat and sound. When bodies stick together, the loss is greatest.
! A ball that hits a wall at v and rebounds at v changes its momentum by 2mv, not zero: the direction reverses.
## Circular motion and gravitation
- Angular speed ω = 2π/T = 2πf, and v = rω.
- Centripetal acceleration v²/r = rω², directed to the centre; centripetal force F = mv²/r. It is supplied by a real force: tension, friction, gravity or an electric force.
- Newton's law of gravitation: F = Gm₁m₂/r², with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². At the surface g = GM/R².
- Orbital speed v = √(GM/r), independent of the satellite's mass. Escape speed √(2GM/R) = √(2gR), about 11.2 km/s for the Earth.
- A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator with a period of 24 hours.
- Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they and their craft are falling freely together; gravity has not vanished.
> Example 2. A 1,000 kg car takes a level bend of radius 50 m at 10 m/s. What sideways friction force is needed?
> F = mv²/r = 1,000 × 10² ÷ 50 = 2,000 N, directed towards the centre of the bend.
## Work, energy and power
- Work W = Fd cos θ (joule). No work is done when the force is at right angles to the motion, such as the centripetal force.
- Kinetic energy ½mv² = p²/2m. Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large.
- Gravitational potential energy near the surface = mgh. Without friction, kinetic plus potential energy stays constant.
- Work-energy principle: net work done on a body = its change in kinetic energy.
- Power P = W/t = Fv (watt). 1 hp = 746 W. The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
> Example 3. A pump lifts 500 kg of water through a height of 12 m in one minute. Taking g = 10 m/s², find its useful power.
! Kilowatt-hour sounds like power but measures energy. A 2 kW heater used for 3 hours uses 6 kWh.
## Fluids
- Pressure at depth h in a liquid: P = P₀ + ρgh. Gauge pressure is ρgh alone.
- Archimedes: upthrust = weight of fluid displaced. A floating body has the fraction ρ(body)/ρ(fluid) of its volume submerged.
- Continuity for steady flow: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Halving a pipe's diameter quarters its area, so the speed rises four times.
- Bernoulli: P + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant along a streamline, so faster flow means lower pressure (aeroplane lift, spray guns, a swinging cricket ball).
- Stokes' law: drag on a small sphere F = 6πηrv. Terminal velocity is proportional to r².
> Example 4. Water flows at 1 m/s in a pipe of diameter 4 cm, which narrows to 2 cm. Find the speed in the narrow part.
> Area depends on diameter squared: the area becomes (2/4)² = ¼ of the original, so v = 1 × 4 = 4 m/s.
! The speed at the top of a projectile's path is u cos θ, not zero. Only the vertical part of the velocity is zero there.
! mgh is valid only close to the Earth's surface. For large heights use −GMm/r.
## Quick check
- Two equal forces at 120° to each other: resultant? (equal to either force)
- Speed doubled: centripetal force on the same circle? (four times)
- Does the orbital speed of a satellite depend on its mass? (no)
- Pipe diameter halved: speed of flow? (four times)
- Unit of impulse? (N s, the same as momentum)

title: Modern Physics
lines: USAT modern physics questions are short: photon energy and the photoelectric equation, de Broglie wavelength, energy levels of hydrogen, half-life and decay equations, binding energy, and basic electronics (diodes, rectifiers, transistors and logic gates). Know the constants and the one-line formulas, and be ready to work in electronvolts.
## Photons
- Planck: radiation is emitted and absorbed in quanta of energy E = hf = hc/λ, with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Halving the wavelength doubles the photon energy.
- A useful shortcut: E(eV) ≈ 1,240 ÷ λ(nm). Photon momentum p = h/λ.
## Photoelectric effect
Light above a threshold frequency f₀ ejects electrons from a metal surface instantly.
- Einstein's equation: hf = φ + K(max), where the work function φ = hf₀.
- K(max) = eV₀, where V₀ is the stopping potential.
- Raising the intensity increases the number of electrons but not their maximum energy. Raising the frequency increases their maximum energy.
- Below f₀ no electrons are emitted, however bright the light. This cannot be explained by the wave theory.
> Example 1. Light of photon energy 5.0 eV falls on a metal of work function 2.3 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons and the stopping potential.
> K(max) = 5.0 − 2.3 = 2.7 eV, so the stopping potential is 2.7 V.
## Other quantum ideas
- Compton effect: an X-ray photon scattered by an electron has a longer wavelength; Δλ = (h/mc)(1 − cos θ). This shows photons carry momentum.
- Pair production: a photon of at least 1.02 MeV (2m₀c² for an electron) can become an electron and a positron near a nucleus. Annihilation is the reverse.
- De Broglie: every moving particle has a wavelength λ = h/p = h/mv. Electron diffraction confirms it, and the electron microscope uses it.
- Uncertainty principle: Δx Δp ≈ h; position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.
- Special relativity: moving clocks run slow, moving lengths shrink along the motion, and mass and energy are linked by E = mc².
## The hydrogen atom
- Bohr: the electron moves only in orbits where its angular momentum is nh/2π.
- Energy levels Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV: −13.6, −3.4, −1.51, −0.85 eV … Radius rₙ = n² × 0.053 nm.
- A photon is emitted when the electron drops: hf = E(upper) − E(lower). The ionisation energy from the ground state is 13.6 eV.
| Series | Final level | Region
| Lyman | n = 1 | ultraviolet
| Balmer | n = 2 | visible
| Paschen | n = 3 | infrared
| Brackett, Pfund | n = 4, 5 | infrared
> Example 2. Find the energy of the photon emitted when a hydrogen electron falls from n = 4 to n = 2.
> E = 13.6(1/2² − 1/4²) = 13.6 × 3/16 = 2.55 eV. It ends on n = 2, so it is a visible Balmer line.
## X-rays and lasers
- X-rays are produced when fast electrons strike a metal target. The shortest wavelength is λ(min) = hc/eV, so a higher tube voltage gives a shorter λ(min).
- The spectrum has a continuous part (braking radiation) and characteristic lines of the target metal.

- LASER means Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. It needs a population inversion, made possible by a metastable state. Laser light is coherent, monochromatic and nearly parallel.
## The nucleus
- A nucleus ᴬ_Z X has Z protons and A − Z neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different A.
- Mass defect Δm = (mass of separate nucleons) − (mass of nucleus). Binding energy = Δm c², and 1 u is equivalent to 931 MeV.
- Binding energy per nucleon measures stability; it peaks near iron-56. Heavy nuclei release energy by fission, light ones by fusion.
- A nuclear reactor uses a moderator (graphite or heavy water) to slow neutrons and control rods (cadmium or boron) to absorb them. Fusion needs temperatures of about 10⁷ K.
## Radioactivity
| Emission | Change in A | Change in Z | Penetration
| α (helium nucleus) | −4 | −2 | stopped by paper
| β⁻ (electron) | 0 | +1 | a few mm of aluminium
| γ (photon) | 0 | 0 | several cm of lead
- Ionising power runs α > β > γ; penetrating power γ > β > α.
- After n half-lives the fraction left is (½)ⁿ. The half-life T½ = 0.693/λ, where λ is the decay constant.
> Example 3. A sample of 64 g of a radioisotope has a half-life of 5 days. How much remains undecayed after 20 days?
> 20 days = 4 half-lives: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 g.
! In a decay chain, find the α count from the change in A first; β particles do not change A.
> Example 4. Uranium-238 (Z = 92) decays to lead-206 (Z = 82). How many α and β⁻ particles are emitted?
> α: (238 − 206) ÷ 4 = 8, which lowers Z by 16 to 76. To end at 82, Z must rise by 6, so 6 β⁻ particles are emitted.
## Electronics

- Pure silicon or germanium is an intrinsic semiconductor. Adding a pentavalent impurity (P, As) gives n-type (electrons in majority); a trivalent impurity (B, Ga, Al) gives p-type (holes in majority).

- A p-n junction conducts in forward bias (p side to +) once the barrier is overcome (about 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium); in reverse bias the depletion region widens and almost no current flows.
- Half-wave rectification uses one diode; full-wave uses two (centre-tap) or four (bridge). On 50 Hz mains, full-wave output pulses at 100 Hz.
- Transistor: I(E) = I(B) + I(C), current gain β = I(C)/I(B). As an amplifier, the base-emitter junction is forward biased and the base-collector junction reverse biased.
- Logic gates: AND gives 1 only if both inputs are 1; OR if at least one is 1; NOT inverts; NAND and NOR are the inverted forms and are universal gates.
! Brighter light does not give faster photoelectrons, only more of them.
! Compare nuclear stability using binding energy per nucleon, not total binding energy.
## Quick check
- Photon wavelength halved: energy? (doubled)
- Ionisation energy of hydrogen from the ground state? (13.6 eV)
- Which series of hydrogen lies in the visible? (Balmer)
- 1/16 of a sample left: how many half-lives? (4)
- Ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz? (100 Hz)

title: Optics
lines: USAT optics questions cover reflection, refraction and total internal reflection, the lens and mirror formula, optical instruments, and the wave ideas of interference, diffraction and polarisation. Learn the formulas with their sign conventions, and know the image formed by a convex lens for each object position.
## Reflection
- Laws: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.
- A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright, same-sized image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Turning the mirror through θ turns the reflected ray through 2θ.
- Spherical mirrors: focal length f = R/2. A concave mirror converges light; a convex mirror always forms a virtual, upright, smaller image, giving a wide field of view.
## Refraction
- Snell's law: n = sin i / sin r, where n is the refractive index of the second medium relative to the first.
- n = c/v: light slows down in a denser medium. Its frequency stays the same, so its wavelength shortens to λ/n.
- Real and apparent depth: n = real depth / apparent depth, so a pool looks shallower than it is.
- Total internal reflection happens when light goes from a denser to a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle C, where sin C = 1/n.
- Uses of total internal reflection: optical fibres (core of higher n than the cladding), prism periscopes and binoculars, the sparkle of diamond.
- Dispersion: a prism splits white light because n is slightly larger for violet than for red, so violet is deviated most.
> Example 1. Glass has refractive index 1.5. Find the speed of light in it and its critical angle (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s).
## Lenses

Pakistani textbooks use the real-is-positive convention: 1/f = 1/p + 1/q, where p is the object distance and q the image distance. Real distances are positive and virtual ones negative; a convex lens has positive f and a concave lens negative f. Magnification m = q/p (size of image ÷ size of object).
| Object for a convex lens | Image
| Beyond 2F | real, inverted, smaller, between F and 2F
| At 2F | real, inverted, same size, at 2F
| Between F and 2F | real, inverted, larger, beyond 2F
| At F | at infinity
| Inside F | virtual, upright, larger (magnifying glass)
- A concave lens always forms a virtual, upright, smaller image.
- Power P = 1/f with f in metres, in dioptres (D). Thin lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂.
> Example 2. An object stands 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Locate the image.
> 1/q = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so q = 15 cm (positive, real). m = 15 ÷ 30 = 0.5: inverted and half size, matching the "beyond 2F" row.
## Optical instruments
- Simple microscope (magnifying glass), image at the near point: M = 1 + d/f, with d ≈ 25 cm.
- Compound microscope: a short-focus objective and eyepiece; the total magnification is the product of the two.
- Astronomical telescope in normal adjustment: M = f(o)/f(e) and length L = f(o) + f(e). It needs a long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece.
- Resolving power improves with a wider aperture and a shorter wavelength.
## Interference
- Interference needs coherent sources: the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
- Constructive (bright) when the path difference is nλ; destructive (dark) when it is (n + ½)λ.
- Young's double slit: fringe spacing Δy = λL/d, where d is the slit separation and L the distance to the screen.
- Thin films (soap bubbles, oil on water) show colours by interference between light reflected from the two surfaces.
> Example 3. In Young's experiment λ = 600 nm, the slits are 0.5 mm apart and the screen is 1 m away. Find the fringe spacing.
## Diffraction
- Diffraction is the spreading of waves through a gap or round an edge; it is most noticeable when the gap is about the size of the wavelength.
- Single slit: the central maximum is the widest and brightest; a narrower slit gives a wider pattern.
- Diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ, where d = 1/N for N lines per metre.
- X-ray diffraction by crystals obeys Bragg's law 2d sin θ = nλ, with θ measured from the atomic planes.
> Example 4. Light of 600 nm falls on a grating with 5,000 lines per cm. Find sin θ for the first order and the highest order seen.
> d = 1 ÷ 500,000 m = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m. sin θ₁ = λ/d = 0.3. Orders need sin θ ≤ 1: n ≤ d/λ = 3.3, so the highest order is 3.
## Polarisation
- Only transverse waves can be polarised; this proves light is transverse.
- Unpolarised light through one polaroid loses half its intensity. Malus's law for a second polaroid: I = I₀ cos² θ; crossed polaroids (90°) let nothing through.
- Reflected light is completely polarised at the Brewster angle, where tan θ = n.
- Uses: glare-cutting sunglasses, LCD screens, stress analysis.
! Convert lines per cm to lines per metre before finding d: 5,000 per cm is 500,000 per m.
! Light entering glass keeps its frequency; only its speed and wavelength change.
! Total internal reflection is impossible when light passes from air into glass, whatever the angle.
## Quick check
- Focal length of a mirror of radius 40 cm? (20 cm)
- Fringe spacing when the slits are moved closer together? (wider)
- Lens of power −2 D: type and focal length? (concave, −50 cm)
- Which colour is deviated most by a prism? (violet)
- Telescope with f(o) = 100 cm and f(e) = 5 cm: magnifying power? (20)

title: Oscillations, Waves and Sound
lines: USAT asks about simple harmonic motion (periods of a spring and a pendulum, speed and energy at a point), wave equations, the speed of sound, stationary waves in strings and pipes, beats, intensity level in decibels and the Doppler effect. Most questions turn on a proportion: what happens to the period, frequency or energy when one quantity is doubled or quadrupled.
## Simple harmonic motion
A body moves in SHM when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement and always directed towards the mean position: a = −ω²x.
- Displacement x = x₀ sin ωt, where x₀ is the amplitude and ω = 2πf = 2π/T.
- Speed v = ω√(x₀² − x²): greatest (ωx₀) at the mean position, zero at the extremes.
- Acceleration is greatest (ω²x₀) at the extremes and zero at the mean position.
- Energy: total E = ½kx₀², shared between kinetic and potential energy. Doubling the amplitude makes the energy four times as large.
| System | Period | Does not depend on
| Mass on a spring | T = 2π√(m/k) | g, amplitude
| Simple pendulum | T = 2π√(l/g) | mass, amplitude (small swings)
- A seconds pendulum (T = 2 s) is about 1 m long.
- On the Moon g is about one-sixth of the Earth's, so a pendulum's period grows by √6; a spring's period does not change.
> Example 1. A 0.5 kg mass hangs on a spring of constant 200 N/m. Find its period.
## Damping and resonance
- Free oscillations happen at the natural frequency. Damping (friction, air drag) makes the amplitude die away.
- Forced oscillations follow the driving frequency. Resonance: when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, the amplitude is greatest.
- Examples: tuning a radio circuit, a microwave oven heating water, a bridge set swinging by marching soldiers.
## Waves
- Wave equation: v = fλ. The frequency is set by the source and does not change when the wave enters a new medium; the speed and wavelength change.
- Transverse waves (light, waves on a string) vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel and can be polarised. Longitudinal waves (sound) vibrate along it and cannot be polarised.
- Speed of a wave on a string: v = √(T/μ), where T is the tension and μ is the mass per unit length.
- Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.
## Sound
- Sound needs a medium; it is fastest in solids and slowest in gases.
- Newton assumed isothermal changes and found about 280 m/s in air, which is too low. Laplace's correction (adiabatic changes) gives v = √(γP/ρ) ≈ 332 m/s at 0 °C.
- v is proportional to √T (T in kelvin). Changing the pressure at constant temperature does not change the speed. Sound travels faster in moist air than in dry air.
- Near room temperature, v rises by about 0.61 m/s for each 1 °C.
- Intensity level L = 10 log(I/I₀) decibels, with I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m². Every tenfold increase in intensity adds 10 dB.
- Loudness depends on intensity, pitch on frequency and quality (timbre) on the overtones present.
## Stationary waves
Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions form a stationary wave. Nodes are λ/2 apart; a node and the next antinode are λ/4 apart.
| System | Fundamental | Harmonics present
| String fixed at both ends | v/2L | all: f, 2f, 3f …
| Pipe open at both ends | v/2L | all: f, 2f, 3f …
| Pipe closed at one end | v/4L | odd only: f, 3f, 5f …
> Example 2. A pipe closed at one end is 0.25 m long. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, find its fundamental frequency and the next frequency it can produce.
> f₁ = v/4L = 340 ÷ 1.0 = 340 Hz. A closed pipe gives only odd harmonics, so the next is 3 × 340 = 1,020 Hz.
## Beats
Two notes of slightly different frequency produce beats at a rate equal to the difference: f(beats) = |f₁ − f₂|. Loading a tuning fork with wax lowers its frequency; filing it raises it.
> Example 3. A fork of 256 Hz gives 4 beats per second with an unknown fork. When the unknown fork is loaded with wax, the beat rate falls to 2 per second. Find the unknown frequency.
> It is 256 + 4 = 260 Hz or 256 − 4 = 252 Hz. Wax lowers its frequency; the beats fall only if it moves closer to 256 Hz, so it was 260 Hz.
## Doppler effect
The observed frequency changes when the source or the observer moves along the line joining them (v = speed of sound).
- Source approaching at u: f′ = fv/(v − u). Receding: f′ = fv/(v + u).
- Observer approaching at u: f′ = f(v + u)/v. Receding: f′ = f(v − u)/v.
- Uses: radar speed guns, sonar, blood-flow measurement, the red shift of receding galaxies.
> Example 4. An ambulance siren of 680 Hz approaches a standing listener at 20 m/s. Speed of sound 340 m/s. What frequency is heard?
! Pendulum period goes as √l: four times the length doubles the period, it does not quadruple it.
! A closed pipe's first overtone is the third harmonic (3f), not 2f.
! A source moving and an observer moving at the same speed do not give the same shift; use the right formula.
## Quick check
- Where is speed greatest in SHM? (at the mean position)
- Amplitude tripled: energy of oscillation? (nine times)
- Intensity multiplied by 100: change in intensity level? (+20 dB)
- Can sound waves be polarised? (no, they are longitudinal)
- Pendulum taken to the Moon: period? (longer, by √6)

title: Algebra and Functions
lines: USAT includes about 4 questions on algebra and functions. They test whether you can simplify and factorise expressions, handle indices (powers), work with function notation, and spot patterns in sequences. The level is SSC to HSSC mathematics; every question is designed to be done by hand in about a minute.
## Indices
| Rule | Example
| aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ | x³ × x⁴ = x⁷
| aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ | x⁸ ÷ x² = x⁶
| (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ | (x²)⁵ = x¹⁰
| a to the power m/n = (nth root of a) to the power m | 27 to the power 2/3 = 3² = 9
- To solve an index equation, write both sides as powers of the same base: 4 to the power x = 32 becomes 2 to the power 2x = 2⁵, so x = 5/2.
## Expanding and factorising
- (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²
- a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b). It also makes arithmetic easy: 51² − 49² = 2 × 100 = 200.
- a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) and a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)
- For x² + bx + c, find two numbers with product c and sum b. For ax² + bx + c, find two numbers with product ac and sum b, then split the middle term.
- Factor theorem: (x − k) is a factor of p(x) exactly when p(k) = 0. The remainder when p(x) is divided by (x − k) is p(k).
- Cancel only factors, never terms: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = x − 3, but (x² + 9)/x² is not 9.
## Functions
A function f takes an input x and gives exactly one output f(x). To find f(3), replace every x by 3, using brackets for negatives.
- Composition: f(g(x)) means do g first, then f. In general f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are different.
- Domain: the inputs allowed. Exclude values that make a denominator zero, and values that make the number under a square root negative.
- Range: the outputs produced. x² is never negative, so x² − 3 has range y ≥ −3.
- Inverse of a linear function: write y = f(x), make x the subject, then swap x and y. f⁻¹(a) is the input that gives output a, so f⁻¹(a) = b exactly when f(b) = a.
## Sequences
- Arithmetic (common difference d): nth term = a + (n − 1)d; sum of n terms = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d], or n × (first + last)/2.
- Geometric (common ratio r): nth term = a × r to the power (n − 1); sum of n terms = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1).
- If neither fits, look at the differences between terms: 3, 5, 9, 15, 23 has differences 2, 4, 6, 8.
## Worked examples
> If f(x) = 3x + 2 and g(x) = x², find f(g(−2)) and g(f(−2)).
> f(−2) = −4, so g(f(−2)) = (−4)² = 16. The order matters.
> Find f⁻¹(x) when f(x) = (2x − 1)/5.
> Check with a number: f(3) = 1, and f⁻¹(1) = 6/2 = 3.
> The 4th term of an arithmetic sequence is 17 and the 9th term is 37. Find the first term.
> Five steps of d take 17 to 37, so 5d = 20 and d = 4. Then a = 17 − 3 × 4 = 5.
! f⁻¹(x) is not 1/f(x). The inverse undoes the function; the reciprocal just turns the output upside down.
! (a + b)² is not a² + b². The middle term 2ab is the most commonly forgotten piece in USAT algebra.
! A negative index gives a reciprocal, not a negative number: 2⁻² = 1/4.
## Quick check
- Can you evaluate 16 to the power 3/4 in your head? (It is 8.)
- Can you factorise x² − x − 12 in under ten seconds?
- Do you always do the inside function first in f(g(x))?
- Can you tell an arithmetic sequence from a geometric one at a glance?

title: Arithmetic
lines: Arithmetic is the largest block of USAT Quantitative Reasoning: about 6 of the 25 questions. Expect number facts (factors, primes, HCF and LCM, remainders), fractions and decimals, percentages, ratio and proportion, averages, profit and loss, and simple interest. There is no calculator, so the test rewards candidates who can see a short route through the numbers rather than grinding through long multiplication.
## Number facts
- A prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. 1 is not prime; 2 is the only even prime.
- HCF is the largest number dividing all the given numbers; LCM is the smallest number all of them divide. For two numbers, HCF × LCM = product of the numbers.
- Events that repeat every 8, 12 and 18 minutes happen together again after the LCM of the intervals, here 72 minutes.
- Divisibility: 3 or 9 when the digit sum is; 4 when the last two digits are; 8 when the last three are; 11 when the alternating digit sum (first − second + third − …) is 0 or a multiple of 11.
## Fractions, decimals and percentages
Learn the common equivalents by heart, because they turn percentage questions into fraction questions that you can do in your head.
| Fraction | Decimal | Percent
- x % of y = y % of x. So 16 % of 25 is the same as 25 % of 16, which is 4.
- A rise of r % multiplies by (1 + r/100); a fall of r % multiplies by (1 − r/100). Two successive changes multiply: +20 % then −20 % gives 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a net fall of 4 %.
- 'A is 25 % more than B' does not mean 'B is 25 % less than A'. If A = 125 and B = 100, B is 25/125 = 20 % less than A.
## Ratio and proportion
- A ratio a : b splits a total into a + b equal parts. Rs 1,200 in the ratio 3 : 5 gives 1,200 ÷ 8 = 150 per part, so Rs 450 and Rs 750.
- Direct proportion: double one, double the other (cost and quantity). Inverse proportion: double one, halve the other (workers and days at a fixed job).
## Averages
- Average = total ÷ number of items, so total = average × number. Most average questions are really total questions.
- When one item is added or removed, compare totals before and after.
## Profit, loss and simple interest
- Profit % and loss % are always on the cost price unless the question says otherwise.
- Selling price = cost × (1 + profit %/100). A 15 % discount means the buyer pays 85 % of the marked price.
- Simple interest = P × R × T ÷ 100, with T in years. Six months is T = ½.
## Worked examples
> A school has 480 students and 37.5 % of them travel by van. How many is that?
> 37.5 % = 3/8. One-eighth of 480 is 60, so 3/8 is 180 students.
> No long multiplication: change the percentage to a friendly fraction first.
> The average of 8 numbers is 25. When one number is removed, the average of the rest is 23. Which number was removed?
> Total before = 8 × 25 = 200. Total after = 7 × 23 = 161. The removed number is 200 − 161 = 39.
> A shirt marked Rs 1,600 is sold at 25 % off. The shopkeeper still makes a profit of 20 %. What did the shirt cost him?
> Selling price = 75 % of 1,600 = Rs 1,200. This is 120 % of the cost, so cost = 1,200 ÷ 1.2 = Rs 1,000.
## Mental-maths habits
- Break awkward numbers: 18 % = 10 % + 5 % + 3 %, or 20 % − 2 %.
- Cancel before multiplying: (36 × 25) ÷ 45 = (4 × 25) ÷ 5 = 20.
- Check the size of your answer against the options; one option is often wrong by a power of ten.
! Percentage change is always measured on the original value. A price that falls from Rs 500 to Rs 400 has dropped by 100/500 = 20 %, not 100/400 = 25 %.
! Profit percentage uses cost price. Dividing the profit by the selling price gives a smaller, wrong percentage that often appears as an option.
! In 'remove one item' average questions, never average the two averages; work with totals.
## Quick check
- Can you say 1/8, 3/8, 5/8 and 7/8 as percentages without thinking?
- Do you know that +x % followed by −x % always leaves a net loss?
- Can you find an LCM by listing multiples of the largest number?
- Do you turn every average question into a total question?

title: Equations and Inequalities
lines: USAT asks about 3 questions on equations: linear equations, pairs of simultaneous equations, quadratics and inequalities, often wrapped in a short word problem. The key skill is turning words into an equation quickly, then solving it with as little arithmetic as possible.
## Linear equations
- Do the same thing to both sides. Clear fractions first by multiplying by the LCM of the denominators; clear decimals by multiplying by 10 or 100.
- Expand brackets carefully: −3(x − 2) = −3x + 6.
- Check your answer by putting it back into the original equation. It takes ten seconds and catches most slips.
## Simultaneous equations
- Elimination: add or subtract the equations so one letter disappears. If 3x + 2y = 16 and 5x − 2y = 16, adding gives 8x = 32.
- Substitution: make one letter the subject (y = 2x − 1) and put it into the other equation.
- Shortcut for symmetric pairs: if 4a + 3b = 260 and 3a + 4b = 230, adding gives 7(a + b) = 490, so a + b = 70, and subtracting gives a − b = 30.
- Two lines ax + by = c have no solution when their x and y coefficients are in the same ratio but the constants are not (parallel lines).
## Quadratic equations
- Rearrange to ax² + bx + c = 0, then factorise or use x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / 2a.
- Never divide both sides by x: x² = 5x gives x(x − 5) = 0, so x = 0 or 5.
- Sum of roots = −b/a; product of roots = c/a. Then α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ.
- The discriminant b² − 4ac tells the nature of the roots: positive means two real roots, zero means equal roots, negative means no real roots. A perfect square gives rational roots.
- An equation with roots p and q is x² − (p + q)x + pq = 0.
## Inequalities
- Solve like an equation, but reverse the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number: −2x > 6 gives x < −3.
- Double inequalities: do the same thing to all three parts. −1 < 2x + 3 ≤ 9 gives −2 < x ≤ 3.
- Quadratic inequalities: find the roots, then (x − a)(x − b) < 0 between the roots, > 0 outside them.
- x² < 25 means −5 < x < 5, not just x < 5.
## Turning words into equations
| Words | Equation
| a number increased by 7 | x + 7
| 5 less than twice a number | 2x − 5
| A is 3 times as old as B | A = 3B
| in 6 years' time | add 6 to every age
| two-digit number with digits a and b | 10a + b
- The 'all of one kind' trick for coin and ticket problems: assume every item is the cheaper kind, then each expensive item adds the price difference.
## Worked examples
> A purse holds 40 notes of Rs 10 and Rs 50, worth Rs 1,200. How many Rs 50 notes are there?
> If all 40 were Rs 10 notes, they would make Rs 400. Each Rs 50 note adds Rs 40 more. 1,200 − 400 = 800, so there are 800 ÷ 40 = 20 Rs 50 notes.
> Bushra is 5 times as old as her son. In 6 years she will be 3 times as old. Find the son's age.
> Solve x² − 2x − 15 < 0.
> (x − 5)(x + 3) < 0, so the expression is negative between the roots: −3 < x < 5.
! Dividing by a variable loses solutions. Factorise instead.
! Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses the sign. Forgetting this is the most common inequality error.
! Read what is asked. Many word problems set x as one quantity and then ask for another (the father, not the son; the notebook, not the pen).
## Quick check
- Can you write the sum and product of the roots of 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0? (7/2 and 3/2)
- Do you flip the sign when dividing an inequality by −3?
- Can you set up an age problem in one line?

title: Geometry
lines: USAT has about 3 geometry questions. Because there are no figures in this app, every shape is described in words, so read slowly and sketch it on rough paper. The questions cover angles, triangles (including Pythagoras), quadrilaterals, circles, perimeter and area, and the volume and surface area of simple solids.
## Angles and lines
- Angles on a straight line add up to 180°; angles round a point add up to 360°.
- Vertically opposite angles are equal. With parallel lines, alternate angles are equal and co-interior angles add up to 180°.
- Interior angles of a polygon with n sides add up to (n − 2) × 180°. Exterior angles of any convex polygon add up to 360°, so each exterior angle of a regular n-gon is 360° ÷ n.
## Triangles
- Angles add up to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
- Isosceles: two equal sides and two equal base angles. Equilateral: all angles 60°.
- Pythagoras (right angle only): hypotenuse² = sum of the squares of the other two sides.
- Common triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, and their multiples such as 6-8-10 and 9-12-15.
- Area = ½ × base × height. For an equilateral triangle of side a, area = (√3/4)a².
- Similar triangles: if lengths are in the ratio k, areas are in the ratio k².
## Quadrilaterals and circles
| Shape | Perimeter | Area
| rectangle l × w | 2(l + w) | lw
| square side a | 4a | a²
| parallelogram base b, height h | sum of sides | bh
| trapezium, parallel sides a and b, height h | sum of sides | ½(a + b)h
| circle radius r | 2πr | πr²
- A rhombus has area ½ × product of its diagonals.
- The angle in a semicircle is 90°. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
- Use π = 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7, otherwise leave π in the answer.
## Solids
| Solid | Volume | Surface area
| cuboid l, w, h | lwh | 2(lw + wh + hl)
| cube side a | a³ | 6a²
| cylinder r, h | πr²h | 2πr² + 2πrh
| cone r, h, slant l | ⅓πr²h | πr² + πrl
| sphere r | (4/3)πr³ | 4πr²
## Worked examples
> A ladder 13 m long leans against a wall. Its foot is 5 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
> This is the 5-12-13 triple: height = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 m.
> Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 150°. How many sides does it have?
> Each exterior angle is 180° − 150° = 30°, so n = 360 ÷ 30 = 12 sides.
> A cylindrical tank has radius 7 m and height 10 m. Find its volume.
## No-calculator habits
- Spot Pythagorean triples instead of squaring large numbers.
- With π = 22/7, cancel the 7 before multiplying anything else.
- When a length is scaled by k, areas scale by k² and volumes by k³. Doubling the radius of a sphere multiplies its volume by 8.
! Pythagoras works only in a right-angled triangle, and the hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle.
! Diameter or radius? Many wrong options come from using the diameter in πr².
! Check units: 1 m² = 10,000 cm² and 1 m³ = 1,000 litres.
## Quick check
- What is the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon? (720°)
- Can you name four Pythagorean triples?
- If a square's side increases by 10 %, by what percentage does its area increase? (21 %)

title: Scenario-based and Mental Maths
lines: About 6 of USAT's 25 quantitative questions are everyday scenarios or quick mental sums: shopping in a bazaar, bus and train timetables, mobile packages, cricket run rates, cooking for guests, calendars and clocks, unit rates, and people or machines working together. None needs advanced mathematics. They test whether you can pick out the numbers that matter and calculate cleanly without a calculator.
## A routine for every scenario
- Underline what is asked (the change, the time, the rate) before reading the numbers.
- Put everything in one unit: grams or kilograms, minutes or hours, MB or GB.
- Estimate the answer, then calculate, then compare with the options.
## Shopping and unit rates
- Compare value by the price of one unit: Rs per kg, Rs per litre, Rs per GB.
- 'Buy 2, get 1 free' means you pay for 2 out of every 3.
- Rate × quantity = cost; distance ÷ fuel per km gives litres.
## Time, timetables and calendars
- Add hours first, then minutes, and carry 60 minutes as 1 hour. Crossing midnight: work out time to midnight, then add the rest.
- A day of the week repeats every 7 days. 45 days later is 45 mod 7 = 3 days on.
- An ordinary year moves dates on by 1 weekday; a leap year by 2.
- Month lengths: 30 days in April, June, September and November; February 28 (29 in a leap year); the rest 31.
- Clock angle at h:m = |30h − 5.5m| degrees, taking the smaller angle if it exceeds 180°.
## Cricket rates
- Run rate = runs ÷ overs. An over has 6 balls, so 12.2 overs means 12 overs and 2 balls, which is 74 balls or 12⅓ overs.
- Required rate = runs still needed ÷ overs left.
- Strike rate = runs ÷ balls × 100. Batting average = runs ÷ number of times out.
## Work and rates
- If A takes a hours and B takes b hours, together they do 1/a + 1/b of the job per hour.
- If rates are given as amounts per hour (boxes, bottles), simply add them.
## Mental-maths toolkit
| Trick | Example
| Near a round number | 99 × 46 = 4,600 − 46 = 4,554
| Difference of squares | 39 × 41 = 40² − 1 = 1,599
| Square ending in 5 | 85²: 8 × 9 = 72, write 25: 7,225
| Halve and double | 16 × 35 = 8 × 70 = 560
| Percent by pieces | 15 % of 480 = 48 + 24 = 72
- Fractions of amounts: find one part first. 3/8 of 320 is 3 × 40 = 120.
- Estimation: round each number to one significant figure and multiply. 302 × 49 is about 300 × 50 = 15,000.
## Worked examples
> A train leaves Rawalpindi at 21:45 and the journey takes 14 h 30 min. When does it arrive?
> 21:45 to midnight is 2 h 15 min. 14 h 30 min − 2 h 15 min = 12 h 15 min, so it arrives at 12:15 the next day.
> Chasing 160 in 20 overs, a team is 70 for 2 after 10 overs. What rate is now needed?
> Runs needed = 90 in 10 overs, so 9 runs per over.
> A recipe for 8 people uses 600 g of meat. How much is needed for 14 people?
> 600 ÷ 8 = 75 g per person, and 14 × 75 = 1,050 g, that is 1.05 kg.
> A 500 ml juice pack costs Rs 90 and a 1.5 litre bottle costs Rs 240. Which is cheaper per litre, and by how much?
> Small: Rs 180 per litre. Large: 240 ÷ 1.5 = Rs 160 per litre. The bottle is Rs 20 per litre cheaper.
! Decimal hours are not minutes: 2.5 hours is 2 h 30 min, not 2 h 50 min.
! 12.2 overs is not 12.2 in arithmetic. Change to balls (74) or to 12⅓ overs.
! In 'every 30 seconds or part of it' charges, round the number of units up.
! Read whether the question wants the total or the rate, the saving per item or the whole saving.
## Quick check
- Can you work out 101 × 47 in your head? (4,747)
- What day is it 50 days after a Friday? (Saturday)
- What is the run rate for 150 runs in 18 overs? (8⅓)
- How many minutes is 0.75 of an hour? (45)

title: Statistics and Probability
lines: USAT includes about 3 questions on statistics and probability: mean, median, mode and range; reading a small table of data; and simple probability and counting. The numbers are chosen to be friendly, so if your working becomes messy, check your method.
## Averages and spread
- Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values.
- Median = middle value after sorting. With an even number of values, it is the mean of the two middle ones.
- Mode = most frequent value. A set can have more than one mode.
- Range = largest − smallest.
- Adding the same number to every value raises the mean, median and mode by that number but leaves the range unchanged. Multiplying every value by k multiplies all four by k.
- Combined mean: (n₁ × mean₁ + n₂ × mean₂) ÷ (n₁ + n₂). It is not the simple average of the two means unless the groups are the same size.
## Reading a table
- Read the headings and units first. Totals and percentages are the usual questions.
- For a frequency table, mean = Σ(value × frequency) ÷ Σ frequency.
- When a table gives percentages, change to counts only when a number is asked for: 35 % of 240 students is 84.
## Probability
- Probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ number of equally likely outcomes. It lies between 0 and 1.
- P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
- Two dice give 36 equally likely outcomes. The most likely total is 7 (6 ways).
- Independent events: multiply. The chance of two heads in two tosses is ½ × ½ = ¼.
- Without replacement, the second draw has one item fewer in the bag.
## Counting
- If one choice can be made in m ways and a second in n ways, both can be made in m × n ways.
- Arrangements of n different objects in a row: n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 1. For example, 4! = 24.
- Choosing r from n when order does not matter: nCr = n! ÷ [r!(n − r)!]. 5C2 = 10.
## Worked examples
> The marks of seven students are 12, 15, 9, 18, 15, 11 and 4. Find the mean, median and mode.
> Sum = 84, so the mean is 84 ÷ 7 = 12. Sorted: 4, 9, 11, 12, 15, 15, 18, so the median is 12 and the mode is 15.
> A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are red?
> Section A has 20 students averaging 60 marks; section B has 30 students averaging 70. Find the combined mean.
> Two coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
> P(no heads) = ½ × ½ = ¼, so P(at least one head) = 1 − ¼ = ¾.
## Mental-maths habits
- To find a mean quickly, guess a central value and average the differences: for 48, 52, 47, 53, 50, take 50; the differences −2, +2, −3, +3, 0 sum to 0, so the mean is 50.
- Simplify probability fractions as you go by cancelling before you multiply.
! Sort the data before finding the median. The middle of an unsorted list is meaningless.
! 'At least one' is easiest as 1 − P(none).
! In a combined mean, weight each group by its size.
## Quick check
- What is the median of 3, 8, 1, 9, 6, 4? (5)
- What is the probability of a total of 7 with two dice? (1/6)
- In how many ways can 5 people stand in a queue? (120)

title: Data and Central Tendency
lines: USAT-GS Statistics opens with the basics of handling data: what kind of variable you have, how data are classified and tabulated, how graphs are read, and how to find an average. Expect short calculations of the mean, median and mode, a weighted or combined mean, and questions on which average suits which data. All of it is HSSC Part I work, done by hand in about a minute.
## Kinds of data
- Qualitative variable (attribute): categories such as blood group, gender or province.
- Quantitative variable: numbers. Discrete if counted (children in a family, goals scored); continuous if measured (height, time, weight).
- Primary data are collected first-hand for your own inquiry; secondary data come from someone else's work, such as a published report.
- Scales: nominal (names only), ordinal (order, e.g. class positions), interval and ratio (equal units; ratio has a true zero).
## Classification and frequency tables
Data can be classified by time (chronological), by place (geographical), by attribute (qualitative) or by size (quantitative). A grouped frequency table needs a few terms:
| Term | Meaning | Example for 20–29
| Class limits | the numbers written | 20 and 29
| Class boundaries | limits moved half the gap outwards | 19.5 and 29.5
| Midpoint | (lower + upper) ÷ 2 | 24.5
| Class width | difference of boundaries | 10
- Relative frequency = class frequency ÷ total. Cumulative frequency adds the frequencies from the top.
- Sturges' rule gives a rough number of classes: k = 1 + 3.3 log n.
## Graphs, described in words
- Histogram: bars on class boundaries with no gaps; area shows frequency. With unequal widths, height = frequency ÷ width.
- Frequency polygon: join the midpoints of the tops of the bars.
- Ogive: cumulative frequency plotted against upper boundaries; used to read off the median and quartiles.
- Pie chart: angle of a sector = (part ÷ total) × 360°.
! Bar charts have gaps between bars and suit categories; histograms have no gaps and suit continuous classes.
## The arithmetic mean
x̄ = Σx ÷ n for raw data and x̄ = Σfx ÷ Σf for a frequency table, using midpoints for grouped classes. Shortcut with an assumed mean A: x̄ = A + Σ(x − A) ÷ n.
- Σ(x − x̄) = 0 always.
- If every value is changed to ax + b, the mean becomes a·x̄ + b.
- Combined mean = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂) ÷ (n₁ + n₂). Weighted mean = Σwx ÷ Σw.
> Example 1. Class A has 30 students with mean 60; class B has 20 with mean 70. Combined mean?
> Example 2. The mean of 20 numbers is 15, but 43 was copied for 34. Correct mean?
## Geometric and harmonic means
- G.M. of n values = nth root of their product; log G.M. = Σ log x ÷ n. It suits growth rates and ratios and fails if any value is zero.
- H.M. = n ÷ Σ(1/x). It suits average speed over equal distances and similar rates.
- For unequal positive values A.M. > G.M. > H.M.; for two numbers G.M.² = A.M. × H.M.
> Example 3. A van goes from Multan to Bahawalpur at 60 km/h and returns at 40 km/h. Average speed?
> H.M. = 2 ÷ (1/60 + 1/40) = 2 ÷ (5/120) = 48 km/h. The tempting 50 km/h ignores that the slow leg takes longer.
## Median and mode
- Median: the middle value after sorting. For n values it is the ((n + 1)/2)th value; for even n, average the two middle values.
- Grouped median = L + (h/f)(n/2 − C), where L is the lower boundary of the median class, f its frequency, C the cumulative frequency before it and h the width.
- Mode: the most frequent value. Grouped mode = L + (f₁ − f₀)h ÷ [(f₁ − f₀) + (f₁ − f₂)], using the modal class and its neighbours.
- Empirical relation for moderately skewed data: Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean.
> Example 4. Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 have frequencies 5, 8, 12, 5. Median?
> n/2 = 15; cumulative 5, 13, 25 puts the median in 20–30. Median = 20 + (10/12)(15 − 13) = 21.67.
## Choosing an average
| Average | Best for | Weakness
| Mean | numerical data without outliers | pulled by extreme values
| Median | skewed data such as incomes | ignores the size of extremes
| Mode | categories, e.g. favourite colour | may not exist or may not be unique
In a symmetrical distribution mean = median = mode. In positive skew (long right tail) mean > median > mode; in negative skew the order reverses.
! Sort the data before finding a median. Reading the middle of an unsorted list is the commonest slip.
! A combined mean is not the average of the two means unless the groups are the same size.
! Class limits and class boundaries are different: boundaries are used for widths, histograms and the median formula.
## Quick check
- Is the number of rooms in a house discrete or continuous?
- What is the midpoint of 40–49?
- Find the G.M. of 3 and 12.
- Which average would you use for shoe sales by colour?

title: Dispersion and Index Numbers
lines: Two classes can have the same mean mark and still be very different: in one everyone scores near 60, in the other marks run from 20 to 100. Dispersion measures this spread. USAT asks you to compute the range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation from small data sets, to compare groups with the coefficient of variation, to judge skewness, and to work simple index numbers.
## Absolute and relative measures
Absolute measures carry the units of the data (kg, rupees). Relative measures, or coefficients, have no units and let you compare groups measured differently.
| Absolute | Relative (coefficient)
| Range = xₘ − x₀ | (xₘ − x₀) ÷ (xₘ + x₀)
| Q.D. = (Q₃ − Q₁)/2 | (Q₃ − Q₁) ÷ (Q₃ + Q₁)
| M.D. = Σ|x − x̄| ÷ n | M.D. ÷ mean
## Quartiles, deciles and percentiles

Quartiles cut ordered data into four equal parts, deciles into ten and percentiles into a hundred. For raw data Q₁ is the ((n + 1)/4)th value and Q₃ the (3(n + 1)/4)th value. For grouped data use Q₁ = L + (h/f)(n/4 − C), like the median formula. Useful equalities: Q₂ = D₅ = P₅₀ = median, and D₇ = P₇₀.
## Variance and standard deviation
Variance σ² is the mean of the squared deviations; S.D. σ is its positive square root. A shortcut avoids working out each deviation:
- σ² = Σx²/n − (Σx/n)².
- Adding a constant changes nothing; multiplying by a multiplies σ by |a| and σ² by a². So Var(ax + b) = a²·Var(x).
- σ is never negative and is 0 only when all values are equal. M.D. ≤ S.D. always.
- For a normal distribution, Q.D. ≈ ⅔σ and M.D. ≈ ⅘σ.
> Example 1. For 10 values, Σx = 50 and Σx² = 410. Find σ.
> σ² = 41 − 5² = 16, so σ = 4. Stopping at 16 gives the variance, not the S.D.
> Example 2. Ali's mean is 40 runs with S.D. 8; Usman's mean is 50 with S.D. 12. Who is more consistent?
> C.V. for Ali = 20 %, for Usman = 24 %. The lower C.V. wins, so Ali is more consistent.
## Moments, skewness and kurtosis
- The rth moment about the mean is mᵣ = Σ(x − x̄)ʳ ÷ n. m₁ = 0 and m₂ = variance. From moments about any origin, m₂ = m₂′ − (m₁′)².
- Pearson's coefficient of skewness: Sk = (mean − mode) ÷ σ, or 3(mean − median) ÷ σ.
- Bowley's coefficient: (Q₃ + Q₁ − 2Q₂) ÷ (Q₃ − Q₁), which lies between −1 and +1.
- Positive Sk: long tail to the right, mean above median. Negative Sk: long tail to the left.
- Kurtosis is peakedness, measured by b₂ = m₄ ÷ m₂². Normal (mesokurtic) b₂ = 3; more peaked is leptokurtic; flatter is platykurtic.
> Example 3. Mean 30, median 27, σ = 6. Pearson's Sk = 3(30 − 27) ÷ 6 = 1.5, a positive skew.
## Index numbers
An index number shows the change in a price or quantity compared with a base period set at 100.
- Price relative = (p₁ ÷ p₀) × 100. An index of 125 means a 25 % rise.
- Simple aggregative index = Σp₁ ÷ Σp₀ × 100 (no weights).
- Laspeyres = Σp₁q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100 (base-year quantities).
- Paasche = Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100 (current-year quantities).
- Fisher's ideal index = √(Laspeyres × Paasche).
- Chain base: link relative = (pₙ ÷ pₙ₋₁) × 100; chain index = previous chain index × link relative ÷ 100.
- A consumer price index measures the cost of living. Real wage = money wage × 100 ÷ CPI.
- Shifting the base: new index = old index ÷ old index of the new base year × 100.
> Example 4. Rice: p₀ = 50, p₁ = 60, q₀ = 10. Sugar: p₀ = 100, p₁ = 105, q₀ = 4. Laspeyres index?
! Var(2x + 5) is 4 × Var(x), not 2 × Var(x) + 5. Constants never change spread.
! Read the stem for the divisor. Descriptive questions divide by n; dividing by n − 1 gives a different variance.
! Percentage changes in a chain compound: rises of 10 % and 20 % give 132, not 130.
## Quick check
- Find the coefficient of range when the largest value is 80 and the smallest 20.
- If σ = 3, what is the variance of 4x − 7?
- Which index uses current-year quantities as weights?
- An index is 90. What happened to prices compared with the base year?

title: Sampling, Regression and Correlation
lines: This topic links samples to populations and one variable to another. USAT asks you to name sampling methods, count possible samples, use the standard error, build a confidence interval, read the vocabulary of hypothesis testing, fit and use a regression line, interpret the correlation coefficient and recognise the components of a time series.
## Population and sample
- A parameter describes a population (μ, σ) and is fixed; a statistic describes a sample (x̄, s) and varies from sample to sample.

- Probability methods: simple random (equal chance for every unit), stratified (random sample from each homogeneous group), systematic (every kth unit after a random start, k = N ÷ n), cluster (whole groups chosen at random).
- Non-probability methods include convenience, judgement and quota sampling.
- Sampling error = statistic − parameter. It falls as n grows; it is not a recording mistake.
- Number of possible samples of size n from N units: Nⁿ with replacement (order counted), ᴺCₙ without replacement.
## Sampling distribution of the mean
- Mean of all possible x̄ values = μ, so x̄ is unbiased for μ.
- Standard error: σ_x̄ = σ ÷ √n with replacement (or for a large population).
- Central limit theorem: for large n (usually 30 or more), x̄ is approximately normal whatever the population shape.
> Example 1. σ = 12, n = 36. SE = 12 ÷ 6 = 2. To halve SE, multiply n by 4.
## Estimation
A point estimate is one number, such as x̄ for μ. An interval estimate gives a range: x̄ ± z·σ/√n.
| Confidence | z
For a proportion, SE = √(p̂q̂ ÷ n).
> Example 2. n = 100, x̄ = 50, σ = 10. SE = 1, so the 95 % interval is 50 ± 1.96 = 48.04 to 51.96.
## Hypothesis testing basics
- H₀ is the null hypothesis of no difference; H₁ is the alternative.
- Type I error: rejecting a true H₀, with probability α (the level of significance). Type II error: accepting a false H₀, with probability β.
- H₁: μ ≠ μ₀ gives a two-tailed test; H₁: μ > μ₀ or μ < μ₀ gives a one-tailed test.
- z = (x̄ − μ₀) ÷ (σ/√n). At 5 %, reject H₀ if |z| > 1.96 (two-tailed) or z > 1.645 (right-tailed).
! Divide by the standard error σ/√n, not by σ. This slip shrinks z and leads to the wrong decision.
## Regression
The regression line of y on x, ŷ = a + bx, is fitted by least squares: it makes Σ(y − ŷ)² as small as possible.
- b = [nΣxy − ΣxΣy] ÷ [nΣx² − (Σx)²], and a = ȳ − b·x̄, so the line passes through (x̄, ȳ).
- b is the change in y for a one-unit rise in x. Use y on x to predict y; use the separate line x on y to predict x.
## Correlation
- r = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ √[Σ(x − x̄)² Σ(y − ȳ)²], with −1 ≤ r ≤ +1.
- r = ±1: points on a straight line; r = 0: no linear relation (a curve may still exist).
- r² = b_yx × b_xy, and r has the same sign as both regression coefficients.
- r is unchanged by adding constants or multiplying by positive numbers.
- Spearman's rank correlation: ρ = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ [n(n² − 1)].
> Example 4. b_yx = 0.8, b_xy = 0.45. r² = 0.36, so r = 0.6.
! Correlation is not causation. A third factor, such as hot weather, can drive two variables together.
## Time series
| Component | Example
| Secular trend | population growth over decades
| Seasonal variation | sweet sales before Eid each year
| Cyclical variation | boom and recession over several years
| Irregular variation | a sudden flood
Trend can be found by semi-averages, moving averages or a least squares line y = a + bt. A 3-year moving average of 10, 14, 12, 16 gives 12 and 14.
## Quick check
- N = 6, n = 2 without replacement: how many samples?
- What is the 99 % z value?
- If b_yx = −0.5 and b_xy = −0.32, find r.
- Which time series component repeats every year?

title: Probability and Distributions
lines: Probability questions in USAT are short but unforgiving: one miscounted outcome and the answer is wrong. Expect counting with permutations and combinations, dice, coins and cards, the addition and multiplication laws, conditional probability, expectation of a random variable, and the binomial, Poisson and normal distributions at HSSC Part II level.
## Counting
- Multiplication principle: if one task can be done in m ways and another in n ways, both can be done in m × n ways.
- Permutations (order matters): ⁿPᵣ = n! ÷ (n − r)!. Combinations (order does not matter): ⁿCᵣ = n! ÷ [r!(n − r)!].
- n objects with p alike: n! ÷ p!. n people round a table: (n − 1)!.
- ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ, so ¹⁰C₈ = ¹⁰C₂ = 45.
! President and secretary are different posts, so use ⁿPᵣ. A committee has no posts, so use ⁿCᵣ.
## Basic probability
For equally likely outcomes, P(A) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, and 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1. The complement rule is P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
| Experiment | Outcomes | Useful facts
| One die | 6 | P(any one face) = 1/6
| Two dice | 36 | total 7 has 6 ways; doubles have 6 ways
| n coins | 2ⁿ | three coins give 8 outcomes
| Pack of cards | 52 | 4 suits of 13; 26 red; 4 kings; 12 face cards
## Laws of probability
- Addition law: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). For mutually exclusive events P(A ∩ B) = 0.
- Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B).
- Multiplication law: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B | A); for independent events P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).
- Total probability and Bayes: if B₁, B₂ split the sample space, P(A) = ΣP(Bᵢ)P(A | Bᵢ) and P(B₁ | A) = P(B₁)P(A | B₁) ÷ P(A).
> Example 1. A card is drawn from 52. P(red or king)?
> 26/52 + 4/52 − 2/52 = 28/52 = 7/13. The two red kings must not be counted twice.
> Example 2. A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls; two are drawn without replacement. P(both red)?
> 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15. With replacement it would be (4/10)² = 4/25.
! Mutually exclusive is not the same as independent. Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities can never be independent.
## Random variables and expectation
A discrete random variable X has a list of values with probabilities that add to 1.
- E(X) = Σx·P(x); Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
- E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b; Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X).
## Binomial distribution
Use it for a fixed number n of independent trials, each with two outcomes and the same chance p of success (q = 1 − p).
- P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ, r = 0, 1, …, n.
- Mean = np; variance = npq, which is always less than the mean. Symmetrical when p = ½.
> Example 4. Mean 6 and variance 4.2: q = 4.2 ÷ 6 = 0.7, p = 0.3, n = 6 ÷ 0.3 = 20.
## Poisson distribution

For counts of rare events with many chances (calls per minute, misprints per page): P(X = r) = e⁻ᵐ mʳ ÷ r!. Mean = variance = m. It approximates the binomial when n is large and p small, with m = np. USAT will give you the value of e⁻ᵐ when needed.
## Normal distribution
- Bell-shaped, symmetrical about μ; mean = median = mode; total area 1; points of inflection at μ ± σ.
- Standardise with z = (x − μ) ÷ σ; Z has mean 0 and variance 1.
| Interval | Area
| μ ± 1σ | about 68 %
| μ ± 2σ | about 95 %
| μ ± 3σ | about 99.7 %
! For one tail, halve what is left outside: above μ + 2σ is about (100 − 95) ÷ 2 = 2.5 %.
## Quick check
- How many arrangements does the word KARACHI have? (Two A's.)
- P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, independent. Find P(A ∪ B).
- A binomial has n = 25, p = 0.2. Find its mean and S.D.
- Marks have μ = 50, σ = 5. About what share score below 40?

title: Analogies
lines: USAT's Verbal Reasoning section usually opens with about five analogy questions. Each gives a pair of words in capitals, such as DOCTOR : HOSPITAL, and four pairs as options. You must pick the pair whose words are linked in the same way as the stem pair. The test is not about hard vocabulary; it is about naming relationships precisely.
## The method in four steps
- Read the stem pair and make a sentence that links the two words: "A doctor works in a hospital."
- Make the sentence specific. "A doctor is found in a hospital" is too loose; "A doctor works in a hospital" is better.
- Put each option pair into the same sentence, keeping the order: "A teacher works in a school" fits; "A school works in a teacher" does not.
- If two options fit, tighten the sentence and test again. Only one option should survive.
! Keep the order. If the stem is PART : WHOLE, an option written WHOLE : PART is wrong even though the link looks similar.
## The common relationship types
| Type | Stem example | Matching pair
| Synonyms | BRAVE : COURAGEOUS | happy : joyful
| Antonyms | ANCIENT : MODERN | generous : stingy
| Part and whole | PAGE : BOOK | brick : wall
| Member and class | SPARROW : BIRD | cobra : snake
| Worker and workplace | PILOT : COCKPIT | chef : kitchen
| Worker and tool | TAILOR : NEEDLE | carpenter : saw
| Worker and product | POET : POEM | baker : bread
| Tool and action | KNIFE : CUT | broom : sweep
| Cause and effect | FIRE : SMOKE | virus : illness
| Degree (intensity) | WARM : HOT | drizzle : downpour
| Object and material | SHIRT : COTTON | ring : gold
| Young and adult | CALF : COW | cub : lion
| Animal and home | BEE : HIVE | horse : stable
| Organ and function | EAR : HEAR | lung : breathe
| Unit and quantity | METRE : LENGTH | litre : volume
| Symbol or sign | DOVE : PEACE | crescent : Islam
| Lack of | DROUGHT : RAIN | darkness : light
## Worked examples
> PUPPY : DOG
> (A) kitten : mouse  (B) foal : horse  (C) nest : bird  (D) lamb : wool
> Sentence: "A puppy is a young dog." A foal is a young horse, so B fits. A kitten is not a young mouse, a nest is a bird's home, and lamb : wool is animal and product.
> DRIZZLE : DOWNPOUR
> (A) whisper : shout  (B) rain : cloud  (C) wind : storm  (D) river : sea

> Sentence: "A drizzle is a much weaker form of a downpour." A whisper is a much weaker form of a shout: A. Wind : storm is tempting, but a storm is not simply stronger wind; it includes rain and lightning. River : sea is a flow into a larger body, not degree.
> SURGEON : SCALPEL
> (A) farmer : wheat  (B) painter : brush  (C) judge : court  (D) author : book
> Sentence: "A surgeon works with a scalpel as a tool." A painter works with a brush: B. Wheat is the farmer's product, court the judge's workplace, and book the author's product.
## How to break a tie

When two options seem to fit, ask a sharper question. For PEN : WRITE, both "axe : chop" and "chair : sit" fit a loose sentence ("used to"). Sharpen it: a pen is a tool used to perform an action on something. An axe chops wood; a chair is not used to act on anything. Choose axe : chop.
Also check the category of each word. If the stem is NOUN : VERB, the answer is usually NOUN : VERB too. If the stem is a person and a place, look for a person and a place.
## Traps to avoid

! Same topic is not same relationship. For DOCTOR : PATIENT, the option nurse : hospital shares the medical topic but shows worker and workplace, not professional and person served. Teacher : student is the right kind of match.
! Do not choose a pair because the words look alike or rhyme. Always test the sentence.
! Degree pairs must move the same way. If the stem goes from mild to strong (ANNOYED : FURIOUS), an option that goes from strong to mild (ecstatic : pleased) is reversed.
! Do not bring in a personal association. ROSE : RED is not a firm rule (roses come in many colours); the test prefers relationships that are always true.
## Quick check
- Make a precise sentence for the stem, then test every option in order.
- Learn the main relationship types and say the type in your head.
- Watch the direction of the pair and the parts of speech.
- If two fit, tighten the sentence; never guess on topic alone.

title: Antonyms
lines: Antonym questions in USAT give a word in capitals and ask for the option most opposite in meaning. They sit with synonyms in the Verbal Reasoning section. The skill is the same as for synonyms, with one extra step: after you know the meaning, you must turn it round.
## The method
- Define the stem word simply: OPTIMISTIC = expecting good things.
- Make the opposite in your own words: expecting bad things.
- Find the option that matches: pessimistic.
- Check that the other options are either unrelated or only partly opposite.
! Many wrong options are synonyms of the stem. Examiners put them in because a hurried candidate sees a familiar meaning and clicks it. Read the instruction: most opposite.
## Ways English makes opposites
| Pattern | Examples
| Negative prefix un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, dis- | able / unable, legal / illegal, regular / irregular, honest / dishonest
| Prefix pairs | include / exclude, increase / decrease, import / export, ascend / descend
| Suffix pairs | careful / careless, hopeful / hopeless
| Root pairs | benevolent / malevolent, maximum / minimum, synonym / antonym
| Separate words | ancient / modern, scarce / abundant, humble / arrogant
! Not every in- word is negative. Inflammable means easily set on fire, the same as flammable. Its opposite is non-flammable. Invaluable means extremely valuable, not worthless.
## Commonly tested opposite pairs
| Word | Opposite
| affluent | poor, needy
| candid | evasive, secretive
| diligent | lazy, idle
| frugal | extravagant, wasteful
| transparent | opaque
| obscure | clear, famous
| hostile | friendly
| verbose | concise, brief
| temporary | permanent
| zenith | nadir
| genuine | fake, counterfeit
| reluctant | eager, willing
## Worked examples
> LETHARGIC
> (A) sleepy  (B) energetic  (C) heavy  (D) cautious
> Lethargic means sluggish and without energy, so the opposite is energetic: B. Sleepy is close to a synonym, which is the trap.
> CONCEAL
> (A) hide  (B) destroy  (C) reveal  (D) protect
> To conceal is to hide; the opposite is to reveal, C. Hide is the synonym trap; destroy and protect are unrelated.
> AMATEUR
> (A) beginner  (B) professional  (C) player  (D) critic
> An amateur does something without being paid or fully trained. The opposite is a professional, B. Beginner is close in meaning, not opposite.
## Building your list of opposites

When you learn a new word, learn its opposite at the same time. Write the pair side by side: generous / stingy, praise / criticise, expand / contract. Pairs are easier to remember than single words because each word reminds you of the other. Group the pairs by idea (size, speed, mood, honesty), and say them aloud. Before the test, revise the pairs that use prefixes, because those are the easiest marks to win back.
Remember that the answer is often a plain word. Examiners make the stem hard and the answer simple, so do not reject an option just because it looks too easy.
## When several options look opposite

Pick the one that reverses the main sense, at the same strength. For FURIOUS the best opposite is calm, not merely pleased, because furious describes anger, not happiness. For SCARCE, the opposite is plentiful (amount), not cheap (price), even though scarce things are often costly.
## Traps to avoid
! Read the stem's part of speech. The opposite of the verb RISE is fall or sink; the noun "fall" works only if it is the same class as the stem.
! Do not choose a word that is only different. For TIMID, "angry" is different, but bold is opposite.
! Words with two meanings: FAST can mean quick or firmly fixed. If the options include slow, the speed sense is being tested.
## Quick check
- Define, then reverse, then match.
- Expect a synonym among the wrong options.
- Use prefixes and suffixes, but beware of inflammable and invaluable.
- Choose the option that reverses the main sense at the same strength.

title: Reading Comprehension
lines: USAT includes about five comprehension questions on a short passage of roughly 150 to 220 words. The passage may be about science, history, society or education. Questions ask for the main idea, a detail, an inference, the author's tone or attitude, and the meaning of a word in context. Everything you need is in the passage; outside knowledge can mislead you.
## Reading the passage
- Read the questions' first lines quickly so you know what to look for, but do not read the options yet.
- Read the passage once at a steady pace. After each paragraph, sum it up in a few words in your head.
- Notice the first and last sentences: the main idea is often stated there.
- Mark turning words (however, but, in contrast) and opinion words (unfortunately, wisely, surprisingly). They show the author's view.
## Question types and how to handle them
| Type | Typical wording | Strategy
| Main idea | The passage is mainly about; the best title is | choose the option that covers the whole passage, not one paragraph
| Detail | According to the passage | find the line and match it; the answer is often reworded
| Inference | It can be inferred; the author suggests | choose what must be true from the text, a small step beyond it
| Tone | The author's attitude is | look at opinion words; tests usually prefer moderate tones
| Vocabulary | The word X in line 5 most nearly means | replace the word with each option in the sentence
| Purpose | The author mentions X in order to | ask why that sentence is there: example, contrast, evidence
## A worked example

> Passage (short): For centuries, farmers in Sindh relied on the annual flood of the Indus to water their fields. The flood brought fresh silt, which kept the soil fertile. When barrages and canals were built, water could be supplied all year, and harvests grew. Yet engineers later noticed a hidden cost: with less flooding, salts built up in many fields and some land became barren. Today, planners try to balance a steady supply of water with methods that wash salts away.
> Q1. The passage is mainly about: (A) the history of Sindh (B) the benefits and drawbacks of controlled irrigation (C) how barrages are built (D) why the Indus floods
> B covers the whole passage: gains (all-year water) and costs (salt build-up). A is too broad; C and D are mentioned only in passing or not at all.
> Q2. It can be inferred that the annual flood: (A) harmed the soil (B) helped to remove salts from the soil (C) was stopped completely (D) has returned
> The passage says salts built up when there was less flooding, so the flood must have helped to wash salts away: B. "Stopped completely" goes beyond the text, which says less flooding.
> Q3. The word "barren" most nearly means: (A) dry (B) crowded (C) unable to produce crops (D) flooded
> Land that becomes barren after salts build up cannot grow crops: C. Dry is close but misses the sense of being useless for farming.
## Eliminating wrong options
- Too broad: talks about much more than the passage.
- Too narrow: true, but only about one detail.
- Extreme words: always, never, completely, only. They are usually wrong unless the passage uses them.
- True but irrelevant: a fact you know, not one the passage gives.
- Reversed: uses the passage's words but flips the relationship.
## Managing time

Give the passage about two minutes and each question under a minute. If a question is hard, answer the others first and come back. Do not reread the whole passage for each question; go to the line you need.
## Traps to avoid
! Do not answer from your own opinion or general knowledge. If the passage says something you disagree with, the passage still wins.
! An option that repeats exact words from the passage is not automatically right; check that it says the same thing.
! For tone, avoid strong labels such as furious or overjoyed unless the language is plainly extreme. Most passages are balanced, informative, concerned or mildly critical.
## Quick check
- Sum up each paragraph as you read.
- Main idea covers the whole; detail matches a line; inference must follow.
- Test vocabulary in the sentence itself.
- Cross out too broad, too narrow, extreme and irrelevant options.

title: Sentence Completion
lines: Sentence completion is the largest verbal item type in USAT, with about six questions. A sentence has one or two blanks, and you choose the word or words that fit best. Some items test vocabulary in context; others test grammar: tense, auxiliary verbs, prepositions, articles and agreement. In every case the sentence itself contains the clue.
## Step by step
- Read the whole sentence before looking at the options.
- Find the clue words that tell you what the blank must mean.
- Predict a word of your own, then pick the option closest to it.
- Read the finished sentence again. It should make sense and be grammatical.
## Context clues
| Clue | Signal words | What it tells you
| Contrast | but, although, however, yet, despite, while | the blank goes against another part of the sentence
| Support | and, also, moreover, in addition | the blank continues the same idea
| Cause and result | because, since, so, therefore, as a result | the blank follows logically from a reason
| Definition or example | that is, such as, for example, a colon | the blank is explained nearby
> Although the medicine was ______, the patient refused to take it.
> (A) bitter  (B) effective  (C) costly  (D) unpleasant
> "Although" signals contrast: the patient refused something good. Effective fits, B. Bitter and unpleasant would be reasons to refuse, so they remove the contrast.
## Two-blank items

Work with the blank that has the stronger clue first, and cross out every option whose word fails there. Then test the survivors in the other blank. Both words must fit; a pair with one perfect word and one wrong word is still wrong.
> The new manager was so ______ that even small decisions took her weeks, and her team grew ______.
> (A) decisive … content  (B) hesitant … impatient  (C) careless … proud  (D) quick … bored
> Decisions taking weeks shows a hesitant manager, and a team kept waiting grows impatient: B.
## Grammar for blanks
- Tense: match time words. "By next June, she ______ her degree" needs the future perfect: will have completed. "Since 2019" usually needs the present perfect: has lived.

- Conditionals: If + present, will + verb (If it rains, we will stay in). If + past, would + verb (If I had time, I would help). If + past perfect, would have + past participle (If he had studied, he would have passed).
- Subject and verb agree: "Each of the students has a book." "Neither the teacher nor the pupils were late" (the verb agrees with the nearer subject).
- Auxiliaries and modals: after can, could, must, should, will and would, use the base verb (must go, not must to go). "Used to" for past habit takes the base verb (I used to walk).
- Gerund or infinitive: enjoy, avoid, finish and suggest take -ing (avoid wasting); want, decide, hope and agree take to + verb (decided to leave).
- Articles: "an" before a vowel sound (an hour, an MBA), "a" before a consonant sound (a university, a one-rupee coin).
## Prepositions often tested
| Correct use | Common error
| good at, interested in, afraid of | good in, interested on
| depend on, insist on, consist of | depend upon is fine; consist from is wrong
| accused of, charged with | accused for
| married to, similar to, different from | married with
| on Monday, in June, at 5 o'clock | in Monday
| prefer tea to coffee | prefer tea than coffee
> The committee insisted ______ a full report before it would approve the funds.
> (A) for  (B) on  (C) at  (D) to
> The verb insist takes on: insisted on a full report, B.
## Traps to avoid
! Do not choose the hardest word because it sounds impressive. The right word is the one that fits the clue.
! Watch negatives: "not", "hardly" and "rarely" reverse the meaning. "The plan was hardly a ______" needs a positive word, such as success.
! A word can fit the meaning and still fail the grammar. "She is capable ______" needs of + -ing: capable of managing.
## Quick check
- Find the signal word: contrast, support, cause or definition.
- Predict before you look at the options.
- In two blanks, use the easier blank to eliminate first.
- Check tense, agreement, verb pattern and preposition before you choose.

title: Synonyms
lines: In USAT, synonym questions give one word in capitals and four options. You choose the option closest in meaning. About four of the Verbal Reasoning questions are synonyms or antonyms, so a strong vocabulary pays off quickly. You cannot learn every word, but you can learn to work out meanings from roots, prefixes and context.
## How to attempt a synonym question
- Say the word in a short sentence of your own: "The lecture was tedious." This fixes the sense.
- Predict a simple meaning before reading the options: tedious = boring.
- Look for the option that matches your prediction; then check the others are weaker.
- If the word is unfamiliar, break it into a root and affixes and guess the direction (positive or negative, more or less).
! The closest meaning wins, not a word that is merely connected. For ARID, "desert" is related but not a synonym; "dry" is.
## Roots that unlock many words
| Root | Meaning | Examples
| bene | good, well | benefit, benevolent
| mal | bad | malice, malnutrition
| chron | time | chronic, chronology
| dict | say | predict, contradict
| duc, duct | lead | conduct, deduce
| scrib, script | write | inscribe, manuscript
| spect | look | inspect, spectator
| voc, vok | call, voice | vocal, invoke
| ver | true | verify, veracity
| loqu, locu | speak | eloquent, loquacious
| amb | both, around | ambiguous, ambivalent
| pac | peace | pacify, pact
## Prefixes and suffixes
| Prefix | Meaning | Example
| in-, im-, un-, dis- | not | inaudible, impartial
| pre- | before | precede
| re- | again, back | revive
| sub- | under | submerge
| circum- | around | circumspect
| omni- | all | omnipresent

Suffixes tell you the word class: -ous, -ive, -ful and -al make adjectives (cautious, decisive), -ity, -ness and -tion make nouns (scarcity, tidiness), and -ify and -ize make verbs (simplify, minimize). The synonym usually belongs to the same class as the stem word.
## Worked examples
> FRUGAL
> (A) careless  (B) thrifty  (C) wealthy  (D) generous
> A frugal person spends little and avoids waste, so frugal means thrifty: B. Generous is close to the opposite, and wealthy is about having money, not using it carefully.
> BENEVOLENT
> (A) kind  (B) clever  (C) famous  (D) rigid
> bene = good, vol = wish. A benevolent person wishes others well, so the answer is kind: A.
> CANDID
> (A) shy  (B) frank  (C) sweet  (D) secretive
> A candid remark is honest and open: frank, B. Do not confuse candid with candy; and secretive is the opposite.
## Shades of meaning

Many words share a general idea but differ in strength or use. Big, large, huge and colossal all mean size, but colossal is far stronger than big. If the stem word is strong, prefer the strong option. Likewise, thrifty (positive) and stingy (negative) both describe careful spending, but they carry different feelings. Match the tone as well as the meaning.
## Synonym groups worth learning
| Idea | Words
| very large | enormous, colossal, immense, vast
| very small | minute, tiny, minuscule
| brave | valiant, intrepid, courageous
| clear | lucid, explicit, evident
| lasting a short time | transient, fleeting, ephemeral
| stubborn | obstinate, adamant, headstrong
| praise | commend, laud, acclaim
| scold | rebuke, reprimand, admonish
## Building your word bank

Keep a small notebook or phone list. Each time you meet a new word in a newspaper editorial or a practice question, write it with a short sentence and one synonym. Revise the list every few days and group words by idea, as in the table above. Ten new words a day for two months gives you about 600 words, which covers most of what USAT tests.
## Traps to avoid
! A word may have several meanings. GRAVE can mean serious (a grave mistake) or a burial place. If the options include "serious", that is the sense being tested.
! Avoid look-alike words: eminent (famous) and imminent (about to happen); credible (believable) and credulous (too ready to believe).
! Watch the part of speech: for the adjective ABUNDANT, choose plentiful, not plenty.
## Quick check
- Use the word in your own sentence, then predict a meaning.
- Use roots and prefixes to judge direction when unsure.
- Match the strength, tone and word class of the stem.
- Choose the closest meaning, not a related idea.
